A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

The fossil was so well preserved that researchers identified a cockroach in the stomach that was likely the owl's last meal.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.

"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Mayr, G., Šmídová, L., Richter, A., & Wedmann, S. (2026). Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

#6339. Mountains rise above a sea of clouds in the Pacific Northwest

A blanket of marine clouds covered the Pacific Northwest, leaving mountain peaks rising above the clouds like islands in the sky.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory captures a spectacular blanket of marine clouds stretching across the Pacific Northwest.

From space, the mountains appear to rise from a white sea.

A broad layer of low clouds covered much of western Washington and Oregon on September 19, 2026, stretching from the Pacific coast toward the foothills of the Cascade Range.

Only the higher terrain escaped the cloudy blanket. Peaks in Washington’s Olympic Mountains and parts of Oregon’s Coast Range poked through the clouds like islands.

NASA’s Terra satellite captured the striking scene at about 10:45 a.m. Pacific Time.

The image was captured by the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), an instrument aboard NASA’s Terra satellite that has observed Earth for more than two decades.

From orbit, MODIS can track clouds, smoke, vegetation, snow, ice, ocean conditions, and other features across large areas of the planet.

On this September morning, its view revealed just how far marine clouds had traveled inland.

Clouds also stretched far offshore over the Pacific Ocean.

Farther north, a different kind of haze appeared over the landscape as smoke from wildland fires collected in valleys of the North Cascades.

The widespread cloud cover over western Washington and Oregon resulted from cool, moist air moving inland from the ocean.

For several nights, marine air had been flowing onshore across the region.

This pattern can produce marine stratus – low, relatively uniform clouds that commonly develop along coastal areas.

The Pacific Ocean provides a huge source of moisture, while differences in temperature between the ocean, land, and atmosphere help determine where clouds form and how far they travel.

During the night and early morning, cool ocean air can move inland beneath warmer air higher in the atmosphere.

That arrangement creates what meteorologists call a temperature inversion.

Normally, air becomes colder with increasing altitude through the lower atmosphere. During an inversion, however, warmer air sits above cooler air near the surface.

The warmer layer acts like a lid, limiting the ability of the cooler air below to rise and mix with the atmosphere above.

When moist air trapped near the surface cools enough, water vapor condenses into tiny droplets. If enough droplets collect, a layer of stratus clouds develops.

The marine push was particularly strong during the early hours of September 19.

Cool, moist air reached well beyond the coastline, carrying clouds eastward until they approached the western foothills of the Cascades.

In some places, the cloud layer reached all the way to the ground.

At that point, what appears from space as a cloud becomes fog for people standing beneath it.

Clouds and fog are essentially the same phenomenon; the distinction largely depends on whether the suspended water droplets are touching the surface.

For residents below, the morning would have looked gray and muted. From hundreds of miles above Earth, however, the same weather pattern created a dramatic landscape.

Mountain summits rose through the smooth cloud deck while lower valleys and coastal terrain disappeared beneath it.

The Olympic Mountains offered one of the most striking examples.

Much of the lower terrain was hidden, leaving the tallest sections exposed above the cloud layer.

Similar features appeared along Oregon’s Coast Range.

Scenes like this also reveal how strongly topography shapes regional weather.

Mountains can redirect airflow, force air upward, influence rainfall, and help determine how far marine air penetrates inland.

The Cascades form an especially important barrier between the moist climate west of the range and the generally drier landscapes farther east.

On September 19, the marine layer had pushed far inland, but it did not last all day.

Several hours after Terra passed overhead, NASA’s Aqua satellite offered another look at the Pacific Northwest.

By about 4:15 p.m. Pacific Time, skies had cleared across much of western Washington and Oregon.

The transformation illustrates the daily rhythm of marine clouds.

As sunlight warms the land during the day, temperatures near the surface rise and atmospheric mixing increases. That process can weaken the inversion and break apart low clouds.

Yet the clearing was not complete. Some marine clouds remained pressed against the Oregon coast, where temperatures stayed cooler than they did farther inland.

The contrast captured during the day demonstrates how quickly coastal weather can change.

A landscape almost completely hidden beneath clouds in the morning can emerge only hours later.

From the ground, that shift might feel like an ordinary transition from a foggy morning to a sunny afternoon.

From orbit, it becomes something larger: an entire region briefly wrapped in a white blanket, with mountains rising above it like islands in the sky.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison

#6338. The 8 Best Hot Tubs That You Can Buy Online

We broke down the best options across sizes, styles, and price points, plus what actually matters before you commit.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

At some point, a hot tub stops feeling like a splurge and starts sounding like a really good idea. It’s one of the few backyard upgrades that actually changes how you use your space, whether you’re dealing with sore muscles, trying to carve out a little quiet at the end of the day, or just want a place to hang out that isn’t your couch.

If you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of new hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up. You can get some simple plug-and-play models up and running in an afternoon, elevating your outdoor space from a simple yard to a true getaway spot. Others are closer to a full installation, though the trade-off is typically stronger jets, better insulation, and more built-in features. You also have options like basic inflatables, molded shells, or acrylic spas with lighting, waterfalls, and app controls.

For our recommendations, we focused on how these tubs are built, their lineups of features, and what you’re really getting for the price. Here are the ones worth considering, plus what to know before you commit to this big purchase.

To guide our selections, we leaned on our own experience owning hot tubs and spas, from basic models to custom setups.

We chose hot tubs that range from just under $1,000 for inflatable models to high-end models that nearly mimic showroom-quality tubs. But all are available to buy online. Beyond price, we looked at features, capabilities, and fun extras like speakers and ice buckets. Some are a must, while others are mere perks that can elevate your time in the hot tub—and the price.

We pored over customer reviews and expert write-ups. We also consulted Jeff Courter, an engineer and former owner of Cache Valley Spas in Logan, Utah, to get his insights on how you should factor price, setup, and features into your decision.

In a crowded field of plug-and-play spa contenders, the AquaRest DayDream stands out for a long list of relaxing reasons. It’s a legit backyard spa without the headache of professional installation and electrical upgrades, which puts this spa in that sweet spot between bargain shopping and custom installs.

We like that it plugs into a standard outlet but still delivers a surprisingly strong massage thanks to 35 jets. AquaRest says the DayDream uses a Jacuzzi-branded pump—and while that doesn’t make it a Jacuzzi spa, it’s still a solid indicator you’re getting a reputable, name-brand component under the hood.

There are so many nice extras, like ozone filtration and a lighted waterfall, that make it feel more like a full spa setup than a starter tub. The trade-off is in the materials and power: The roto-molded shell isn’t as luxe as pricier acrylic models, and heating can be slow on 120 volts. There is the option to use a 240-volt setup, if you’ve got the capacity. Given the price and host of features, this hot tub is a great choice for those looking to make a long-term investment.

More: Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Bliss

If you’re looking for a solid hot tub without overspending, we like the Coleman SaluSpa line. The Sicily AirJet is a great choice within that line because it gives you a larger soaking area, 180 AirJets, and a 314-gallon water capacity without jumping into hard-sided spa pricing. This is still an inflatable model, so it does not have the same insulation, jet pressure, or long-term durability you get from a permanent acrylic spa, but the feature set is strong for the price.

Our family has been using a SaluSpa for several months now, and I find it easy to maintain as well. We especially like that the package includes the pump, cover, chemical floater, two filter cartridges and repair patch, which makes the first setup feel simple and straightforward.

We have found the hot tub is hard to connect to the companion app, but we also have no problem controlling it from the panel and do not find a need for an app. For shoppers looking for a quality inflatable that won’t break the bank and has solid reviews, this is a roomy, feature-heavy pick that feels like a better value than many smaller inflatables.

Inflatable hot tubs are a great option for folks who want to relax at home without making a more permanent decision (and investment). If you’re looking for a roomy, tricked-out inflatable hot tub to enhance your wellness, the Intex PureSpa Greywood Deluxe checks quite a few boxes.

With 170 bubble jets, a multifunction heater, filter, blower, and hard water treatment system, this model has more features than many inflatables. With a capacity of 290 gallons and included headrests, there is plenty of room for lounging. If you like the features of this tub, but have less space to work with, there is also a smaller four-person model available.

We like that—for the price—this hot tub includes a lot of fun extras. In addition to the water treatment and jet specs, there’s also a multicolor LED light system and wireless touch button control panel. There are two headrests, a cover, ground tarp, and storage bag included as well.

We do wish there were more than two headrests for a hot tub advertised for six people, but it’s not a deal breaker. One note: Check your available ground space before ordering, too, as this hot tub has a larger footprint than some other popular models.

This hot tub solves a lot of the issues folks face when seeking a therapeutic experience at home—they may not have the space or ability to upgrade the electrical system.

The hard-sided LifeSmart plugs into a standard outlet, skips complicated installation, and still delivers a solid massage with 13 jets, all in a compact, patio-friendly footprint. If you’re hoping to place this hot tub on an elevated surface, though, it’s important to consult a professional and check the load your deck can bear.

Even compact four-person models like this one can weigh over 3,000 pounds when filled with water, which is more than most standard decks can handle without added support. And while it’s listed as a four-seater, many users say it's comfiest with two to three adults.

If aesthetics matter as much as performance, this Comfort hot tub leans into both. The acrylic shell and clean wood-look cabinet design give it a more built-in, high-end vibe than most entry-level spas (which typically have rotomolded, all-in-one shells). We love the details like LED lighting and water features that make the whole experience feel a bit fancy.

It’s not just about looks, though. With 51 jets and a lounger seat, this tub delivers a more immersive soak than simpler plug-and-play models. The trade-off is in installation. For this model, you’ll need a 240-volt hookup, but that also means those jets will pack a lot of therapeutic power at the end of a long day.

If you want a five-person hot tub that doesn’t require rewiring your backyard, the LifeSmart LS500 keeps things simple. It plugs into a standard outlet, sets up quickly, and still delivers a comfortable soak with 23 adjustable jets and a lounge seat. We wish there were more, but other features (and price) make up for the lack of bubbles.

The full-foam insulation and thermal locking cover do a solid job holding heat, which helps keep operating costs in check, and the built-in ozonator cuts down on chemical maintenance. We also like the simple look of this spa, which feels a little high-end for the price bracket. It’s not the most powerful spa in this size range, and heat-up times can be slow, but for an easy, low-hassle setup, it’s a practical upgrade.

While Bestway’s Toronto was our pick for overall best inflatable hot tub, the foam walls do require some extra setup—the process takes two people several hours to complete. On the other hand, the Hot Springs model fully self-inflates in under five minutes and is truly plug-and-play, making it a great choice for those who are purchasing their first hot tub and are not yet familiar with some of the intricacies involved with setting one up and maintaining it.

Everything you need to set it up is included right in the box, with just a level, dry surface and access to an outlet (without an extension cord) required. Despite the lack of foam inserts, this hot tub is still rated for year-round use with Bestway’s Freeze Shield technology. One caveat: While this tub says it's for four to six people, it's really most practical for just four.

The DoCred inflatable hot tub delivers solo relaxation without swallowing up a small patio or using a ton of water. Think of it as an outdoor bathtub, perfect for homes with only showers or those with very limited outdoor space. The oval shape actually makes it easier to fully stretch out compared to some two-to-four-person circular models, and the included side table and mat are a nice touch.

A few drawbacks: Because the heater and bubble jets share the same pump and limited electrical power, activating the bubbles pauses the heating function until the massage cycle ends. That just means you’ll need to make sure the tub is at your desired temp before turning on the jets. This tub also isn’t rated for cold-weather use outdoors, so think of it as a fun addition to your warm-weather outdoor vibe.

There are two main types of hot tubs: plug-and-play models and hardwired spas. When we reached out to Courter, he recommended considering several factors before making a decision about which type of hot tub you should go for.

“The right choice depends less on preference and more on your setup, budget, and how much installation you’re willing to deal with,” says Courter. “There are many things specific to the hot tub being purchased. Things such as whether it is insulated, and what R-value does that insulation have?” R-value measures how well a hot tub’s insulation resists heat loss. The higher the R-value, the better it holds heat, and the less energy it uses to stay warm.

He notes that some hot tubs run on gas, though for this guide we’ve chosen only electric models. Where you live matters, too. “Ambient temperature will play a big part in operational costs,” he says. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain.”

Plug-and-play hot tubs are the easiest way in. Most run on a standard 110-volt outlet, so setup is straightforward. They require no electrician, no buried lines, and no major prep beyond a flat surface.

They’re typically made from molded plastic and are widely available online, which helps keep prices down. There are also some inflatable models on the market for less permanent use.

The trade-off, however, is performance. These models often have slower heating and less powerful jets compared with higher-end models. Still, for many homes (and especially rentals), this is the most practical option.

Hardwired spas require more planning. These usually run on 240 volts and need professional installation, but they deliver stronger jets, faster heating, and a more refined overall experience.

Most hardwired tubs have acrylic shells and insulated cabinets, which improves durability and efficiency. They also cost more upfront (and installation adds to that), but they feel closer to a traditional showroom spa experience.

If you’re worried about party-hosting capabilities, be wary. Capacity numbers can be misleading. A “six-person” tub will rarely feel comfortable with six adults. If you have the space, it’s usually worth sizing up.

A four-person model works well for one or two people who want room to stretch out, while six- or seven-person tubs are better for families or hosting. If you’re mainly using it for relaxation or hydrotherapy, a smaller tub is easier to maintain, and often more comfortable day to day.

Take time to think about jet count, but that’s not always a straightforward metric on which to judge a hot tub. What matters just as much is the placement, variety, and adjustability of those jets. Higher-powered pumps will provide stronger flow, as well. A lounger with carefully placed jets is a must if you’re seeking physical relief for aches and pains.

It’s fun to have perks like lights and sound systems, but those matter less than the features that keep a hot tub up and running for years. A good cover in particular makes a big difference. It helps retain heat, reduce energy use, and keep maintenance manageable.

But once you’ve chosen the size and key mechanical specs that meet your needs, it’s okay to jazz up the experience a bit with neat extras like waterfalls and lights. Just be mindful of additional maintenance. It’s easier to buy a new portable Bluetooth speaker than it is to repair one integrated into a hot tub.

Courter said that the exact operational cost is hard to guesstimate—a lot of factors come into play. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain,” he says. “In Northern Utah, we can get down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit in the wintertime. In that same timeframe, the average temperature in Miami is going to be in the mid-70s. A hot tub in northern Utah is going to need to run much more often to maintain its temperature.”

When it comes to chemicals and cost, that also varies depending on the size of the hot tub and how often you use it. General online user reports vary between $40 and $100 a month, but it’s not a number that’s easy to estimate. The initial setup will cost a bit more as you invest in the chemicals and supplies you’ll regularly need.

While hot tubs certainly are not a set-it-and-forget-it luxury, they are easier to maintain than a pool—and upkeep should not be a major deterrent. “Maintenance of a hot tub isn’t too bad if you stay on top of it,” says Courter. “Usually, it takes 10 to 20 minutes once a week to adjust your chemicals and clean your filters.”

When it comes to chemical options, whether you choose chlorine, bromine, copper, a salt system, or an ozone generator, they all work just fine—as long as you keep your pH in line. “A pH of 7 on the pH scale is neutral, but the pH of a human eye is 7.5, so I always suggest to my customers that they aim for around 7.5,” says Courter.

Other maintenance will involve keeping an eye on the water level, the condition of the hardware, and any signs of malfunction. Some hot tub repairs are simple and you can even DIY them, but many require calling an expert.

Other than structural considerations if you want it on an elevated deck, the options are virtually endless.

“A factory-built hot tub can go just about anywhere, as long as whatever you are putting it on can hold the weight,” says Courter. “A dry hot tub can weigh around 1,000 pounds, but remember that water weighs 8.34 pounds per gallon.” That means an average-sized spa could weigh nearly two tons.

When it comes to ground placement, a flat and level surface with a good base is fine for most uses. If you do choose to place a plug-and-play spa inside your home, be prepared to consult an expert about ways to mitigate moisture damage.

This is another one of those tricky metrics to guesstimate. We’ve listed the warranty windows for each tub we’ve included, but these spas should last longer than that.

“As with most items, it really depends on the quality of the product you buy,” says Courter. He says not all hot tubs are created equal and that consumer research goes a long way. That being said, spending more doesn’t guarantee a longer life for the hot tub.

“If a customer buys the highest-quality tub on the market and doesn't take care of it, it will fail quickly,” says Courter. “I have seen many hot tubs fail in just a couple of years if not maintained the way they should. In contrast, my wife and I still use a Watkins Hot Springs that is over 25 years old. Moral of the story: Buy the best quality that you can and take care of it.”

#6337. School playgrounds may have shade in all the wrong places

Researchers found that only one of nine playground areas met standards for shade, comfort, and play, raising questions about schoolyard design.

A shade sail stretched over a school playground looks like a job done. But children play where the fun is, not where the shade is.

When the two don’t line up, the shade covers an empty patch of ground while the children play in the sun.

Researchers in New Zealand have built a way of grading playgrounds that treats that mismatch as a design problem.

It scores every part of a schoolyard on whether it blocks the sun, whether it’s comfortable, and whether a child would want to play there.

On its first test, at a primary school in Christchurch, New Zealand, one of nine play areas passed.

Anupriya Sukumar of the School of Landscape Architecture at Lincoln University in New Zealand led the work. Her co-authors are at Lincoln and in the Department of Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning at Texas A&M University.

Sun protection is especially important in New Zealand. The country and neighboring Australia have the world’s highest rates of skin cancer, with about 100,000 New Zealanders affected each year.

Roughly a third of a person’s lifetime exposure to the sun comes before age 18.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sukumar said the schools she has mapped tend to put their shade in the wrong place.

“While shade was available in many schools, it was most commonly located around the perimeter of playgrounds, particularly along school boundaries,” she noted.

Those shaded strips often went underused, she said, because they weren’t where the children played.

Sukumar’s team starts by dividing a playground into activity zones, each one a place for a particular kind of play.

The Christchurch school had nine, from a sports field and a tennis court to a sandpit and a covered outdoor classroom.

Around each zone with a fixed purpose, the team drew a buffer of about 6.5 feet (2 meters) for the children waiting their turn.

Shade was measured for the worst moment of the school day. The team built a 3D model of the school and simulated its shadows for 1:30 p.m. on February 1.

That is the end of the summer lunch break, close to solar noon.

A zone passed on sun protection only if at least 80% of it was in shade dense enough to block most of the sun’s ultraviolet light for about an hour.

A thin tree canopy, which lets 70% of that light through, doesn’t count.

The surface underfoot reflects ultraviolet light back up at a child’s face.

Grass reflects about 2% of it and dry sand 20%, so a sunlit sandpit reflects ten times as much as a sunlit lawn. Asphalt and concrete fall in between.

The team assessed comfort separately, using five years of records from a nearby weather station to identify prevailing wind patterns.

They then mapped the areas sheltered from wind by buildings and trees.

Running children need shade with a breeze to stay comfortable, while children sitting down to eat need shade out of the wind. So each zone is scored against what happens there.

The third test is the simplest. A zone counts as attractive if it holds something that draws children in, such as climbing equipment, sand, or balls.

Only the covered outdoor classroom met all three tests. Four zones met one of them, and four met none. On sun protection alone, one zone was adequate, four were moderate, and four were low.

The sports field, the tennis court, and the basketball court all failed the attraction test.

School policy restricts balls at break time, so these large spaces lacked the equipment needed for their intended activities.

Asked what surprised her most, Sukumar singled out those big sports areas.

“One of the most surprising findings was that large portions of school playgrounds were dedicated to sports fields and hard courts, yet these spaces often lacked access to sports equipment, such as balls, due to lunchtime restrictions or school policies,” she said.

Smaller spaces such as sandpits and nature play areas took up much less of the playground, she said, and were often used more.

The grades lead to a repair plan the authors call the three Rs. A zone that nearly passes gets a retrofit, meaning a simple, low-cost change.

More serious failures call for a longer-term redesign. Schools can relocate or repurpose areas that fail every test and see little use.

A school can work through that list as money allows instead of rebuilding everything at once.

Sukumar told Earth.com that schools with funding for only one project this year should improve their busiest play area first.

The method was tried at one school, and the team hasn’t yet measured whether the children there spend more time in protected zones or get less sun.

“At this stage, we have not directly measured how much time children spend in shaded or sun-protected areas,” Sukumar said. “However, this represents an important next step for future research.”

The authors wrote that the attractiveness scores rest on what a zone contains rather than on watching children use it.

The pass marks come from earlier research, not from measurements at this school.

The comfort rules were set for Christchurch’s temperate climate and would need adjusting elsewhere, and the authors called the whole process complex and potentially time-consuming.

What would settle the open question is a count of where children actually go during outdoor play.

Sukumar said direct observation, or tracking children’s movements across a playground, could show whether the protected zones are used as intended and where shade is needed most.

The full study was published in the journal Cities & Health.

#6336. Record-breaking X-ray flash pushes the limits of ultrafast science

Scientists created a record-breaking attosecond X-ray flash that could help reveal how electrons move inside atoms and molecules.

A camera flash can freeze a sprinter’s motion in a photograph because its light lasts only an instant.

Inside an atom, electrons rearrange themselves in attoseconds, and there are more attoseconds in one second than there have been seconds since the Big Bang.

X-ray flashes that short are hard to make, and physicists have now made one about ten times more intense than any attosecond X-ray laser pulse reported before it.

Researchers at the European XFEL, an X-ray laser in Schenefeld, Germany, focused the flash into a spot a few hundred times narrower than a human hair.

They then checked the record by watching copper atoms do something only extreme light makes them do.

“This is a world record in intensity and fluence for a hard-X-ray attosecond pulse,” said Ichiro Inoue of the University of Tokyo, the first author of the paper. The team ran the experiment in April 2026.

Hard X-rays are the most energetic kind of X-ray, with wavelengths about the size of an atom. Physicists judge a flash by two numbers once it reaches a sample.

One is how much energy lands on each bit of area, which is called fluence. The other is how fast that energy arrives, which is intensity.

A high fluence matters for samples smaller than the beam. A high intensity makes matter respond in ways that weak light can’t trigger.

“A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL,” said Jiawei Yan of the German research center DESY, one of the corresponding authors.

“But generating powerful pulses is only the first step.”

“For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample,” Yan added.

“With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter.”

The machine starts with a tightly packed bunch of electrons lasting just a few femtoseconds.

A long line of magnets with alternating poles makes the bunch give off an X-ray flash.

Measured just past those magnets, each flash carried 140 microjoules on average, more than ten times the energy of earlier hard X-ray attosecond pulses.

A pair of mirrors brought in from Japan focused the beam nearly 1 kilometer (0.6 miles) beyond the magnets.

Each flash bounced four times, one mirror focusing it vertically and the other horizontally, inside a vacuum chamber.

Scanning fine gold wires across the beam showed a focal spot about 7 by 13 millionths of an inch (180 by 330 nanometers). A human hair is a few hundred times wider.

A curved diamond crystal recorded the spread of energies in every flash without disturbing it.

Ordinary X-ray laser pulses, which last femtoseconds, typically show several tens of spikes in that spread.

Of 74,000 flashes here, 13.7% showed a single spike, consistent with the light coming from one ultrashort slice of the electron bunch.

At the focus, the single-spike flashes carried an average of 45 microjoules, with some reaching 100 microjoules.

Their energy spread of 6 electronvolts implies a duration of about 300 attoseconds, if each pulse is as short as its spectrum allows.

That is a flash so brief that light itself travels less than the width of the spot before it ends.

From those numbers, the fluence came to 67,000 joules per square centimeter and the peak intensity to 210 billion billion watts per square centimeter.

Both are roughly ten times the previous best for attosecond X-ray laser pulses.

They also rival the best focused femtosecond pulses, with one very recent exception that reached roughly 50 times higher.

The team wanted an independent check on that intensity. They put a copper foil less than one thousandth of an inch (20 micrometers) thick at the focus, with a detector about 2 feet (600 millimeters) behind it.

A 10,000-electronvolt X-ray photon can knock an electron out of the innermost shell of a copper atom.

When another electron drops into that hole, the atom gives off an X-ray of its own.

At high enough intensity, those X-rays stimulate neighboring excited atoms to emit in the same direction. Physicists call it amplified spontaneous emission, or ASE.

“It is almost magical to see this happening,” said Anders Madsen, group leader at the European XFEL’s MID instrument, where the study was conducted.

“Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction.”

The copper glow climbed steeply as pulse energy rose to about 20 microjoules, slowed after that, and leveled off above 50 microjoules.

One possible reason for the leveling is that the pulse strips electrons out of the atoms faster than the atoms can glow.

The estimated intensity was close to the level at which this electron stripping should occur, supporting that explanation.

The 300-attosecond figure is an inference from the energy spread, not a direct measurement of the pulse in time.

Only about one flash in seven came out as a single spike, and the leveling of the copper glow has one possible explanation rather than a proven one.

The team wrote that pulses this intense could drive higher-order interactions between X-rays and matter and capture a structure before the X-rays damage it.

Split into two timed flashes, they might also control how electrons move in atoms and molecules. This paper reports just the flash and the copper test.

Flashes this short and intense are meant to show what electrons do before the X-rays change the sample.

European XFEL expects its own focusing mirrors in early 2027, funded with the University of Hamburg and Germany’s research ministry.

The new mirrors would make these flashes available to researchers worldwide, opening more opportunities to study electrons in motion.

The full study was published in the journal Optica.

#6335. Why some cities embrace new technology faster than others

A study of 3.2 million Americans links residents’ openness to new experiences with earlier adoption of Airbnb, Uber, and Flickr.

Why does a new app catch on quickly in one city but struggle in another? Income, internet access, and nearby universities may help explain the difference.

A study of 3.2 million Americans points to another factor: residents’ openness to new experiences.

Across 349 metropolitan areas, regions whose residents scored higher on openness took up Airbnb, Uber, and Flickr earlier.

That held even after income, education, internet access, and a long list of other differences were accounted for.

Tobias Ebert of the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland and Martin Obschonka of the University of Amsterdam led the work.

The findings show an association, but they do not establish that openness drives adoption.

“What stood out was the consistency of the pattern,” Ebert said.

“Psychological openness was the only factor reliably associated with adoption across all of the three innovations we studied.”

Psychologists sort personality into five broad traits. One of them covers curiosity, a taste for new ideas, and a willingness to try unfamiliar things, and they call it openness. It is partly shaped by genes.

The survey measures it with plain statements like “Is curious about many different things,” rated from strongly disagree to strongly agree.

Between 2004 and 2015, 3,234,899 people in the United States answered a 44-statement version of that survey online and gave their zip code.

The team averaged the scores for each of 349 metro areas in the lower 48 states.

The smallest regional sample, Victoria, Texas, had 406 people, and New York had 127,859. The co-authors include researchers at the University of Cambridge, the University of Texas at Austin, and the IT University of Copenhagen.

The averages ran from 3.48 out of 5 in Bismarck, North Dakota, to 3.93 in Santa Fe, New Mexico. That gap looks small until it is counted in people.

Counting anyone who scored 4 or higher as open, the share of open residents ranged from 21% in the least open region to 48% in the most open one.

The companies’ own early numbers are patchy, so the team turned to tax records.

The team used tax records for businesses without employees in accommodation and passenger transportation as indicators of hosting and driving activity.

The team counted new accommodation filings for the five years after 2009, when Airbnb took its current name and landed its first major funding.

Uber launched city by city and reached 142 regions in its first five years.

In each of those regions, taxi and ground transport filings were flat before Uber came and rose sharply in the five years afterward.

For Flickr, the photo-sharing site that peaked around 2008, the team sampled 80 million photos uploaded between 2005 and 2015.

It counted how many different people in each region posted during the site’s first five years.

In the five years after Airbnb launched, San Diego gained 9.5 new accommodation businesses per 100,000 residents, more than four times the 2.2 in Minneapolis.

Regions that were early on one platform tended to be early on the others, and openness tracked that general readiness. Its correlation with early adoption was about 0.4 for each platform and 0.49 for the three combined.

A region one standard deviation higher in openness gained about 2.4 more accommodation hosts per 100,000 residents and about 48 more ride-share drivers.

For a region the size of New York, the team calculated, that is roughly 450 more hosts and more than 9,000 more drivers over five years.

San Francisco, Portland, and Austin were repeatedly among the strongest adopters, and El Paso, Flint, and Jackson among the weakest.

The association weakened somewhat but remained when the team adjusted for age, gender, race, income, education, and unemployment.

It also held after adjusting for internet access, tourism, housing, transportation, politics, religiosity, social ties, and the other four personality traits.

Openness was the only variable linked to adoption of all three platforms.

All three platforms asked ordinary people to do something unfamiliar. An Airbnb host let strangers sleep in the spare room.

An Uber driver gave rides in the family car. Flickr users posted their photos in public before that was common online.

None of those services works until enough people in one place are willing to go first.

“Someone has to be willing to try a new behavior before everyone else regards it as normal,” said Obschonka, of the Amsterdam Business School.

“This can be especially important for platforms, which need enough local users, hosts, drivers or content creators to generate the network effects that make them useful and viable.”

The team calls regional openness an invisible social infrastructure. It can’t be seen the way roads and fiber lines can, but it may shape how readily a place takes to something new.

Openness does not replace those familiar factors, the authors wrote, but it may help explain why otherwise similar regions adopt new services at different rates.

The data are a snapshot, so they can’t say whether open people make a region quick to adopt, or whether something else produces both.

The team checked two alternatives: open people moving to places that already had the platforms, and the platforms raising a region’s openness.

Neither explained the pattern, and Uber’s choice of cities didn’t either, since its launch order tracked population and income, not openness.

The surveys were taken by whoever chose to answer online, a group skewed toward women and younger people, with an average age of 27.

Reweighting the sample to match the population did not change the results.

The team also treated each region’s openness as fixed across the decade, and the data could not show how the trait turns into a decision to rent out a room.

The study did not look at artificial intelligence either, and the authors cautioned against stretching the result to it.

“When a genuinely new technology arrives, its future does not depend only on the technology itself,” Obschonka said.

“It also depends on whether people are ready to experiment with it.”

The authors wrote that studies following regions over time, or treating a platform’s launch as a natural experiment, could help clarify whether openness influences adoption.

The full study was published in the journal Research Policy.

#6334. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6333. A jellyfish rots in days, so why did the first soft-bodied animals leave so many fossils?

Collagen-eating microbes spread into oxygen-rich seas as animals diversified, and that shift may explain why Ediacaran fossils are so common.

A jellyfish that washes up on a beach is gone within days, and nothing of it ends up in a rock. Yet the oldest animals known, soft-bodied creatures with no shell, bone, or tooth, left fossils so often that whole seafloor communities survive in stone.

Half a billion years ago, the microbes that rot a carcass may not yet have been able to digest the protein holding it together. A new study traces when they acquired that ability.

The protein is collagen, which gives animal tissue its strength. Microbes break it down with enzymes called collagenases, and the new work follows the genes for those enzymes through 700 microbial genomes.

The genes are far older than animals. For most of Earth’s history, though, only microbes that can’t live around oxygen had them.

Philip Vixseboxse led the study as a Ph.D. student in the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Cambridge, and at the University of Edinburgh.

In an interview with Earth.com, he described the result as a one-way change in how fossils form. “Once collagenases proliferated into microbes in those environments, there was no going back,” he said.

Most fossils are shells, bones, and teeth, because hard parts last long enough to turn to stone. Soft tissue has to be sealed off from decay quickly, and that rarely happens.

The exception is the late Ediacaran Period, from about 579 million to 539 million years ago, when soft-bodied animals were preserved in many kinds of seafloor sediment.

Ediacaran fossils are the oldest animal fossils known, and some sites preserve whole communities. Researchers have argued for decades about why.

The usual explanations point to unusual seawater chemistry, different kinds of tissue, or a mat of microbial slime across the seafloor. Each works at some sites but not at all of them.

In 1999, paleontologist Jerzy Dzik proposed a different cause. The microbes of the time hadn’t yet evolved collagenases, he argued, so a carcass kept its shape for long enough to fossilize.

There was no way to test it then, but genome sequencing has since made it testable, and the new study did just that.

Vixseboxse’s team searched the 700 genomes for two collagenase genes and found the main one in 242 species.

They then compared the enzymes’ family trees with a dated tree of microbial life. Where a gene turned up in a lineage that couldn’t have inherited it, another microbe had passed it sideways, and the dated tree says roughly when.

The main collagenase arose billions of years before animals, in microbes that live without oxygen, such as methane-producers and fermenters. So Dzik was wrong about one thing. Collagenases didn’t first appear when the Ediacaran fossils stopped. They had been around for ages, working only in the oxygen-free zones deeper in the seafloor mud.

In an oxygen-rich Ediacaran sea, a dead animal would have kept its collagen until the oxygen in the surrounding sediment ran out.

The authors put that delay at years, which is long enough for minerals to build up on the tissue and preserve its shape. The collagen scaffold of the body, flexible and slow to decay, would have acted as a kind of organic skeleton.

Starting in the Neoproterozoic, the era in which animals arose, the gene for the main collagenase began jumping between lineages far more often.

The team counted an average of 63 sideways transfers across its larger set of trees. Oxygen-tolerant and oxygen-using microbes picked it up, including the groups that dominate decay today.

Vixseboxse told Earth.com the pace of that change was the surprise. “I was shocked by just how stark the increase in diversity of collagen-degrading microbes was when animals first appeared on the scene!” he said.

The timing matters because the microbes that dominate the rotting of an animal carcass in modern oceans acquired collagenases in the latest Neoproterozoic or afterward. Before the Cambrian, the authors wrote, the main agents of modern decay couldn’t efficiently digest collagen at all.

That shift coincides with a sharp drop in soft-bodied fossils. “These results suggest there may be an overarching biological mechanism that has shaped the fossil record of soft tissues across Earth’s history,” said co-author Alex Liu, a professor in the Cambridge Department of Earth Sciences.

Collagen is far from the only material that lasts until something evolves to eat it. The authors wrote that decay-resistant polymers should pile up in sediments before the enzymes that digest them spread, and more sparingly afterward.

Asked by Earth.com about other findings, Vixseboxse pointed to plastics as a modern case, with a fossil record that may one day decline the same way.

Microbial enzymes that break down some plastics already exist, the authors wrote, but they’re not yet common across environments.

The team tracked genes, not decay itself. The gene trees can’t say how fast an Ediacaran carcass rotted, only that the microbes present lacked a tool that modern decomposers have.

Other changes around the same time, including animals that burrow, scavenge, and hunt, also made soft-tissue fossils rarer. The authors call the enzymes a major driver rather than the only one.

The dated tree also gives ranges, not dates. The moment any one group gained the enzyme can be a window of more than a hundred million years.

Vixseboxse said the next test would be a community of microbes that can’t digest collagen, and then a look at how an animal body decays among them.

“It would be really neat to produce a microbial community that was incapable of degrading collagen,” he said. His team came close by soaking a soft coral in a strong soap solution for three days, which stripped out the cells and left only the collagen framework behind.

Until a microbial version of that experiment runs, the case rests on gene trees, and on the fossils that stopped appearing when the genes spread.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6330. Japan is encouraging people to use AI, but small businesses are falling behind

Japan is promoting AI to ease labor shortages, but a new review highlights a wide gap between experimentation and everyday business use.

When governments set out to govern artificial intelligence, most of them reach for rules. Japan reached for a law whose central word is promotion.

Passed in May 2025, Japan’s AI Promotion Act carries no penalties, no licensing and no registration requirements.

It exists because too few people in Japan were using AI.

Two researchers have reviewed Japan’s approach as AI use has grown sharply. In 2023, 9.1% of people in Japan said they had used generative AI. By 2025, the figure was 58.8%.

A large gap remained between large and small companies in putting AI to work.

The review comes from Hiromi M. Yokoyama of the Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe at the University of Tokyo and Shuo Wang of Tsinghua University.

“The instruments a government chooses reveal its assumptions about the nature of the problem,” Yokoyama said.

“The urgency of Japan’s governance problem comes not from the risks of AI being used, but from the economic and social cost of AI going unused.”

In the same 2023 government survey, 46.3% of people in the United States had used generative AI. In Germany the figure was 34.6%.

The shortfall came in a country short of workers. As of July 2025, 29.3% of Japan’s population was 65 or older. Farming, nursing, construction, retail and logistics all report labor shortages.

Japan’s industrial computer systems were aging too. The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry warned of a “2025 Digital Cliff,” a large stock of custom-built legacy systems whose maintenance engineers were nearing retirement.

The law promotes AI as one way to ease Japan’s labor shortages.

In cross-national surveys run by the authors’ own team, Japanese respondents scored among the highest on objective tests of AI knowledge.

They ranked lowest in confidence about their own understanding.

A separate 47-country study found 28% of Japanese respondents willing to trust AI, below the global figure. Acceptance of AI was 60%, so the hesitation is about trust.

Yokoyama and Wang point to a Japanese idea called anshin-kan, an expectation that things will behave predictably.

A society that values predictability may hold back from a technology it can’t anticipate, so clear rules work as encouragement.

Elsewhere, people have been found to place too much trust in AI.

The AI Promotion Act creates no AI-specific duties that carry a fine. It asks users to make an effort to use AI properly, a duty recognized in Japanese law that carries no sanction.

The government can publish the names of companies that ignore its guidance.

Agencies steer private companies through non-binding recommendations, and a long record of cooperation between ministries and organized business lets voluntary guidelines act as real constraints.

The law’s main organizational tool is an AI Strategy Headquarters inside the Cabinet Office, set up on September 1, 2025, with the prime minister in charge.

Its job is to overcome the divisions between ministries that have slowed Japanese policy in other fields.

It commits the government to revising its AI plan every year, and that schedule held even as Japan changed prime ministers in 2026.

The EU AI Act sets penalties of up to 7% of a company’s global turnover. A 2023 Cabinet Office paper judged that burden too heavy for firms already struggling with digital change.

Personal use of generative AI, the tools that write text and generate images, posted the largest rise among the four countries surveyed.

Among companies, 86.4% of Japanese firms reported trying generative AI in at least one business function, close to the United States at 90.9%.

Trying is not the same as using. In an Information-technology Promotion Agency survey of 1,799 firms, companies with more than 1,000 employees had deployed AI in their operations at a rate of around 80%.

Among firms with 101 employees or fewer, the figure was 16.6%.

The deployment gap by company size runs to more than 60 percentage points.

“Adoption is not a single quantity,” Wang said. “Trial and organizational integration respond to different instruments. Promotional instruments lower the cost of trying.”

“They do not supply the capital, technical personnel or managerial authority that system replacement and process redesign require – and these are precisely what smaller firms lack,” he added.

The government appears to have read the data the same way. Its second AI Basic Plan, adopted on July 14, 2026, sets its goal at changing how decisions are made and how work is organized.

Whether humans and AI work better together is now a question for every small firm in Japan.

A year and a half is a short record, Yokoyama and Wang wrote. Some of Japan’s climb may reflect AI spreading everywhere at once.

The researchers identify three areas where Japan’s approach remains untested. First, voluntary compliance may prove less effective against rare but severe events.

These could include a major data breach, an AI failure in critical infrastructure, or AI-generated disinformation spread during a crisis.

The alignment between government and business has not been tested on hard questions like liability, data sharing or job losses.

And the AI Strategy Headquarters has produced two plans on schedule but has not yet had to settle a conflict between ministries.

“A governance model may succeed on its own terms while the underlying problem persists in a form its instruments cannot readily reach,” Yokoyama said.

“Japan’s case shows that where adoption is low, the governance problem has a different structure from the innovation-versus-risk balance that dominates comparative debate, and it calls for different instruments.”

Whether small Japanese companies can close the deployment gap remains an open question.

Future plans and surveys may help reveal whether efforts to reorganize work can address barriers that promotion alone has not overcome.

The full study was published in the journal Risk Sciences.

#6329. Women who used menopause hormone therapy had less brain vessel damage later in life

Women who had used menopause hormone therapy showed fewer signs of damage to small brain blood vessels at 70.

Estrogen helps regulate the menstrual cycle and supports pregnancy, but it also helps keep blood vessels healthy, including those in the brain.

That second job may still matter decades after menopause.

Women who had used menopause hormone therapy showed fewer signs of damage to the brain’s smallest blood vessels at age 70.

Women whose menopause came later showed a similar but weaker pattern.

Damage to these tiny vessels becomes more common with age, and it’s linked to a higher chance of stroke and dementia.

Giulia Lorenzon, now at the Yale School of Medicine, and Anna Marseglia of Karolinska Institutet in Sweden led the work.

The team compared each woman’s hormone history with her brain scans but never gave anyone hormones, so the study can show links but can’t prove cause and effect.

Doctors use the word cerebrovascular to describe the brain’s blood vessels.

“Our results suggest that hormonal exposure across different periods of a woman’s life may have cumulative effects also on the cerebrovascular health in later life,” said Marseglia, one of the study’s senior authors.

“The findings suggest that the brain’s blood vessels may play an important role in the link between estrogen and brain aging.”

The women all took part in the Gothenburg H70 Birth Cohort Studies, a long-running study of aging in Gothenburg, Sweden. Between 2014 and 2016, 352 women born in 1944 had MRI brain scans at about age 70.

None had dementia. On a common 30-point test of memory and thinking, the women averaged just over 29.

Staff asked each woman about her reproductive history and used her answers to work out her reproductive span, the number of years between her first period and menopause.

A woman whose first period came at age 13 and whose menopause came at age 50, for example, had a span of 37 years. That’s close to the group’s average.

The ovaries make most of a woman’s estrogen. For women who had both ovaries removed, the researchers used their age at surgery to calculate their reproductive span.

Most of the women had also used hormones. About 73% had taken birth control pills, and about 61% had used menopause hormone therapy.

That level of hormone use fits Swedish history, the authors wrote. The pill caught on in the mid-1960s, and hormone therapy use rose sharply in the 1990s, as these women reached menopause.

The brain depends on a dense network of small blood vessels. Damage to them is called small vessel disease, and it often causes no symptoms, so many people learn they have it only from a brain scan.

Radiologists checked each scan for four common signs. Large bright patches in the brain’s white matter can mark areas where blood supply has suffered.

Lacunes are small holes often left behind by tiny strokes, and microbleeds are pinpoint spots of old bleeding.

The fourth sign is widened fluid-filled spaces around the vessels themselves.

Each woman got one point for each sign that passed a set threshold. About 59% of the women scored zero, and 12% scored two or more. No one scored four.

The team also measured the white matter itself, the bundles of nerve fibers that carry signals between brain areas.

In healthy white matter, water tends to move along nerve fibers rather than across them. The scans measured this movement to assess the tissue’s structure.

Women with more years between their first period and menopause were less likely to score two or more. Each extra year was tied to about 8% lower odds of that higher score.

The team found the same pattern after accounting for education, pregnancies, and breastfeeding.

The age at menopause mattered more than the age at a first period. A later menopause was tied to a lower score and to fewer lacunes.

Still, this was one of the weaker results. When researchers run dozens of comparisons, a few can look real by luck alone, so the team applied a stricter test that allows for that.

The reproductive span link weakened under that test, and it weakened again when the team left out the 31 women who’d had a stroke or a mini-stroke.

Women who had used menopause hormone therapy had less than half the odds of scoring two or more, compared with women who never had. Their white matter also looked more orderly.

Both of those links passed the stricter test. They held after the team accounted for high blood pressure, heart disease, and diabetes, and when women with a past stroke were left out.

Birth control pill use was linked to more orderly white matter but not to a lower score, and that white matter link faded under the stricter test.

Women who had used birth control pills when younger and menopause hormone therapy later had the most favorable scans.

Compared with women who had used neither, they had about a third of the odds of scoring two or more.

The researchers found no clear interaction between birth control pill use and menopause hormone therapy.

They described the combined pattern as preliminary and called for studies in more varied groups of women.

Women make up about two-thirds of dementia cases. Earlier studies of hormone therapy and dementia have reached opposite conclusions, with some finding lower risk and others higher.

So the team also measured four areas of the brain that tend to thin early in Alzheimer’s disease. Overall, none of the hormone measures was linked to the thickness of those areas.

One exception involved a version of a gene called APOE. Its ε4 version raises the risk of Alzheimer’s, and about a third of the women carried at least one copy.

Among those carriers, hormone therapy users had thicker tissue in the Alzheimer’s-prone areas than nonusers. That result didn’t pass the stricter test, and the authors wrote that it should be read with caution.

Among the 205 women scanned again five years later, hormone history made no clear difference to how fast the bright patches grew or the Alzheimer’s-prone areas thinned.

Hormone therapy users had a hint of slower growth in the bright patches, but it wasn’t strong enough to rule out chance.

To the authors, the split between these results suggests that estrogen’s link to brain aging in these women may mostly involve the blood vessels.

The women recalled their hormone use decades later, and researchers recorded whether they had used birth control pills or menopause hormone therapy.

The study didn’t capture the products, doses, or treatment start dates.

“Furthermore, the study is an observational study, and we cannot therefore determine cause and effect,” Lorenzon said. “The results cannot therefore be used as a basis for recommending hormone therapy for preventive purposes.”

The volunteers were also a healthy, well-educated group from one city.

Among the women with white matter measurements, only 46 had used neither the pill nor hormone therapy, so that comparison group was small.

Some earlier research suggests hormone therapy may help the brain most when it starts close to menopause.

The team couldn’t test that idea, because the study didn’t record when each woman began.

Nor did the researchers check whether healthier-looking vessels made any difference to memory or thinking.

Answering that will take studies that record exactly which hormones women took and when, then follow their thinking skills along with their brain scans.

The full study was published in the journal Neurology.
