#6327. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?

Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?

[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?

Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard examples of the good that’s been created by these technological leaps. In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: Some pretty bad stuff’s happening, right? So let’s just go through a few of these. So first, you’re seeing massive types of fraud. Everything from romance scams to people calling parents and saying your kids have been taken, pay a ransom, to geopolitics. People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6326. A honey bee’s stinger keeps pumping venom after the bee flies off, and now scientists know how

Video shows that a honey bee stinger works as a tiny, double-piston pump, with collapsing valves that keep pushing venom after the bee has gone.

A honey bee stings once, leaves its stinger in your skin, and flies off to die. It looks like the end of the attack. It isn’t.

The stinger left behind is a self-contained unit, with its own venom sac, muscles and nerves. It keeps digging in and pumping venom on its own after the bee has gone.

Scientists have now filmed that happening at high speed. Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel of Macquarie University in Sydney and her colleagues watched detached stingers push into a clear gel that stands in for skin. The gel is not living tissue, but it lets a camera see what skin would hide.

The stinger, they found, works as a pump but is unlike most pumps that people build: two flexible pistons sliding in opposite directions inside a single chamber.

“We’ve known since as early as 1910 that the venom sac of a honey bee stinger empties into a chamber with little pumping elements called valves, but until now we didn’t know exactly how they work,” said Ramirez-Esquivel.

The honey bee is one of only a handful of insects whose stinger is built to tear away from its body. When the bee pulls free, the stinger stays put, along with its venom sac, several glands, a cluster of nerve cells, and the muscles that drive it.

The team, from Macquarie and UNSW Canberra, took stingers from live worker bees. Each tip went into a small block of clear gel about a sixth of an inch (4 millimeters) long.

A stinger is partly see-through, so a strong light shone through it let cameras running at up to 500 frames a second record the parts moving inside.

The stinger only pumped properly when it had something to push into. Without gel, its pumping parts barely moved. In the gel, strong pumping lasted from 15 seconds to just over a minute in a sample of 10 stingers.

It then faded to twitches that went on for two to five additional minutes. In an interview with Earth.com, Ramirez-Esquivel said the speed of the stinging made it hard to film.

“There is no time to adjust, you either catch it or you don’t,” she said. “I still did not expect the sheer number of attempts we had to go through to capture this footage.”

Inside the stinger, the venom sac empties into a small chamber at the base. Two long, sharp blades called lancets slide back and forth through that chamber along a rail.

Their backward-facing barbs anchor the stinger in skin and work it deeper with each stroke. Scorpions and spiders deliver venom differently, by squeezing muscles around a venom gland.

Each lancet carries a small, flexible flap, called a valve, inside the chamber. The two valves move in opposite directions: when one travels down toward the tip, the other travels up.

A single stroke moves a valve about a sixtieth of an inch (0.45 millimeters), roughly the thickness of four sheets of paper, in about seven tenths of a second. The venom then leaves through a canal about half the width of a human hair.

On the downstroke, each valve inflates like a parachute and pushes venom ahead of it. On the upstroke it collapses, so venom can flow past it and refill the chamber below while the other valve is pushing.

The top of the chamber is also wider than the valves can seal, which leaves a space where fresh venom keeps entering even while pumping goes on.

Then the two valves meet. “Finally, and perhaps most dramatically, as the valves meet in the middle of the stroke, they change shape again to push past each other,” said Ramirez-Esquivel.

“This is a remarkable strategy to pump fluid since maintaining a seal is vital to transmit pressure effectively.”

There are no muscles inside the chamber or the valves, so every change of shape is passive.

To test the idea, the team scanned stingers from a Canberra hive at the Australian National University and 3D printed a scaled-up chamber with flexible plastic valves pumping glycerol. Its valves moved like the real ones.

A syringe shows why that matters. Its one rigid piston can’t refill without pulling back, so it can’t deliver a steady flow. The stinger’s two collapsing pistons pump and refill at once.

“The stinger pump design is quite unusual in having two pistons in a single pumping chamber,” Ramirez-Esquivel told Earth.com.

She said that, as manufacturing advances, the design may become practical to produce at scale for uses such as medical pumps for drug delivery.

The stinger has already inspired microneedle designs, and mosquito mouthparts have inspired 3D printing nozzles.

Asked by Earth.com the best way to remove a stinger, Ramirez-Esquivel said the stinger empties the venom sac within about 30 seconds to two minutes.

Taking it out as quickly as possible limits how much venom gets into the skin, she said. Near a hive, though, it is better to get away calmly and quickly first.

The reason is in the stinger itself. It carries glands that release alarm pheromones, chemical signals that recruit other bees to sting. “If there is something worse than getting stung once it is getting stung multiple times,” she said.

The stinger’s independence also makes sense for the bee. A worker that leaves its stinger behind dies, but the stinger keeps delivering venom whether or not the bee survives.

The authors wrote that this suits an insect that defends its colony with its life.

The team could not directly see venom flowing inside the chamber. The refill space at the top is inferred from the shapes and timing of the valves.

Whether the collapsing valve fully stops venom from being sucked back up is also unknown, and the authors wrote that more work is needed to measure that.

How the valves squeeze past each other is unresolved too. The video suggests the cup-shaped part of each valve collapses sideways, while in the printed model the valve’s wings flipped upward. The authors wrote that future work is needed to settle which happens in the real stinger.

In addition, the authors have not measured what the valves are made of, because each one is small and fragile enough to damage on removal. And every stinger was filmed in gel, not living skin.

The next step the authors proposed is to freeze stingers in liquid nitrogen in mid-sting and scan them, catching the valves in whatever shape they take as they pass.

The scans from this study are public on MorphoSource for anyone who wants to look.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

#6324. When eco-friendly advertising backfires: More green claims can make a product less appealing

Advertising both eco-friendly ingredients and sustainable packaging can lower a product’s appeal among shoppers who care less about buying green.

A product made with eco-friendly ingredients and sold in sustainable packaging sounds like an easy sell.

But a new study suggests that advertising both benefits can make it less appealing to some shoppers.

People who care a lot about buying green rated a product higher when its ad mentioned both. People who care less rated it higher when the ad stuck to just one.

At least with these ads, more green information wasn’t automatically more persuasive.

Miyuri Shirai, a professor at Keio University, tested this in three experiments with 1,729 people in Japan. The products were made up for the study, and people rated ads instead of buying anything.

Soap, cereal, detergent and other things people buy over and over are called consumer packaged goods. A growing number of them are sold as better for the planet.

In 2023, 18.5% of these goods sold in the US were marketed as sustainable, according to the NYU Stern Center for Sustainable Business. That’s up 4.8 percentage points from 2015.

McKinsey & Company and NielsenIQ found that products with sustainability claims grew their sales by 28% over five years, compared with 20% for products without those claims.

Growth like that leaves companies with a choice. They can make the product itself greener by changing what goes into it or how it’s made. Or they can work on the packaging, using better materials, a new design or a package that can be recycled.

Sustainable packaging gets a lot of attention because these products are bought and thrown away so often. All that packaging uses up raw materials and energy and adds to pollution.

Doing both often costs more and makes production harder. So it helps to know whether shoppers actually reward the extra effort.

At first glance, two green features should beat one. Researchers call this the more-is-better pattern, where the more good things an ad says about a product, the better people tend to rate it.

A much older finding suggests otherwise. In a 1992 study, Daniel Kahneman and Jack Knetsch looked at how much people were willing to pay for environmental services.

People tended to value something less when it came as part of a bigger package than when it was judged on its own. This is called the embedding effect, and it’s where Shirai’s question started.

“My interest in this research began when I read articles about the embedding effect, which suggest that adding more positive information does not always make an option seem better,” Shirai said.

“I became curious about whether communicating multiple sustainability benefits might sometimes be less effective than highlighting just one, depending on the consumer,” she added.

At Keio’s Faculty of Business and Commerce, Shirai studies the psychology of how shoppers judge products. For this project, she recruited people through Freeasy, a Japanese online survey panel.

Each person saw one ad for a made-up product. Some ads talked only about what the product was made of, others only about the packaging, and the rest about both.

People then rated the product. Shirai also measured how much each person cares about buying things that are good for the environment, which researchers call green consumption values.

The first experiment used laundry detergent. Of the 750 people recruited, 124 failed a check meant to catch careless answers, which left 626.

The second used organic granola, a food that’s widely sold and already seen as sustainable.

Switching from detergent to food helped test whether the pattern held across different product categories.

This time, 600 of the 750 recruits made it through the same check.

Body wash was the product in the third experiment, which included 503 people. Those people also answered extra questions to help explain why they reacted the way they did.

In all three experiments, the results came out the same way.

People who cared more about green buying rated the product higher when the ad covered both the product and its packaging than when it covered only one.

People who cared less did the reverse. They rated the product higher when the ad stuck to a single feature.

That second group’s response was consistent with the embedding effect.

For them, one green feature may have seemed less impressive when it came bundled with another.

For the first group, Shirai had a different explanation. It’s hard to tell how green a product really is from an ad or a label, so people look for small clues.

For someone who cares a lot about the environment, details about the product and details about its package may work as two clues that back each other up.

“Emphasizing sustainability in both the product and its packaging may not always be the most effective strategy,” she said.

In the body wash experiment, people also rated how useful they found the green information and how sustainable they thought the product was.

Both ratings were linked to how people felt about the product, and those links depended on each person’s green values.

The analysis couldn’t show which came first, though, so this is a possible explanation rather than proof.

There’s one catch in how the ads were built.

The ads that mentioned both the product and its packaging had four green statements, while the single-focus ads had two each.

So the results can’t show for sure what people were reacting to. It could have been the number of claims, or whether the claims covered one feature or two.

Everyone in the study was in Japan, and participants rated fictional products without spending real money.

Whether tailoring ads to shoppers’ green values would increase sales or benefit the environment remains untested.

The full study was published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology.

#6323. The 7 Best Fireproof Home Safes Protect Your Valuables from Extreme Heat

Your standard safe may stop burglars, but can it also withstand fires and floods?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A good home safe will protect your most important items from theft and damage, but if you want one that will also offer protection from heat, direct flames, and even water (in some cases), you need a fireproof home safe. This protection isn’t just limited to non-flammable items like jewelry or firearms, either. High-quality fireproof safes keep cash, important documents, photographs, and passports safe, too.

To go one step further, home safes rated as fireproof will protect your belongings from house fires and sprinkler systems, but if you're looking for protection from natural disasters, there are solutions out there. A safe rated for extreme temperatures will safeguard your things in the event of a wildfire, and those with airtight seals should prevent water from seeping in even during a flash flood.

We’ve reviewed the best fireproof home safes below with picks that cover your needs regardless of what you’re storing or how much space you need.

We made our choices on this list based on extensive research, looking closely at key features, brand reputation, and of course, each model’s temperature and fireproof rating. We also looked through customer reviews, making note of how well their safes held up in real-world situations. Beyond this, we took into account recommendations from professional firefighters. Because of these factors, you won’t see a wide variety of brands on this list.

In previous versions of this article, we featured fire safes and chests that were tested out by our team. While these models have since been discontinued or are out of stock, we used this experience to inform new choices for this list. All the safes on this list are “true” fireproof options, meaning that the safe itself will hold up, not just an included fireproof envelope. Each safe we selected is rated to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 degrees Fahrenheit.

More to Explore: Best Outdoor Security Cameras • Best Video Doorbell Cameras • Best Carbon Monoxide Detectors • Best Smart Locks

As you’ll see throughout this list, we believe in SentrySafe as a top brand for fireproof safes—for its lifetime warranty, $50,000 fire protection guarantee, and reliably high levels of fire protection across all products. This mid-sized, 1.23-cubic-foot option is the perfect choice for most people.

Alongside a fire rating of up to 1,700 degrees F for a full hour, the safe boasts a fully waterproof design that protects internal items completely for up to 24 hours in up to 8 inches of submerged water.

Beyond the powerful protection it offers, the fireproof safe also has internal organization features like key hooks, a shelf, and a lockable drawer for especially valuable items. The interior of the safe is even lit to help you see inside. That said, both the lights and the digital keypad are battery-operated, so you'll need to periodically replace them.

The safe, as a whole, weighs close to 90 pounds. While this is a great deterrent from a thief trying to simply steal the entire safe, it can make it quite difficult install or carry up stairs on your own.

As an affordable yet durable alternative to some of the higher-end models on our list, this safe from Amazon Basics checks a lot of our boxes. At 1.24 cubic feet, it's actually slightly larger than our Best Overall choice from SentrySafe, leaving you with just as much space inside, including a top shelf for organization.

The safe also comes with a digital keyboard for easy access. If the keyboard is damaged during a fire, the safe also comes with a backup emergency key that unlocks the mechanism manually.

The biggest detractor for this safe is its durability. The safe is only rated to handle up to 1,200 F for 20 minutes. This is considerably lower than many other safes on this list both in temperature and duration.

If you require more space and organization than our previous recommendations, this safe provides plenty. With over 2 cubic feet of space, there is significantly more room to store larger valuables, such as photo albums or antiques.

Furthermore, the internal organization boasts a top tray and a large bottom drawer, as well as key hooks and a small storage cubby on the door. Unlike other models on this list, the safe uses a dial lock which doesn't require batteries, but it can be cumbersome to use.

Like all SentrySafe models, this one will protect your items for up to an hour at 1,700 F and prevent moisture damage for 24 hours in 8 inches of water. This impressive durability extends to the outer strength of the safe, as well, which can handle a fall from 15 feet without significant damage. Because of its size and strength, the safe weighs a hefty 125 pounds.

Unlike the more traditional safes we recommend, this option from SentrySafe functions more like a secure file cabinet than a traditional safe. The chest holds up to 40 hanging files for easy document organization and has a small space on the lid for handheld items like passports or electronics.

While the safe gives up some fire protection compared to the classic options on our list (it’s rated for 30 minutes at 1,550 degrees), it more than makes up for this with its robust water protection. The file storage box can be fully submerged in water for up to 72 hours without the items inside seeing any water damage at all.

At 39 pounds, this safe is slightly more portable than the bulkier home options, though it is still relatively cumbersome to transport given the lack of handles or wheels.

This Sanctuary model stands out as the gold standard for fire protection. It’s capable of withstanding a blistering 1,800 F for 90 minutes. That makes it the best home safe to protect your valuables from the extreme heat of wildfires.

Additionally, with ETL-rated waterproofing, it can hold out for 7 days in up to 6 inches of standing water. The company also provides a lifetime warranty against fire, natural flood, and theft.

The LED-lit interior has two upholstered shelves and is California DOJ-certified for firearm storage. For security, the electronic lock has a timed lockout mode and tamper indicator. You can also enable an optional silent entry mode for added discretion.

Once you get this compact safe situated, at over 62 pounds, it’s not likely you’ll want to move it again. But, its sturdiness and heavy-duty construction are worth the extra money.

If you only need to protect a few small items, like your passport, a USB drive, and some jewelry, there’s no need to invest in such a large safe. This lock box safe from SentrySafe is small enough to be hidden away on a shelf in your closet, but it doesn’t sacrifice fire protection in the name of being compact.

Rated to handle up to 1,550 degrees F for up to 30 minutes, the lock box should be able to withstand house fires without much issue. The carrying handle also makes it easy to take this safe with you if you are evacuating the fire quickly.

Of course, because of its small size, there’s no internal organization. Everything just sits in the same compartment. But it’s not a feature-less safe. If you are interested in additional theft prevention, it comes with a bolt-down kit for securing the safe to your floor.

For security beyond just the physical integrity of the safe, the Mycube offers a biometric fingerprint scanner as the primary way to unlock its door. The safe saves up to 10 unique fingerprint IDs, so you can program it to open for you and your immediate family with ease.

If someone else needs access to the safe, you can also program a backup password they’ll enter from the digital keypad. Internally, the safe has a removable drawer for storing documents, small valuables, and watches. This also leaves the main compartment of the safe open for larger items.

The Mycube fire safe is quite durable with the company claiming it is capable of withstanding 1,700 F for up to an hour. Its worth noting that Mysafe does not use UL for its fire rating, though the company does report that the rating it has would be the equivalent of one from UL.

To withstand high temperatures, choose a safe that is completely fireproof rather than a security safe with a fire-resistant envelope. Unless all of your valuables fit comfortably in a fire-resistant envelope, the risk of damage to other items in the safe is far too high. Even in the envelope, your items will not be protected to the same degree as a completely fireproof safe.

For advanced protection, fireproof safes should withstand temperatures of at least 1,150 F for 30 minutes or more. In the case of wildfire risk, a fireproof safe that protects at temperatures up to 1,800 F is your best protection. Keep in mind, though, that wildfires get as hot as 2,000 degrees, which would melt most of the safes included here. Any safe you purchase should have fireproof ratings certified by either the Underwriter’s Laboratory (UL) or the inspection firm Intertek, designated by an “ETL” mark.

There are several different types of locking mechanisms available depending on the level of security you desire. Among our recommendations, you’ll find models with traditional keys, combination locks, and electronic keypads. Some safes also come with biometric locks that only unlock to your specific fingerprint, which may offer an additional layer of security.

The size of the valuables you need to store and the available space in your home will dictate the ideal dimensions for your fireproof safe. Look for a deeper safe if you need to protect a large cache of valuables or a variety of different-sized items.

Some smaller safes, like the Honeywell Small Safe Box Chest, are shaped like briefcases and work best for holding important documents. Similarly, if you are looking to store jewelry, look for deeper safes equipped with drawers or trays to better organize your items.

For a fireproof safe you can transport, look for a fireproof chest or document box that weighs 30 pounds or less. These safes are also light enough to be placed on a shelf. Heavier fireproof home security safes (upwards of 75 pounds and designed to deter thieves) usually specify and provide hardware for floor mounting.

Many fireproof safes that are water-resistant or waterproof may only be so under certain conditions, such as standing water of 5 to 8 inches, and possibly for only a certain duration of time. This ensures added protection of the safe’s contents when sprinklers go off in an apartment complex, or if the safe is in the direct line of heavy-duty hoses. Some fireproof security boxes or chests offer waterproof ratings anywhere from 8 to 72 hours spent submerged, which are optimal for homeowners who may face flood risks.

Fireproof rating is easily the most important feature to consider. An independent testing agency must rate the safe, and it should be able to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 F. However, we recommend much higher for those who are worried about wildfires.

Beware of home security safes that companies list as fireproof, but aren't rated by a testing agency. Many of these safes do not have fireproof bodies and instead just include a small fire-resistant envelope to store sensitive items in.

Once the temperature on the safe interior gets above 350 F, any paper inside (including all your hard-earned cash) is at risk of scorching. Even rooms in a burning house that aren’t on fire can get above 600 degrees F at eye level, which is definitely hot enough to soften steel.

There are many things you can and should keep in a fireproof safe, but if it you need to keep the items chilled or temperature controlled, it shouldn’t go in the safe long term. Avoid storing volatile chemicals or batteries in a safe as they can deteriorate or spill and damage other valuables.

You might assume most safes are lock it and forget it, but they do require some maintenance. You should “air out” your safe to avoid moisture build-up every few weeks to a few months depending on the climate where you live and the contents of your safe. You should also replace the batteries in battery-powered safe locks once a year.

Avoid installing a safe in the master bedroom, where security experts indicate thieves are most likely to check for valuables first. Fireproof safes are heavy, so it’s preferable to store them on the floor even though it might make it harder for you to access.

In fact, large standing safes often have mounting hardware included so you can bolt them into the floor of your basement or garage for additional security and stability.

#6322. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6321. Construction crews in California accidentally unearthed the bones of a large mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago

Fossils found during construction in Oceanside, California, may belong to a giant hoofed mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago.

During routine excavation for a city infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, Joseph El Adli, a principal paleontologist with Helix Environmental Planning, spotted fossil bones about 12 feet (3.7 meters) below the surface. He recognized their importance and secured the area.

The bones belong to a large, hoofed mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago, the City of Oceanside announced on September 22, 2026.

The animal may be a titanothere, nicknamed “thunder beast,” or Amynodon, historically called a “swamp rhino.” Laboratory work should settle which.

He was monitoring the dig as the project’s paleontologist. The city places monitors on major infrastructure work as standard practice and to comply with California environmental laws.

The find includes several limb bones, ribs and numerous other bones and fragments. The largest piece appears to be a femur.

El Adli’s team worked for seven days to expose the bones from beneath several tons of hardened mudstone and sandstone.

The fossils were then wrapped in a plaster field jacket and moved to an off-site laboratory.

The exact location has not been disclosed, to protect public safety and the integrity of the site.

The bones came from Member C of the Santiago Formation, a thick sequence of sedimentary rock in northwestern San Diego County.

Paleontologists based the age estimate on the known age of that rock and the types of organisms found in it. The range falls within the Eocene Epoch, in a stretch of time called the Uintan North American Land Mammal Age.

According to the city, the animal roamed ancient floodplains in the area.

The same rock unit in the city has yielded Diegoaelurus vanvalkenburghae, a predator named in a 2022 description of Diegoaelurus. It belongs to the machaeroidines, the oldest group of sabertooth mammals.

Known from a nearly complete lower jaw with most of its teeth, it is the youngest machaeroidine on record. Its authors tentatively tie the group’s extinction to faunal change at the shift from the middle to the late Eocene, part of a wider turnover among mammal predators.

The fossil site that produced it, known as Jeff’s Discovery, also holds a tapir relative called Hesperaletes and a hyaenodontid predator, Limnocyon.

The paper was led by Shawn Zack of the University of Arizona College of Medicine in Phoenix, with Ashley Poust of the San Diego Natural History Museum.

Both candidates belong to Perissodactyla, the order of odd-toed hoofed mammals that includes today’s horses, rhinos and tapirs. Titanotheres are also known as brontotheres.

Oceanside officials describe them as animals roughly the size of a black rhino, with deep chests, a distinct shoulder hump and small horns.

In 2001, paleontologists collected brontothere remains from a sandstone layer at another construction site in Oceanside, near Rancho del Oro Road.

That animal, Parvicornus, stood about 5 to 6 feet (1.5 to 1.8 meters) at the shoulder, according to the San Diego Natural History Museum. It had only a very small horn, more of a bump, near each eye.

Brontotheres began as dog-size animals in the early Eocene and grew larger over roughly 20 million years. Those in South Dakota’s Badlands, about 38 to 34 million years ago, reached around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and 16 feet (4.9 meters) long.

The Badlands animals carried blunt, paired horns on their noses, sometimes more than 3.3 feet (1 meter) long. Males had larger horns than females.

These herbivores most likely ate soft leaves in Eocene forests. The group died out at the end of the Eocene, likely as the climate turned cooler and drier, the National Park Service notes.

Amynodon is the namesake of the amynodonts, which the American Museum of Natural History describes as large-bodied, hornless rhinos. Amynodon itself had a squat, hippo-like body, city officials say.

Their nickname comes from an older idea that they spent much of their time in water. Evidence for that is very limited.

Only Metamynodon, the last North American amynodont, may have been semi-aquatic. Its fossils turn up in sandstone laid down by rivers.

Amynodonts lived in Asia and North America from the middle Eocene through the early Oligocene. They have no living relatives and sit far from today’s species on the rhino family tree.

Amynodon had a large hollow in the skull in front of each eye socket. It likely anchored muscles for an enlarged upper lip.

At the laboratory, preparators will remove the plaster jackets. They will then harden and stabilize the fossils with museum-grade glues and resins.

Once the bones are fully freed from the surrounding rock, paleontologists expect to narrow down the animal’s precise identity.

The specimens are expected to join a museum collection, where they will be preserved and available to scientists and the public. The museum has not been named.

Several jacketed blocks have not been opened yet, and a skull may be inside one of them.

The information was obtained from the City of Oceanside.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6319. Helping children reach healthier weights may start with one change

An afterschool program focused on replacing sugary drinks with water helped shift children’s BMI in a healthier direction after one year.

Most programs that try to help children reach a healthier weight ask families to change a lot at once: more exercise, better meals, earlier bedtimes. Those plans are hard to keep going at home.

A team at Boston University School of Public Health tried asking for one change instead.

Children in an afterschool program were coached to drink fewer sugary drinks and more water.

After a year, their body mass index had moved in a healthier direction compared with children at clubs that ran their usual activities.

“One of the most striking findings from this study is that we were able to shift our study participants’ BMI in a healthier direction at a time when childhood obesity trends nationally were moving the opposite way,” said Monica Wang, the corresponding author and an associate professor of community health sciences.

“That tells us that well-designed, community-based behavioral interventions can make a meaningful difference, even against a difficult broader backdrop.”

In the United States, childhood obesity affects nearly 1 in 5 school-aged children. Sugary drinks include regular soda, fruit-flavored drinks, sports drinks, and energy drinks.

They are the largest source of added sugar in children’s diets, but drinking them may do little to satisfy hunger.

Wang said the single target came from listening to families before the study began.

“Our formative work with families and community partners taught us that asking families to change many dietary behaviors at once can quickly become overwhelming, particularly for families facing competing time and financial pressures,” she said.

The program, called H2GO!, was built with Boys & Girls Clubs of America, which runs afterschool and summer programs at about 5,500 sites. Trained club staff led 12 group sessions over about six weeks.

Kids did taste tests and watched demonstrations of how much sugar a drink holds. They made print, music, and video projects about why water mattered to them.

They took activities home to do with a parent, and the program ended with a community event where they showed their work.

The trial ran from 2020 to 2025 at 11 clubs across Massachusetts. Researchers randomly assigned clubs to offer H2GO! or continue their usual activities, such as lessons on online safety.

In all, 437 children aged 8 to 13 took part, each with a parent or caregiver. About two-thirds qualified for free or reduced-price school lunch.

At the start, about 17% had overweight and about 37% had obesity.

Staff measured each child’s height and weight. The team turned those into a BMI z-score, which shows how far a child’s BMI sits from the average for children of the same age and sex.

Researchers use it to track BMI in children who are still growing.

The average z-score fell by 0.11 among children in the program and rose by 0.08 at the other clubs. On its own, neither change was large enough to rule out chance.

The gap between the two groups was the result the trial was designed to test. It came to 0.19 after a year, a difference the authors reported as statistically significant.

They noted that it is similar to or slightly larger than the effects reported in other childhood obesity prevention trials.

The gap had not appeared at two months or at six. It held when the team left out children who enrolled in 2020, early in the pandemic, and when it accounted for siblings.

One alternative analysis pointed the same way but fell short of significance.

In a further analysis, which the authors label exploratory, the team looked at weight categories.

Among children who started with overweight, 44.4% of those in the program reached the healthy-weight range, compared to 31.6% at comparison clubs.

Fewer of them moved up into obesity, 5.6% compared to 21.1%. Children who began at a healthy weight mostly stayed there.

“Community organizations are critical partners in prevention because they are where children spend time, build relationships, and learn from one another,” Wang said.

Children in the program reported drinking about 3.7 fewer ounces (108 milliliters) of sugary drinks a day after a year. They also reported about 6.6 ounces (196 milliliters) more water.

At the start, the average child reported drinking about 12 ounces (355 milliliters) of sugary drinks a day.

But the difference in drinking between the two groups was not statistically significant. The authors wrote that this calls for caution about what drove the change in BMI.

Children recalled how much they drank, making those estimates less precise than the height and weight measurements.

The authors suggested that the focus on sugar may have shifted other habits too, such as eating sugary foods or getting enough sleep.

Attendance was uneven. Children came to about half of the sessions on average, often missing them for schedule conflicts or illness. About 69% of children were still in the study at 12 months.

Families knew which kind of club they were in. All the clubs were in one state.

One comparison club stopped enrolling partway through and was replaced, and the authors wrote that unmeasured differences between sites may have affected the results.

The team also expected the program to work by boosting children’s sense of empowerment, measured with a survey. It did not find that link.

Next, the researchers want to test the approach in other community settings and on other habits, such as eating ultra-processed foods.

“What I find most encouraging about H2GO! is that it shows we do not have to wait for large-scale policy or environmental change to make progress,” Wang said.

“Those changes are essential, but we can simultaneously give children and families tools to make healthier choices within the environments they live in now.”

The study was funded by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6318. Researchers tested what happens to student grades when schools completely ban cell phones in classrooms

Students who dropped their phones in a box before every lecture earned higher grades, and the phone ban helped struggling students most.

Schools around the world are taking phones away at the classroom door, mostly in the belief that such a ban has to help. Almost no large randomized experiment had tested whether it does. Now one has, and the phones went into wooden boxes.

College students in eastern India who dropped their phones in a box at the start of every lecture finished the semester with slightly higher grades than classmates who kept theirs. Attendance didn’t change, so the researchers read the gain as better attention in class rather than more time in it.

Alp Sungu of the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania led the study. His co-authors were Pradeep Kumar Choudhury of Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi and Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen of the University of Copenhagen.

The trial covered 16,683 students, 742 teachers, and 2,305 courses.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sungu said the gains were largest for lower-performing students, and he was careful about what that means for schools elsewhere.

“That doesn’t guarantee the same ban will work everywhere,” he said. “Banning phones is not a silver bullet, but it is plausibly a simple, low-cost policy lever worth considering.”

The experiment ran at 10 colleges and universities in Odisha, an eastern Indian state of more than 40 million people. There, more than 70 percent of people aged 15 to 29 own a smartphone.

The team had about 1,000 wooden deposit boxes built from recycled materials and put one in every classroom. A full-time research assistant at each campus kept the protocol running.

Departments were split by year of study into 420 groups, and a random draw assigned 198 of them to the ban. In those groups, every student handed over their phone before each lecture for the whole spring semester of 2024, from February to May. The policy wasn’t optional.

Students with a documented emergency or caregiving duty could tell the teacher beforehand, and everyone else went without. Students in the other groups kept their usual access.

The boxes stood in their classrooms too, so the only difference between the two arms was whether a teacher enforced the rule.

The participants averaged 19 years old, ranged from 16 to 22, and about a third were women. Grades came from end-of-semester exams that outside examiners wrote and marked, with no devices allowed for either group.

Across everyone in the trial, the ban raised grades by a small amount. It came to about a third of the difference that a very good teacher, rather than an average one, makes over a school year.

That puts it in the same range as large curriculum reforms and teacher training programs, which the authors use as the benchmark.

The average hides where the change happened. Students whose earlier grades fell below the middle of the pack improved, and so did first-year undergraduates.

Students who were already doing well, postgraduates, and students in science, technology, engineering, and math fields showed no measurable change.

Because the weakest students moved most, the spread of grades grew less in the banned classrooms than in the others. Attendance, measured from the colleges’ own records, didn’t shift in either direction.

The grades themselves are hard to inflate.

Under Odisha’s rules, 60 to 80 percent of each course mark comes from external exams graded off-site by people who don’t know the student. The ban’s effect was largest in non-STEM courses, where that outside share is 80 percent.

So teachers going easy on their own students is an unlikely explanation, though the authors couldn’t rule it out entirely.

A subset of 2,557 students answered two surveys over the semester. Students who had spent the term under the ban became more supportive of phone restrictions than those who hadn’t.

They also rated the restrictions as more beneficial and were less likely to want a classroom with no rules at all.

Given five options, from an all-day ban to no ban, the banned students favored stricter policies than the control group did, with the biggest shift toward an all-day ban. The trial only ever tested a lecture-only ban.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him about how students felt, Sungu pointed to that shift in support. “That’s encouraging for implementation, since policies students support are easier to sustain,” he said.

The surveys found no change in how distracted students felt, how much they thought they were learning, their well-being, or their motivation. Students under the ban reported a mild rise in the fear of missing out, and no change in how much time they spent on their phones.

Women in the banned groups backed the policy more strongly, while men reported a small rise in missing-out feelings and in screen time.

Research assistants also made random spot checks, glancing into each classroom through a window or doorway and ticking off a list of behaviors without interrupting the lecture.

In banned classrooms, they recorded less disruptive behavior and less chatter unrelated to the lesson, and teachers who were busier keeping order and more engaged with their material.

The checks also caught something the team hadn’t planned to measure. “To our surprise, our random classroom spot checks showed that teachers also used their phones in class, and the ban reduced their phone use as well,” Sungu told Earth.com. Teachers were never subject to the rule themselves.

One reading came out the other way. To the observers, students in banned classrooms looked more distracted than students who had their phones.

The authors suggested that with the phone gone, a student’s attention goes to whatever is next most noticeable, such as background noise. That kind of restlessness is easier for an observer to spot.

The students in this trial were in college, having already passed entrance hurdles, and the policy fight in most countries is about younger children.

Since first-year students and weaker students gained most, the authors think the effect could be larger at earlier ages, but that remains to be tested. The study itself ran for one semester in one Indian state.

The ban covered lectures only. Whether a bell-to-bell ban, phones locked away through breaks as well, changes how students treat each other or use their phones at home is an open question.

So is whether the result holds in richer countries, where students often have other devices alongside the phone.

Sungu’s next question is about a different technology. “There have been recent proposals to ban AI in classrooms, but such bans could be a double-edged sword, and we need more scientific evidence to guide policy,” he said.

He also named delaying young people’s exposure to social media and AI companions as an area worth studying.

Until a trial like this one runs in a middle school, the evidence for phone bans rests on a semester of wooden boxes in Odisha. It also rests on students who ended that semester more in favor of the rule than their classmates who kept their phones.

The full study was published in the journal Science.
