#6252. The 50 Best Restaurants For 2026 Have Been Announced—With a Remote European Spot in First Place

The 50 Best Restaurants for 2026 have just been announced as part of a prestigious awards ceremony in Lima on Wednesday, November 5, 2026. As with every year, we wait for the release—an indicator of which restaurants will be topping travelers' lists in the year ahead, and the trends that will shape the experiences they offer. Below, we cover which restaurant snagged the top spot, which restaurant led on every continent, and the industry stars celebrated with individual awards like Best Pastry Chef, Best Sommelier, and more.

Read on for the full list, and notable takeaways from the winners. (For more on the trends revealed at the Lima event, read our reporter's conversation with winning chefs here.)

The Best Restaurant in the World for 2026 is hidden away in sleepy Basque village, Axpe.

Climbing up from its number two spot in last year's list, this year’s winner is Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, in Spain's Basque Country.

Basque wood-fired cooking is at the heart of this rustic fine-dining restaurant. Chef-owner Víctor Arguinzoniz (also known as Bittor Arginzoniz) is considered a pioneer of grilling and live-fire cooking. At Asador Etxebarri, every course of Bittor Arginzoniz's €300 euro (about $337 USD) tasting menu touches the wood and charcoal grills—from Palamós red prawns to smoked milk ice cream.

Hidden away in the sleepy mountain village of Axpe, about 45 minutes by car from Bilbao, foodies have been making the pilgrimage to try Arguinzoniz's signature grilled dishes since the restaurant opened in 1990. It's been an 18-year journey to the top, as Asador Etxebarri has been a mainstay on The World's 50 Best Restaurants list since 2008, starting at number 44.

Once a restaurant gets the coveted number-one trophy, it is ineligible for nomination in forthcoming years—with the intention of allowing other restaurants a chance to earn top billing. Top-placing restaurants are then inducted into a new list, called the Best of the Best. This list includes such legendary eateries as Chef Thomas Keller's The French Laundry in Yountville, California, and Disfrutar in Barcelona, Spain. Last year’s winner, Maido in Lima, Peru, is the most recent inductee to this prestigious list.

It’s tempting to imagine the enviable job held by a panel of judges that sample every restaurant in the world. But that’s not quite how the 50 Best works. Rather, the 50 is an international media company that taps the expertise of over a thousand hospitality experts from around the world to weigh in on the industry that they know best. Chefs, restaurateurs, food journalists, and well-traveled gourmets all anonymously nominate restaurants that they have dined at within the last 18 months. (Members can’t vote for a restaurant they have a financial interest in.) Professional services consultancy Deloitte has access to the voting data to ensure the validity and fairness of the process.

Because of the voting-style nature of the awards, a restaurant might fall off the list one year only to return later. This year, previous entries to the list such as The Ledbury—a fine-dining beauty in London, United Kingdom where chef Brett Graham marries British produce, Japanese flavours, and French culinary techniques—returns to the list in the number 83 spot. Similarly, Luxe Mosu in Seoul, South Korea—home to chef Sung Anh's elevated interpretations of traditional Korean fare—returns to the list at number 78.

“Every year The 50 Best Restaurants list gives us a snapshot of where more than 1,100 individuals who live and breathe this industry have had their most memorable restaurant experiences over the previous 18 months," explains Rikki Tidball, managing director of awards and rankings for The 50. “And I think that’s what makes it so special. Each Academy member votes independently, so nobody at The 50 or any of our partners has a say in who makes the list, and restaurants can’t nominate themselves. This means every restaurant on the list has genuinely earned it.”

Gaggan in Bangkok climbed up to Number 2 after placing at Number 6 the year prior.

As always, the highest-ranking restaurants on each continent have been given a special mention during tonight's awards—and there are a few repeats from last year. Gaggan in Bangkok (this year's number 2) won the best restaurant in Asia again. Mexico City's Quintonil (4) was the best restaurant in Latin America again, while New York City's Atomix (11) was the best restaurant in North America. Dubai's Trèsind Studio (28) was named the best restaurant in the Middle East for another year. The best restaurant in Africa was Cape Town's La Colombe (35). Sydney's Saint Peter (50) was the best restaurant in Oceania, while top spot Asador Etxebarri took the best restaurant in Europe award.

Every year, the panel awards special prizes to chefs, front-of-house staff, and activists who are leading the charge in hospitality. In 2026, the Best Female Chef Award went to Jessica Rosval, head chef of Al Gatto Verde. Bangkok’s Dej Kewkacha won Best Pastry Chef Award, and Lesley Liu of Odette in Singapore won the Best Sommelier Award while the Estrella Damm Chefs' Choice Award went to Junghyun ‘JP’ Park from Atomix in New York City. Doris Lam won The 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship. Spanish chef Ferran Adrià of El Bulli won the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Restaurants given a special mention during the 2026 ceremony included Tuju in São Paulo, which earned the Highest New Entry Award. Copenhagen's Kadeau won the Highest Climber Award after soaring 33 places this year, and Naar in Kasauli, India, won the Sustainable Restaurant Award.

This year, only one US restaurant made the top 50: Atomix, in New York. It came in 11th place, rising one place from 2025, when it ranked 12.

#6251. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

Laura Burns is a frequent traveller with an affinity for fine coffee, delicious food and the world's most beautiful sights. If she's writing about it, it's worth exploring. Happiest in Tokyo, Melbourne,... More by Laura Burns

This method sounds as irritating as the coupon-book BS. As soon as you use a benefit, you are dinged for it.

#6250. American Airlines business class to Prague for just 55,000 points: Here's how you can do it, too

It's not often that you can fly from the U.S. to Europe in business class for just 55,000 points, but sometimes, deals are out there — especially if you use American Airlines AAdvantage miles or Atmos Rewards points.

I found a great award using Atmos Rewards Points on American Airlines' newly resumed nonstop flight from Philadelphia to Prague. As mentioned, I paid just 55,000 points (and $5.60 in taxes and fees).

I'll get into some detail on how to find these kinds of deals, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

I wanted the chance to check American's European service and compare the business-class products on the older 787-8s (like the one I flew to Prague) and the new premium-heavy 787-9P planes I've flown to London.

American Airlines relaunched its Prague service in May of this year. It had previously served the route for a few years, in 2018 and 2019, before abandoning it during the coronavirus pandemic.

AA now operates the route seasonally during the busy summer period, from May to October, between Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) and Václav Havel Airport Prague (PRG). The airline has already said the route will return for summer 2027.

Another good sign for the route: AA is adding more European destinations from Philadelphia next summer, including Vienna and Porto, Portugal. American Airlines calls Prague part of "the airline's Central European network."

I kicked off my journey with a few days in Philadelphia before heading to the airport.

A post shared by Clint Page Henderson (@clintpage1)

American Airlines' Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia opened in May of last year, after years of delays. It is a lovely space to spend a few hours before your flight, though it can get crowded at times. I could access it because I was flying long-haul business class.

A great American Airlines agent named Thomas Doersam, who has been with AA for 38 years, gave me a quick tour of the Flagship and the adjacent Admirals Club.

The Flagship lounge (American's fifth) is near Gate A15, where AA's long-haul flights depart. Eligible passengers flying long-haul business class can use the Flagship Lounge, which includes those in business class on these flights.

Others have access to the Admiral's Club just across the way.

It has been lovely to see American Airlines invest so much in its lounge product. In fact, a sixth Flagship lounge was announced for Charlotte, along with a massive new Admiral's Club that will clock in at more than 40,000 square feet.

I had seat 1L on this 11-year-old Boeing 787 Dreamliner, with the ship number N806AA. This is a legacy interior that will eventually be phased out.

TPG reported that these planes will receive new Flagship business-class suites and a full cabin refresh, though AA didn't say when that would start.

I was on the smallest Dreamliner variant, and the business-class cabin had just 20 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration. All the seats had aisle access.

These lie-flat seats were 21 inches wide and featured American's version of the Safran Concept D seat (formerly known as Zodiac).

I found them to be fairly comfortable, if a bit narrow, during the overnight journey.

Some flyers complain about these seats since some are rear-facing. The seats are attached to each other, and some people say they feel it when the person seated next to them moves. (Some flyers even refer to them as "rocking chairs.") It never bothered me on my previous trips in these seats, and it didn't this time either, even though I was in the first row.

There were also 28 premium economy seats on this plane — a comfortable and potentially more affordable option.

There were also 186 economy seats, including 48 Main Cabin Extra seats.

Inflight entertainment was provided by a 15-inch screen that could pop out with the push of a button. There were plenty of shows and movies to choose from.

Still, these screens are showing their age, especially now that more innovative 4K screens are rolling out across many fleets (including American's).

Inflight Wi-Fi was provided by Panasonic and cost $35 for the full flight. It was just OK, and I was glad I wasn't relying on it for important work. American Airlines will begin rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi in 2027, but in the meantime, representatives say there are plans to improve Wi-Fi speeds on its 787s, too. I expect the overall tech picture to improve dramatically over the next few years.

The airlines have had some pretty major connection problems recently.

Remember, these seats are a decade old and show a bit of wear and tear. Still, it's a comfortable cabin, and because there are so few business-class seats, it does feel a bit special.

My seat had plenty of other bells and whistles that I won't go into too much detail here, but I appreciated the overhead air vents and some of the nooks and crannies for storing items.

I also loved American's newer bedding. The zipper bag held a large blanket and pillow; mattress pads were also available at each seat. While it may not look as fancy as United's Saks bedding, I found it super comfortable.

Amenity kits were made in honor of the World Cup, featuring a clear design filled with standard amenities.

You can read more details about the hard product on these planes in the reviews linked above, but I think, in general, I'm a bigger fan than most when it comes to the seats on these Dreamliners.

As I mentioned, I don't mind the older 787s, but there's no question: American's new 787Ps are a fresher product.

TPG's Eric Rosen and I reviewed the new product last year, and we were both pretty impressed. AA unveiled its all-new Flagship Suite business class in May, and Eric and I were eager to experience the new planes and try out the Flagship Suite Preferred and Flagship Suite business-class seats. He took a flight from London to Chicago, and I was flying from Chicago to London.

Unlike the 787-8s, which have just 20 business-class seats, the new 787Ps have a whopping 51 Flagship Suites.

It will be interesting to see whether AA expands the business-class and premium-class cabins during the retrofit of these planes.

You can really see the differences in the photos below.

Aside from the size of the business-class cabin, the biggest difference is the sliding doors on the 787Ps.

There are eight Flagship Suite Preferred seats on the 787Ps — an upgraded version of the new suites with additional space.

Finally, the new 787Ps have updated designs, more storage, a lounger mode on the seat controls, wireless charging and dramatically better 17.3-inch IFE screens with both Bluetooth and touchscreen capability.

While I love the new planes, I wouldn't choose a more expensive redemption just to fly them.

I had a great crew on my flight to Prague, with friendly service and generally good food and beverage.

Not only did we get a predeparture beverage, but service was prompt, friendly and efficient.

Dinner started with warmed nuts and a beverage of your choice. Appetizers included a small romaine salad, along with citrus-poached shrimp and ceviche-style fish. For a main course, I finally tried American Airlines' new "sliders and fries." It was only available as a pre-order, but I'm so glad I took the time to select it because it was delicious.

Dessert was the classic sundae which I ordered with extra whipped cream. How can you resist?

Breakfast was yogurt with granola and fruit that AA calls a "fresh fruit bowl" — perfectly fine for an airplane breakfast. The best part was the multiple cappuccinos I drank. (American brought back espresso drinks in business class in 2025, and I've made full use of the perk.)

I even received a thank-you note from my flight attendant, Daniel — a rare and lovely touch that I don't often find with U.S. airlines.

As I mentioned, I scored my business-class seat for just 55,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in taxes and fees. Remember, you can book American Airlines flights using Alaska points, and it can often be an even better deal.

Related: Why American Airlines AAdvantage has become my most valuable rewards currency

Often, when a new route is launched or resumed, you'll see airlines make award tickets more available than usual. That's just what happened here, when the airline made business-class redemptions on both Prague and its newly resumed Budapest route widely available, even on partners like Alaska.

When a new route starts or an old one resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

To start, flexibility is key. If you can be flexible on dates and destinations, the world literally opens up. Let the deal guide where you go.

Try booking as soon as schedules open up. For carriers like Japan Airlines, you'll find the best availability 11 months in advance, as that's when seats open to partner airlines.

Award search tools have also become a huge part of my process. Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel are my favorites. I also love the award tool Points Path, which sits on my browser, so I see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

American Airlines also has a great tool that I use to find deals. I use the airline's award search calendar to find business-class seats for months at a time. Here's an example of that for flights from New York City to Rome, Paris and Amsterdam for next year.

I wouldn't book any of these because of the high taxes and fees for partner awards, but it at least gives an idea of what's out there.

My last suggestion: Keep checking flights in case the price drops.

Sometimes, it can make sense to lock in a coach redemption and then keep checking to see if business class opens up at a reasonable rate.

If you are willing to be brave, more availability often opens up at the last minute, and you can find some great deals.

#6249. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.

#6248. I Found $1.70 Burritos At Denver Airport. Thank You, Taco Bell.

While I usually just make a beeline for the Capital One Lounge while in Denver International Airport, I recently noticed that Taco Bell is back…now airside instead of landside..and from a cost perspective, probably the best deal for food in DEN.

If you’ve flown from Denver for years, you might remember that there used to be a Taco Bell in the Jeppesen Terminal in the food court above the security checkpoint. At some point that closed while the airport was refurbishing that area and did not re-open.

But was I (very pleasantly) surprised to see a Taco Bell Cantina in Concourse A (near Gates A47 and A49) during a recent trip through DEN. I had no idea!

Even better? The prices were street pricing, not airport pricing. $1.70 for a burrito? What a lovely way to get your junk food fix without breaking the bank.

And street pricing not ubiquitous in the airport. I had a salad with some pulled brisket at Brothers BBQ and it was almost $20….

I also want to note that I tried the more “local” option, called Denver Street Eats, located in The B Gates, which offers street tacos. A steak taco was $6.25. That may seem reasonable at first glance, but it was just a small flour tortilla with very little to it: a bit of steak, a couple spinach leaves, and a few tiny slices of picked onions. It was good, but sorry, Taco Bell is better.

So if you’re looking for an affordable meal at Denver Airport, Taco Bell is your best bet.

And for new readers, yes, I have a strong affinity for Taco Bell…wherever I am in the world. Check out the archive.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

I was going to patiently wait for LALF Taco Bell analysis after this morning’s VFTW “should Denver Taco Bell workers get paid while they are standing in the security line” analysis of state labor law disguised as an article, but oh man, never expected this. 10 points to LALF.

And this comment is not taking a position on whether those workers deserve security line pay, nor is it taking a position with respect to whether the $1.70 burrito price will now have to rise should those workers receive increased compensation. It is simply an acknowledgement of a 10 out of 10 counterpoint to the VFTW article, replete with competing Mexican food analysis and consumer guidance, all from TB’s #1 fan. As the stock ticker says, YUM.

LOL. Seriously, is this all just sponsored content?

This is awesome to know…an alternative to the C1 and UC lounges!

I used to fly through Detroit a lot and went to the Taco Bell airside. 99 cent bean burritos. That wasn’t in the days of the DC-6 but in the current Delta terminal. I tend to never eat fast food except while traveling.

Cheaper at DEN than most places in LA 😀 !

I love it, please use the kiosk to order so we can save on labor, but kiosks don’t take currency, so we’ll charge you to use a credit card. At least no tip prompt (unless I missed it).

Matthew, Taco Bell taco explains perfectly why on my flight departing DEN, you took up one of the toilets for the entire flight!

#6247. The Food Trends We’ll See in 2027, According to the World’s 50 Best Chefs

On November 4, Lima, Peru, was a playground for global palates. Star chefs from across the world flocked to the culinary hotspot for the 50 Best Restaurants 2026, a prestigious awards ceremony that crowns the top restaurants around the globe based on anonymous nominations from over a thousand industry experts. Restaurant Asador Etxebarri, which is located in Spain's Basque Country, won top billing as the World’s Best Restaurant 2026 at the event held at the ornate Teatro Municipal de Lima. And before the winners took the stage, we were on the ground as Lima and its top restaurants buzzed with excitement all week.

In addition to knowing which spots came out on top, we also wanted to understand what these results signaled about dining in the year ahead—so we asked chefs for their hot takes. After the plates, tastings, and pisco sours (so many pisco sours), these the top dining trends and places to look for in 2027, according to the world's best chefs.

Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants in 2026 here.

Lobster from Kjolle in Lima, which was just named No.7 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list.

Chef-owner Pía León of Kjolle in Lima—a fine-dining wonder that showcases the megadiversity of the host nation with startlingly beautiful tasting odysseys—snagged the number seven spot this year, making it the top restaurant in the host country. With the global spotlight on her, León looks to the growing importance of knowing specifically where your food comes from, beyond just a vague sense of ‘local.’ “To me, traceability means understanding where each ingredient comes from, who produces it, and the knowledge behind it,” she told Condé Nast Traveler. “Many of the products we work with come from local producers and communities who have kept their techniques alive for many years. As cooks, we have a responsibility to recognize their work and the value of what they grow.”

It’s a feeling that chef and co-owner Josh Niland of Sydney's Saint Peter (which also appeared on our 2025 Hot List of the best new restaurants in the world) emphasizes even further. The restaurant, founded by chef-owner Niland and his wife Julie Niland, focuses on whole-fish cookery and placed at number 50 this year, also earning the title of Best Restaurant in Oceania. “I think it [will be] ridiculous,” he says, if, in 10 years, restaurants are not telling us exactly on paper where things are from. “Like I think it's non-negotiable,” he said. “If you're writing a menu right now, let alone 10 years from now, I want to know why I'm paying $60, $70 for this chicken. Where is it from? That's how I feel about it. You know, we've got QR codes on the menu that you can scan and watch a fisherman pull a fish out of the water. Like, that's probably a very drastic leap, but I feel like that's where, to a degree, the premium end of dining needs to be. We need to be incredibly transparent about our labor, how we're paying people, like where things are from, all that.”

Saint Peter in Sydney came in at No. 50 on the list, and was named the Best Restaurant in Oceania.

At New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen—number eight on the list and also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June—head chef and co-owner Nicolai Nørregaard plays with time, drawing on both seasonal, hyper-local fresh produce, and preserved beauties from seasons past. Kadeau—where the team includes chef Francisco “Pancho” Cardenas supervising the kitchen, and Kyumin Hahn serving as partner—also won the Highest Climber award for jumping from number 41 in 2025 to its placement this year.

La Colombe in Cape Town debuted a Secret Cellar in 2024, an intimate subterranean enclave where guests hand over their phones before the meal begins. While chef James Gaag understands that some people want to take photos of their food—and certainly that Instagram traffic helps restaurants—he hopes for, but isn't counting on, more phone-free restaurant experiences.

So what, exactly, does “seasonality” mean when the seasons seem so different lately? Condé Nast Traveler asked Nørregaard just how climate change is impacting the menu, and what adjustments the team is making: “Some meals are shit,” Nørregaard said, “or some ingredients that we are relying on [are], so we need to change plans. But then maybe something else is in abundance, and then we just switch to that direction.” During Kadeau’s growing season, when it relies on produce from its garden on the Danish island of Bornholm and from what can be foraged nearby, adding more nutrients and water to the soil allows them to step in and give Mother Nature a helping hand, ensuring a better product. During the preservation season, in the colder months, the team showcases products like preserved onion that have been stored since spring and summer—but even that process is changing. Take the pine cone: A dry year might produce very few of the beauties, while a wet year will see abundance. “We sometimes need to think ahead and plan two years in advance,” he continued. “So we have to preserve something for more than one season because it might not come the next season.”

Around the globe, more nimble menus—shifting ingredients, planning well ahead of time—are on the way to account for increasingly unpredictable weather. This is a further expression of adaptations already underway, including a reduced focus on meat, due to its environmental impacts, and broadened waste-reduction efforts. For diners, this means that no two tasting menus, even at the same restaurant, may be exactly the same; that talked-about dish may be swapped out for something else when the seasons or weather requires. But this commitment to the best, and the possibility for newness on menus, presents an arguably more interesting fine dining experience. Each menu, and dish, may represent a singular moment in time.

The Sardine Pie at New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen, which placed number eight on the list.

Kadeau was also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June.

Sprawling menus as an indicator of abundance; dozens of items on a single plate—foams, sauces, sprigs of herbs placed with tweezers; narrative-driven tasting menus that span six or seven hours. These used to scream luxury. Now? Simplicity speaks louder. It’s a trend noted by executive chef James Gaag of La Colombe in the Constantia Valley near Cape Town, owned by chef-proprietor Scot Kirton. La Colombe landed at number 35 and also took home the title of Best Restaurant in Africa.

La Colombe in South Africa placed No. 35 on the list.

At La Colombe and elsewhere, Gaag is energized by “less courses, fresher courses, lighter courses, less time at the table.” His innovative menus might be inspired by both his German upbringing and world travels, but that doesn’t mean trying to fit the entire globe in one menu. “We used to put 100 ingredients on each plate, and I think the longer I run the restaurant, the more confident I am in putting less on the plate,” he continued.

Chef Jeremy Chan, who owns Michelin-starred Ikoyi in London with co-founder Iré Hassan-Odukale, continues to rise. Ikoyi landed at number 48 this year, owing to its contemporary global menu that is inspired by both British microseasonality and meticulously sourced global spices. For Chan, though, fine dining doesn’t mean frigid. “Fine dining is about creating a refined experience, rather than a sense of preciousness or formality,” he told Condé Nast Traveler. “For me, it is about the refinement and technique of the craft, alongside the responsibility and precision in what we do to make people feel special.”

Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Royer, placed at number 15 this year—one of the many high-ranking spots across Asia, including Gaggan in Bangkok (number 2, and also the Best Restaurant in Asia), Wing in Hong Kong (number 5), and the Chairman (number 6), also in Hong Kong. Condé Nast Traveler asked Chef de Cuisine Sheng Xiong—who blends his Asian heritage with French training for Odette’s menus—if there’s a fine dining trend he’d be happy to see vanish. “You mean we’re going to lose our jobs?” He joked. After his laughter subsided, the chef at the Three Michelin-starred restaurant echoed Chan’s sentiments: “I think moving forward, maybe the white-glove service [will go], because in our restaurant we treat everyone coming in like [they are] coming back home as a family member. It can be a bit too casual sometimes, and at the same time, it makes them feel comfortable. Guests are happy. At the start, Singaporeans, the older generation couldn't understand what we are doing, but as time goes by, they actually prefer that to a very stiff kind of environment.”

A Bluefin Tuna Rhubarb dish at London's Ikoyi, which landed at No. 48 on the list this year.

Chef Niko Romito of the lauded, three Michelin-starred Reale—which placed at number 27 this year—is seeing a difference in the way travelers experience his restaurant. Reale, which he co-owns with his sister Cristiana Romito, sits within a 16th-century monastery nestled in a remote medieval town in Abruzzo, Italy. As Niko Romito explained to Condé Nast Traveler, because of Reale’s remote location, tourists would often get there at the tail-end of a food tour of Italy—a tough situation to be in, when perhaps a meal at the end of a trip might feel less memorable after a string of stellar meals. “Today, it’s the exact opposite,” Romito said. “The location—tucked away in the provinces—was once a major limitation. Yet, this very constraint pushed me to create a style of cooking that transcends the distance, making the journey—the hours spent in the car—fully justified. I could say that the region where I live, Abruzzo, is beginning to emerge as a top destination for tourists. A territory rich in nature, parks, and hidden gems.”

At Singapore's Odette, number 15 on the list, Kampot Pepper Crusted Pigeon is served.

Inside Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Roye

Many restaurants within this year’s list support the growing trend that rurally set tasting menus are sometimes more interesting than their big-city counterparts, luring an increasing number of diners. This year’s number one restaurant and also the Best Restaurant in Europe is Asador Etxebarri, which calls Atxondo, a village of less than 1,500 inhabitants in Spain’s Basque Country, home. Vyn, the number 23 restaurant, is located within a pastoral fishing village of about 7,000 people in southern Sweden. While Naar, number 50 and also the winner for this year’s Sustainable Restaurant Award, sees diners traveling deep into the foothills of the Himalayas for its open-flame-cooked dishes. As food tourism continues to boom, expect even more meteoric restaurants to shine from beyond bustling metropolitan areas.

Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 here.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6246. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

It’s one thing to read about an exciting welcome offer and another to see what it can actually do in real life. So when the IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (see rates and fees) launched with a generous limited-time launch offer, I mapped it onto a weekend in New York City with my mom.

The card, now open to applicants, comes with a launch offer of 200,000 bonus points, earned after you spend $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening (apply by Nov. 18, 2026). Beyond the bonus, its benefits include automatic Platinum Elite status and up to $300 per year in food and beverage rewards at IHG Hotels.

But the real question for many IHG fans is how the welcome offer, benefits and earning rates stack up against an actual getaway.

My mom and I recently spent a mother-daughter weekend in New York City, staying two nights at the Kimpton Era Midtown New York and spending Saturday soaking up the city's art and culture. If you’re considering this card, here’s how our trip played out so you can see just how far all of these perks can go.

My mom had not visited New York in a long time, and I wanted to make sure we were right in the middle of the action while also being near great dining and activities. The Kimpton Era Midtown, which opened in early 2026 in a 33-story tower on West 48th Street, proved to be the perfect home base for us. The Theater District was within walking distance, and we were able to grab a quick subway ride uptown to the Met.

Our two-night weekend stay in New York would have cost 64,600 points per night, or 129,200 points total — versus $1,354 (including taxes and fees) if we'd paid cash.

That means the 200,000-point welcome offer would have covered our entire stay, and I would still have 70,800 points left over to put toward a future trip.

One thing to keep in mind: While we only had a weekend, you can plan a longer trip and take advantage of the fourth-night-free benefit (redeem points for three consecutive nights, get the fourth free) to make your points go even further.

Plus, each year on your cardholder anniversary, you get one free night certificate worth up to 60,000 points. If a night costs more than 60,000 points, IHG allows you to top off the additional points you need. For my stay at the Kimpton Era Midtown, I would have only needed an additional 4,600 points to cover one night, which would have been easy to earn as someone who frequently stays at IHG properties.

Nothing makes me feel more like a VIP at an IHG Hotel than my Platinum Elite Status. Cardholders get automatic IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite status for as long as they keep the card. That comes with perks such as room upgrades and early check-in when available.

Thanks to my loyalty, I applied for a Confirmable Suite Upgrade, one of the Milestone Rewards IHG One Rewards members can choose after reaching certain night thresholds in a calendar year. That means we checked in knowing a premium high-floor room with a view of the Empire State Building was waiting for us.

The surprises and delights didn’t end there, though. We were also given a welcome amenity as a thank-you for my status. I had the option to choose between 5,000 bonus points or a welcome beverage. I usually opt for points when I stay with IHG, but since we were celebrating our mother-daughter weekend, we decided to have some fun and treat ourselves to the welcome drinks.

One of the coolest perks on the IHG Premier Select Card is the $300 in annual Food and Beverage Rewards at IHG hotels, issued as a $75 voucher each calendar quarter. So before heading out for a full day of adventuring on Saturday, my mom and I enjoyed an awesome breakfast at Bar Rocco, and the $75 voucher would have covered our entire meal.

It’s important to note that any charges paid with a Food and Beverage Reward don't earn IHG points, but there are also a few other rules worth knowing to get the most out of this perk:

I booked our round-trip nonstop flights from Orlando International Airport (MCO) to LaGuardia Airport (LGA) directly with JetBlue for $422.85 per person. The IHG Premier Select Card offers a $200 statement credit each calendar year when you spend at least $250 on flights booked directly with an airline through Dec. 31, 2027.

Unlike some travel credits that tie you to a single carrier or a booking portal, this one works with any airline as long as you book directly, as I did. Plus, it’s a win-win because the remaining balance can be paid with the IHG Premier Select Card and earn 6 points per dollar since it counts as a travel purchase.

A weekend in New York City goes beyond the hotel stay. The IHG Premier Select Card helps you earn rewards on your flights, hotel stays and everything in between. This card gets you:

And these earning rates worked out well for our trip, right down to the experiences.

We spent Saturday morning at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where admission for the two of us came to $60, and admired works by my personal favorite painter, Claude Monet, and explored the Temple of Dendur.

Our biggest splurge of the weekend, though, was on two tickets to see "Hamilton" at the Richard Rodgers Theatre, totaling $560. This was a real treat because original Broadway cast member Christopher Jackson (George Washington) temporarily rejoined for a limited engagement.

Since the IHG Premier Select Card earns 3 points per dollar on all other purchases, it will help you make the most of those experiences (and your souvenirs) too.

Our mother-daughter New York City weekend getaway is exactly the kind of trip that the new IHG One Rewards Premier Select Card was built for. And the welcome offer is the best way to make the most of it.

Right now, new cardholders can earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, but this limited-time launch offer is only available to those who apply by Nov. 18, 2026.

Beyond the welcome offer, the card's earning rates and benefits, such as the food and beverage reward and the $200 airline credit, keep the value coming long after you’ve used your points.

So if you stay at IHG hotels even a couple of times a year, then this card will likely be worth your while — and now is the perfect time to apply.

#6244. American Airlines Vs. United First Class: Boring Chicken Dinners That I’d Happily Order Again

I realize if you just read my blog it looks like I’ll eat anything thrown in front of me and to some extent that is true on airplane, but a pair of flights, one on American Airlines, the other on United Airlines, featured chicken dinners much closer to my what I usually eat at home. Let’s compare them in this week’s Meal of the Week.

Let’s start with American Airlines. I was flying from Los Angeles to Chicago and received a same-day upgrade (as a mere Advantage Gold!) and thus was not able to pre-ordered. Onboard the choices were chicken or pasta (described as a chicken breast with rice or pasta shells with tomato sauce). I chose chicken.

The chicken breast was covered in a white sauce and served with white rice on the side and green beans on top. On the side, a small green salad with sun-dried tomatoes and a ramekin with what appeared to be parsnips, carrots, and cabbage with croutons…at least I think so (whatever it was, it was nice).

While not an exciting dinner, I really appreciated just eating a lean chicken breast and green beans…it’s very similar to what we eat at least a couple nights per week at home.

Dessert was raspberry sorbet…I miss the Häagen-Dazs ice cream that used to be on these flights (and the real ice cream sundaes before that).

On to United. Same route. The current “signature entree” out of Los Angeles is described as:

Pollo asado chicken thigh Pollo asado chicken thigh with charred corn farro, street corn style zucchini and asado sauce

The AA dish was fine, but this folks was excellent. The flavor of the chicken was excellent and the corn farro and zucchini were really nice…we grow zucchini in our garden at home and cook it in the oven with our chicken so this really felt close to home. The corn was a nice treat and I ate every bit of it.

The sale on the side had sun-dried tomatoes and sliced cucumbers and the meal also came with a cornmeal roll and a slice of “hot chocolate” cheesecake, which I passed on.

Both were rather boring meals, but both were very delicious. Simple is often better.

My Meal of the Week feature examines an airline meal from my travels over the years. This may be a meal from earlier in the week or it may be a meal served over a decade ago.

#6243. Ask a Local: Where to Go in Nairobi According to Runner Emily Chepkor

"Nairobi is a city best understood in motion," says Emily Chepkor, founder of We Run Nairobi, the city's biggest and most popular run club. She's from a small town in Kenya, Kapsabet, that has produced more world-class runners per square mile than anywhere else on earth. While the country is known worldwide for its running heritage, Nairobi hadn't quite caught up to the hype until Chepkor came along.

She runs as a hobby, and is a 12-time marathoner (and two-time Boston qualifier) who felt that, though Kenya's running reputation was unmatched internationally, the runner lifestyle itself wasn't accessible to everyday Kenyans—elite athletes only. She set out to change that and bring running closer to all Nairobians, starting with a weekly run club that began with just her and three friends. It slowly grew through word of mouth and especially TikTok, into something bigger, built on a simple idea: no registration, no fees, you just show up and run alongside Emily.

That run has become a defining weekly ritual for Nairobians, drawing over 1,200 people every Saturday morning. It's now etched into the city's identity. The same way New York is known for its bagels, Nairobi is known for the We Run Nairobi neighborhood runs, a cultural landmark for locals and tourists alike.

Below, Emily tells us about some of her favorite things to do in the city she calls home.

Karura Forest is “without a doubt” the best place to run in Nairobi, if you ask Emily.

"Karura Forest, without a doubt, is the most scenic route in the city”, she says. “I run the Sigiria side, through Gate F; it's quieter, more canopied. My dog Biscuit and I do the 10-kilometer loop most Sundays, crossing little rivers every kilometer. If you want something gentler, the 5-kilometer route is just as lovely." Her Saturday club runs the same way: "We're completely pace-agnostic. First-timers run next to marathoners".

Karura is the second largest urban forest in the world after the Tijuca Forest in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and provides the perfect place for an outdoor run.

“Kengele's is always a safe bet whatever's on, whether it's World Cup, rugby, athletics, you'll find a good crowd," says Chepkor. "What I love is how the embassies get involved: around big sporting events, they'll partner with venues across the city to host public watch parties. I'll never forget the British High Commission's watch party in Karura Forest, the day Sebastian Sawe broke the two-hour marathon barrier. The whole country was locked in, and experiencing that moment surrounded by hundreds of people felt incredibly special.”

The McMillan Memorial Library is one of her favorite places for some peace and quiet, and some history.

“The McMillan Memorial Library is a perfect little time capsule of Nairobi, architecturally and literally—it's currently being renovated by Book Bunk, founded by two Kenyan women committed to restoring our public libraries," she says. "I also love the Nairobi Gallery, home to Point Zero, the spot from which all distances in Kenya are measured.”

“Tigoni is a small town only 30 to 40 minutes from Nairobi, but it feels much farther away. The city gives way to rolling tea plantations and narrow country roads. I start at Brackenhurst with coffee from Muna Tree Cafe on the terrace, then rent a bicycle and ride through the plantations, stopping wherever the view is too good to pass.” Back at Brackenhurst, she'll spread a blanket on the lawn to read, maybe doze off, then finish with tennis or a walk through the Indigenous forest. "It's the itinerary I'm proudest to take an out-of-towner on," Chepkor says.

"Sigiria Coffee House is my default—small, intimate, and full of dogs on Sunday mornings. On tennis mornings it's Waitabit, same easy vibe." For souvenirs, she sends visitors to two spots near each other: "Spinners Web has beautiful rugs, a café, and a used-books library. Just up the road, Tribal Gallery has grander pieces—restored Swahili doors, oversized mirrors—alongside smaller suitcase-friendly finds like ceramics and jewelry."

"Fig & Olive in Tigoni is part bodega, part restaurant, with a lawn where no one blinks if you swap your chair for the grass. In the city, it's the Tin Roof Café in Karen—moving from table to grass and back, especially post-run, and the salad bar is iconic. For something dressier that still softens outdoors, Matteo's: white tablecloths, al fresco seating, and little intimate corners I'm still discovering."

The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart.

Scoring a place by the fireplace is a coup.

"The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart. Scoring a corner table by the fireplace on a chilly evening is a date-night dream. For something more stylish, Inti has skyline views in every direction—some Friday nights it turns into an intimate DJ set." For the rest of the evening, she splits the city in two: “If you're after energy, Geco, alive with Nairobi's music scene, especially on Wednesdays. For actual conversation, Cave-à-Manger has an expansive wine list and keeps the music in the background.”

"Toi Market, with one caveat: Nairobi isn't really a vintage city in the curated, boutique sense— we're much more of an open-air, flea market vibe, with thousands of stalls. Toi is sprawling, busy, and a little chaotic. You'll need patience and a willingness to dig, but if you put in the time, you'll almost always come away with something great for a fraction of what you'd pay elsewhere."

“Nai Nami is properly off the beaten track; it's a walking tour of Nairobi's CBD led by former street children. You see downtown Nairobi through the eyes of people who know it intimately, and leave with a completely different understanding of the city. The Alliance Française is an unexpected answer, but it's one of Nairobi's great cultural hubs—plays, concerts, exhibitions, most of which are free, and the original stomping ground of Sauti Sol, our biggest boy band.”

A view of the city from Nairobi National Park

"Nairobi is the only city in the world with a national park so if you’ve only got one day, make it a wildlife day. I’d go for a game drive through Nairobi National Park at sunrise, then the elephant feeding at Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, and the Giraffe Centre to finish. Afterwards, a slow lunch nearby at either Cultiva, Talisman, or Matteo's. "

"I'd highly recommend coming to a We Run Nairobi Saturday. One of my favorite traditions is that we 'brand' every first-timer with a little sticker, so everyone knows it's your first Saturday. I'll encourage people to say hello, ask where you're visiting from, and recommend a coffee spot. You're moving together with actual Nairobians, in neighborhoods where we actually live. You're not being shown the city, you get to experience it alongside the people who call it home.”

#6242. The Parking Spot Promo Code: Save 10%

As a New Yorker without a car, I don’t often put much thought into airport parking. However, a few years ago, my mom texted me raving about The Parking Spot, a service available near Connecticut's Bradley International Airport that allows you to park your car near (but not directly at) the airport in a secure lot, then shuttle over to the terminal. She effusively recommended the process for its ease and convenience, and has continued to rave about it since. Its reach extends far beyond Bradley—with more than 70 locations at 45+ airports, it’s a service that’s available across the US for fliers looking to reduce some of the hassle that comes with travel.

Here’s how it works: You can reserve a spot ahead of time on the company’s website or app, securing your place to park and sorting out the cost up front. Once you arrive at the airport and park your car (avoiding the dreaded terminal traffic), you’ll hop in the bright yellow, polka dot-covered shuttle (whimsical!) and head over. While you’re traveling, you can get your car washed or detailed if you so wish, a nice added value. Then, when you return, you can track the shuttle in real-time using the app to get back to your car quickly.

If all of that sounds appealing—or you’re a regular to the service and are just looking for the latest promo codes—read on for ways to save on your next booking.

(Looking to rent a car instead? Take a look at active promo codes for Budget, Avis, and Hertz first.)

Fall is a great time to squeeze in a long weekend getaway—or even a full week to yourself, if you've got the PTO days to spare—ahead of the holiday busyness. If you're headed off on a trip, know that for reservations that begin by November 15, you can save 10% or more on your airport parking with promo code FALL10.

An easy way to score The Parking Spot discounts: Sign up for the company's mailing list. New users will automatically receive 10% off their first reservation. You’ll also gain access to 10–20% off promo codes on parking reservations for select cities—right now, that includes Austin, Denver, Columbus, Houston, and Salt Lake City.

Like many brands, The Parking Spot offers a military discount for active duty military and veterans. A less common, though fitting, discount is available for airline crew members. Both groups can get 25% off a reservation with a Spot Club account. As for the fine print, discounts don’t apply to Basic parking reservations and can’t be combined with other offers. Airline crew will need to submit a photo of their work badge; similarly, proof of military affiliation must be submitted to receive the discount.

If a Parking Spot promo code isn’t working at checkout, there are a few things you can do to troubleshoot. First double-check the basics—typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization can all prevent a code from working correctly. You'll also want to confirm that the code is still valid, as expiration dates and location exclusions may apply.

#6241. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6240. Cheers At The Gate As American Airlines Pilots Save My Flight From Cancellation

Never have I been so happy to board a delayed American Airlines flight…because we actually took off when I thought we were certain to face cancellation. And it culminated in a way that left me smiling.

American Airlines is famous for its rolling delays and I recently encountered one on a flight from Chicago to Los Angeles. While AA has promised that it going to do a better job of communicating delays and trying to predict actual departure time based on aircraft placement, it still has some work to do.

My flight was originally supposed to leave at 7:10p but I received a text message in the afternoon that it would be delayed until 8:15p, which actually was idea for me. I showed up to the airport at 7:30p, had a quick bite to eat in the Admirals Club, and prepared to board…but boarding never began. Instead, the delay was pushed to 8:45p. Then it was pushed to 9:00p. Then 9:30p. Then 10:15p. Then 11:30p. Then 11:55p.

The other AA evening flight to Los Angeles was facing similar delays.

Why? The aircraft was on the ground and at the gate. It had been there since 7:45p.

One of the agents in the Admirals Club turned her screen to me and said, “See look, you’ve got no pilots.”

Sure enough, no pilots were assigned to my flight, though it made no sense to me…this was an A321 and were in Chicago O’Hare, a hub. Does AA have no reserve pilots there that can fly an Airbus?

During this time I went back and forth between the gate and the lounge, because the rolling delays notifications often came late and while I know you usually get a text message when boarding starts, that is not always the case and I did not want to miss the flight (like Andrea Sachs).

The poor gate agents were fielding the angry mob…people were livid and many were freaking out that the flight would not cancel. The gate agent didn’t exactly help by stating his belief the flight would cancel, but I appreciated his candor.

Back in the Admirals Club, suddenly the pilot positions were filled. They were being flown in from Dallas, said the agent.

Seems like a product of poor planning, but okay. I was offered a hotel room if I wanted to bail and rebook for tomorrow (“But it aint gonna be at the Hilton”) but I really wanted to get to LA without a short night in a hotel room.

Back at the gate, we were told that though the pilots had been assigned, it would be up to them determine whether they wanted to accept the overtime assignment and fly the flight…the gate agent once again was on the pessimistic side. Many passengers were (understandably) irate.

But around 11:15p, the Dallas flight pulled up to the gate. We all waited anxiously.

Suddenly, a first officer rounded the corner and the whole gate area broke out into cheers. Someone called out, “Are you our pilot?!” and he flashed the thumbs up sign.

Moments later, the captain showed up to another chorus of cheers.

The trip was on! Boarding soon commend and we were on our way…very late, but on our way.

And as an added bonus, since so many passengers bailed, I got a first class upgrade at the gate, minutes before boarding. Better than three seats in economy class? Probably not, but certainly better than just an open middle in Economy Extra and I ended up enjoying a delicious salmon dinner enroute to LAX and still enjoying a nap for a couple hours due to the late hour.

I wish AA would get their act together, but after hours of rolling delays, I was just thankful to get home without having to overnight in ORD.

I have friends who work for major carriers here in the US, my question is how long was the food sitting on the plane? When a rolling delay happens in most cases the plane is catered for the original delayed departure time which in this case was 8:15 pm. However due to rolling delays it appears they didn’t leave the gate until 11:55 pm. At that time of night is it highly unlikely catering came back and re-catered the flight. Several of my friends have told me one of the most frustrating things they face as flight attendants during rolling delays is trying to get a flight re-catered and 9 times out of 10 the operation center refuses the request to re-cater the flight.

It is quite possible the food sat on the airplane for at least 4 hours without refrigeration if catering catered the flight for a 8:15 pm departure.
