#6208. 11 US Vacation Rentals Where the Hot Tub Comes With a View

Travelers love to debate window vs. aisle, or whether or not a group trip is a good idea, but I’ve never met anyone who didn’t love a hot tub. It’s the amenity that separates a good vacation home from a great one—the ultimate way to wake up your system in the morning or relax tired muscles in the evening, no matter the season. The rentals on this list, from cozy log cabins in Tennessee to glassy beach houses in coastal Oregon, all promise steamy hot tubs worth planning a trip around. Whether you want to experience the stillness of the New Mexican desert, breathe in the Blue Ridge mountain air, or look out for wildlife in Texas Hill Country, you can do it all from the comfort of your very own bubbling sanctuary. For a rejuvenating weekend away, where the agenda is resetting your nervous system or simply sharing a few laughs with friends, these hot tub–included rentals in the US are just the ticket.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, game room, outdoor space

Just a short drive away from some of Tennessee’s best theme parks (including Dollywood), this Smoky Mountain retreat is a home the entire family will love. The 2,100-square-foot cabin is divided into three levels, each with its own bedroom (all have king-size beds) and bathroom (one has a freestanding bathtub). Kids will love the game room in the loft, as well as a few hours spent at nearby Wild Bear Falls Indoor Water Park, Anakeesta, or Ripley's Aquarium of the Smokies. After all that fun, adults can end their days in the outdoor hot tub, perfectly positioned for watching the sun set over the mountain ridge.

Location: Gatlinburg, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Historic Ogle Log Cabin, Hillbilly Golf, Herbert Holt Park

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, floor-to-ceiling windows, forest views

Ideal for a couples getaway in the woods, this glassy cabin, with its soaring, floor-to-ceiling windows, is sure to provide a nature-friendly reset. It’s located just a five-minute walk away from Hocking Hills State Park and has all the modern comforts you need: a newly renovated kitchen and dining area, a queen-size bed upstairs, and, of course, an outdoor patio with a firepit and hot tub for nights spent nestled in the trees. Many reviewers gush over how spotless the place is and how close it is to hiking trails. One thing to note: AWD/4WD vehicles are recommended due to the rugged landscape.

Location: Laurelville, OhioThings to do nearby: Hocking Hills State Park, Conkles Hollow State Nature Preserve, Cedar Falls

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Game room, home gym, lake views

This modern masterpiece of a home, perfect for large family gatherings, was voted a 2026 Vrbo Vacation Rental of the Year. And it’s pretty easy to understand why, between the gorgeous views of Squam Lake from nearly every corner; the private dock from which to swim, kayak, or paddleboard; and the hot tub that’s built into the property. There are dozens of hiking trails nearby, whether you want to go on an easy lakeside stroll or trek to Mount Morgan. Suitable for any season, the house invites you to either laze a sunny day away on the patio’s sun chairs or curl up by the fireplace on a cooler night.

Location: Center Harbor, New HampshireThings to do nearby: Lake Winnipesaukee, White Mountain National Forest, Loon Mountain Resort

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Cold plunge, meditation spaces, outdoor shower

For a Hudson Valley hideaway just minutes from Catskill State Park, this two-bedroom home is bound to bring you peace, with reading nooks, meditation spaces, and even a room for massages, which you can book alongside a sound bath. There’s plenty to do outside too, whether that looks like meandering along the nearby Mill Stream, stretching out on the “flying saucer” hammock, or engaging in a little hydrotherapy (there’s a cedar cold plunge and hot tub situated right next to each other). In the warmer months, roast some s’mores by the firepit, and in the winter months, read a book by the wood-burning stove.

Location: Woodstock, New YorkThings to do nearby: Catskill State Park, Hunter Mountain, Kaaterskill Falls

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Private balcony, barbecue, secluded location

Tucked away on six acres of Texas Hill Country, this cozy cabin is the ultimate Lone Star escape, with its vaulted ceilings, log walls, and cowhide rugs. Beyond the expansive living room and fully equipped kitchen, there’s a bedroom downstairs with a queen-size bed, plus another one upstairs with a king-size bed and private balcony. When night falls, take in the stars from the hot tub on the outdoor patio and keep an eye out for local wildlife, which can include deer, turkeys, birds, and the occasional fox. Enjoy the local shops and breweries of nearby Wimberley Square, or go swimming or hiking at Jacob’s Well and Blue Hole Regional Park.

Location: San Marcos, TexasThings to do nearby: Devil’s Backbone Tavern, Canyon Park, Jacob’s Well Natural Area

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, in-unit washer/dryer, pool

Experience the beauty of the Yucca Valley desert from this spacious one-bedroom home. Just a 5-minute drive to Yucca Valley Community Park and a 15-minute drive to Joshua Tree National Park, it’s conveniently located for all kinds of desert excursions—there’s even a mountain of boulders right behind the home that guests can climb. Enjoy sunrise or sunset views from the outdoor stock tank pool or hot tub, and be sure to look out for animals. Previous guests have recorded a few sightings, from lizards and rabbits to coyotes and roadrunners.

Location: Yucca Valley, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Yucca Valley Community Park, Hi-Desert Nature Museum, Desert Christ Park

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Ocean views, in-unit washer/dryer, proximity to beach

Located just north of Manzanita in Tillamook County, this massive, five-bedroom home offers spectacular views of Neahkahnie Beach. Suitable for a family reunion or bachelorette weekend, it can sleep up to 12 guests and has large spaces built for gathering, whether that’s the grand dining table near the kitchen or the patio outside that includes the gorgeous hot tub. There’s plenty to do nearby, from strolling down Manzanita’s Laneda Avenue in search of a quaint coffee shop to visiting the historic Nehalem Bay Winery for a tasting.

Location: Nehalem, OregonThings to do nearby: Sunset Beach, Oswald West State Park, Nehalem Bay State Park

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Terrace, desert views, earthy interior design

At this El Prado property, you’ll have to make the tough call between hopping in the Japanese-style bathtub, the outdoor hot tub, or nearby Manby Hot Springs—but who says you can’t do all three? Located on 15 acres of land where juniper, piñon, and sage grow wild, the architectural home features cast-earth walls, a corrugated metal roof, radiant heat, and mahogany woodwork. Explore the many trails at Rio Grande Gorge National Monument, a minute’s walk away, then have a soak under the stars.

Location: El Prado, New MexicoThings to do nearby: Rio Grande del Norte National Monument, Manby Hot Springs, Taos Plaza

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Game room, pet-friendly, forest views

For a moment away in the Blue Ridge Mountains, look no further than Bear Pause Cabin, a three-bedroom retreat perfect for a multigenerational clan. Whether you want to play pool in the game room, take in views of the forest from the hot tub, or explore nearby Grandfather Mountain State Park, there’s no shortage of ways to spend your days. The fully equipped kitchen has everything you need to prepare meals at home, while the patio has a barbecue for outdoor entertaining. The wood-burning fireplace and blanket ladder in the living room make movie nights especially cozy.

Location: Seven Devils, North CarolinaThings to do nearby: Grandfather Vineyard & Winery, Grandfather Mountain State Park, Hawksnest Tubing Park

Number of guests: 16Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, in-unit washer/dryer, game room

This spacious four-bedroom home in Interlochen, Michigan, provides access to both Green Lake and the Betsie River. Inside, you’ll find vaulted ceilings, exposed beams, and large windows that give way to hues of blue and green. There are also a few dedicated spaces, like the “Mutt Room,” which features a custom dog shower, and the game room, with its ping-pong table. The house can fit up to 16 guests, thanks to the additional twin-size beds in a few of the bedrooms. Outside, you’ll find a hot tub, a firepit, a floating dock on the lake, a smaller riverside dock, and an anchored swim raft; guests can feel free to use the provided kayaks for a fun excursion.

Location: Interlochen, MichiganThings to do nearby: Green Lake, Interlochen Center for the Arts, Crystal Mountain

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Proximity to ski resorts, private deck, in-unit washer/dryer

If you’re planning a ski trip to Utah’s Deer Valley or Park City Mountain Resort, this bright and airy condo is an ideal place to retreat to after a day on the slopes. It boasts an entryway designed for gear drops, a spacious living area with a stone fireplace, and, the best part, an outdoor hot tub for the ultimate aprés-ski soak. While there are only three bedrooms, the home can actually sleep up to 10, thanks to the help of bunk beds and sleeper sofas. It’s time to take that ski trip out of the group chat.

Location: Park City, UtahThings to do nearby: Deer Valley Resort, Park City Mountain Resort, Homestead Crater

#6207. British Airways Boeing 787 Stranded In Pittsburgh For 2 Months Due To Complicated Repairs

A Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner has been stranded at Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) in Pennsylvania for over two months after reportedly sustaining significant damage during a ground-handling incident. The aircraft, registered as G-ZBJF, arrived at PIT from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) in August, operating as BA171. However, instead of a routine transatlantic arrival, a ground service vehicle collided with the aircraft, damaging its underside and leaving it unable to return to the skies.

More than 70 days later, the 12-year-old Dreamliner remains in Pittsburgh. According to Turbine Traveller, the repair process has proven to be much more complicated than initially anticipated. As several travelers reported, potential damage to the aircraft’s landing gear system continues to delay the repair process.

G-ZBJF arrived in Pittsburgh on August 28, after completing its roughly 3,233-nautical-mile (5,987 km) journey across the Atlantic Ocean. The aircraft departed Heathrow five minutes early, at 4:40 PM, and landed at PIT at approximately 8:23 PM local time. However, G-ZBJF never operated its return service to London later that night, and subsequent reports indicate the 787-8 sustained severe damage while on the ground. Flight tracking data and visual sightings confirm the aircraft is still on the ground.

According to discussions among aviation enthusiasts on Reddit, the incident that led to G-ZBJF’s grounding involved a mobile baggage belt loader that reportedly struck the airframe underneath one of its bulk cargo doors. The belt loader, a piece of ground service equipment used by ramp personnel to load and unload luggage from the 787’s cargo hold, was raised into position but pierced the fuselage, leaving a hole in the cargo bay’s exterior. Although the exact details beyond this have not been confirmed, the aircraft's continued presence in Pittsburgh suggests a major structural issue requiring a significant engineering solution.

The repair process could be particularly challenging given the 787’s construction. Unlike older aircraft that primarily use conventional aluminum structures, about 50% of the Dreamliner’s primary structure is made from composite materials. This includes significant portions of its fuselage and wings, requiring specialized inspection and repair procedures in the event of substantial structural damage.

Depending on the severity, British Airways maintenance engineers may have to construct a specialized patch to apply to the exterior of the Dreamliner. This would allow the plane to be ferried to a larger maintenance base capable of handling the 787, where more extensive work can be completed. In order to be transported to one of these locations, however, the aircraft would have to be approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to complete a one-off ferry flight via the use of a special flight permit (SFP).

Since the initial damage to G-ZBJF, several people have reported that the aircraft may also have damage to the landing gear system. According to one person on Reddit, a British Airways engineer who worked on the Dreamliner, repair work was well underway, but technicians encountered additional complications involving damage to the jet’s landing gear system. While this account has not been independently verified, it could help explain why the Dreamliner has remained grounded for so long.

A separate report suggests that British Airways could be preparing to reposition the airplane to Cincinnati Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG) after completing temporary repairs in Pittsburgh. The reported plan could allow the 787 to be moved to a larger facility operated by FEAM Aero, a maintenance services provider, where the aircraft could be repaired more permanently before returning to the United Kingdom. Ferrying the jet to Boeing’s 787 facilities in Seattle could also be another option, as the planemaker would be well-equipped to handle any repairs to the aircraft’s composite structure if needed.

For British Airways, getting G-ZBJF back into the skies is a high priority. Currently, the UK flag carrier operates a total of 12 examples of the 787-8, according to Planespotters.net. G-ZBJF is about 12 years old, first flying in April 2014 before being delivered to British Airways the following month. While it is not uncommon for airplanes to be parked for routine maintenance checks, the prolonged grounding of G-ZBJF is costing the airline not only potentially millions in repair fees, but hundreds of thousands in lost revenue potential and roughly $175,000 in gate parking charges, according to the Allegheny County Airport Authority (ACAA), which operates PIT. While British Airways likely is not paying the full amount given insurance coverage and the ground service operator's fault, it goes without a doubt that the airline would rather have its aircraft flying passengers than sitting on the ground in Pittsburgh.

The incident delayed the flight's departure by several hours.

Interestingly, the Pittsburgh incident is not the first time this year G-ZBJF has spent an extended period away from flying passengers. Before its latest grounding, the Dreamliner already spent nearly eight months at Cardiff Airport (CWL) in Wales, where British Airways operates a major maintenance facility, before being placed into long-term storage while D-checks were completed. Aircraft tracking records show that G-ZBJF arrived in Cardiff on December 19, 2025, and remained there until August 6. After nearly eight months in Cardiff, the aircraft returned to commercial operations on August 7, meaning it had been back in service for only about three weeks before being stranded in Pittsburgh.

G-ZBJF ferried to Cardiff for long-term storage and maintenance checks.

G-ZBJF completes D-check at Cardiff maintenance base.

G-ZBJF returns to operational service after being ferried from Cardiff to London.

G-ZBJF operates BA171 from LHR to PIT and is subsequently grounded in Pittsburgh after a ground service vehicle collided with the aircraft's underside.

The timing makes the latest incident particularly unfortunate for British Airways. Having spent much of the previous eight months undergoing extended maintenance, G-ZBJF had only recently returned to its regular flying schedule before the incident in Pittsburgh. Meanwhile, the prolonged grounding underscores the heavy logistical challenges of repairing a widebody thousands of miles from primary maintenance facilities. Whether the 787 can eventually return to service directly from Pittsburgh or must first be repositioned to another city remains one of the biggest unanswered questions.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I hope BA's insurers are going after the ground services provider for every farthing in damages.

Obviously its extended time in Cardiff at the BA maintenance base was due to its RR engines and the repair/upgrade of them. BA was smart to switch to GENex engines for its 787-10s.

I’ve held the (see rates and fees) for eight years, and despite carrying more than 25 credit cards, it’s one I’ll continue renewing year after year.

The reason is simple: World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and this card makes it even more rewarding to stay with the brand. Between an annual free night, automatic elite status and the ability to earn valuable Hyatt points on spending, I consistently receive far more value than the card’s affordable $95 annual fee.

It isn’t the right fit for everyone. Hyatt has a much smaller global footprint than Marriott, Hilton and IHG, so travelers who rarely stay at Hyatt hotels may be better served by a more flexible travel rewards card. However, if Hyatt is already part of your travel plans — or you’d like it to become one — the World of Hyatt card is one of the best mid-tier hotel cards on the market. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

If you’re comparing several hotel credit cards, here’s what you need to know at a glance:

Unlike cards that earn transferable rewards, this is very much a Hyatt-focused product. If you’re loyal to Hyatt — or want an affordable way to accelerate your progress toward higher status — it deserves serious consideration.

If there’s one reason why I continue paying the World of Hyatt card’s annual fee, it’s the anniversary free night certificate.

Each cardholder anniversary, you’ll receive a free night award valid at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort. Since Hyatt prices these properties between 3,000 and 25,000 points per night, there’s plenty of opportunity to extract well over $95 in value. Free nights expire 12 months after issuance.

I’ve redeemed my certificates at The Standard, Brussels, Hyatt House Manchester in the U.K. and Andaz Mexico City Condesa. In each case, paying cash would have cost considerably more than the card’s annual fee.

Even better, you can earn a second Category 1-4 certificate after spending $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

That’s the spending threshold I personally target each year. It unlocks another free night and an additional six elite night credits toward Hyatt status for even more value beyond the points you'll earn from that spending.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

Simply holding the card gives you complimentary Discoverist status.

While Discoverist isn’t Hyatt’s most rewarding elite tier, I still appreciate benefits like preferred room upgrades and late checkout (when available) and a 10% bonus on eligible Hyatt spending.

That said, for frequent Hyatt guests, this perk probably won’t be all that enticing since they’re likely to earn Discoverist status organically. The card becomes more valuable when working toward a higher status level.

Every calendar year, you’ll receive five qualifying night credits automatically, and you’ll earn another two qualifying night credits for every $5,000 spent.

I’ve found those elite night credits incredibly valuable. By combining the five annual elite nights from the card with my Hyatt stays and strategic spending to earn an additional six nights, I qualified for top-tier Globalist status in August 2025, which I’ll enjoy through February 2027.

Related: Was going all-in on Hyatt Globalist worth it? My honest take

These protections aren't as extensive as those you'd receive with a premium travel card, but that's to be expected given this card's modest annual fee.

Related: Is the World of Hyatt credit card worth the annual fee?

One of my favorite things about the World of Hyatt program is that earning and redeeming points is refreshingly straightforward.

Unlike most major hotel loyalty programs, Hyatt still publishes an award chart, making award pricing more predictable.

When you stay at Hyatt hotels, these earnings stack with the points you earn as a World of Hyatt member. Since cardholders receive complimentary Discoverist status, you’ll also earn a 10% bonus on your base points, meaning you can earn up to 9.5 total points per dollar spent on eligible Hyatt purchases. That represents a solid 16% return on Hyatt purchases, per our November 2026 valuations.

I generally use this card for Hyatt stays and tax payments that help me reach the $15,000 annual threshold for the second free night certificate.

Otherwise, I typically use my  (see rates and fees) for most travel and dining purchases, then transfer those Chase Ultimate Rewards points to my Hyatt account whenever I need to top up my balance for an award stay.

That gives me the best of both worlds: I earn more rewards on everyday travel and dining while keeping my points flexible until I’m ready to book. If I don’t end up needing Hyatt points, I can always transfer them to one of Chase’s 13 other airline or hotel partners instead.

Related: 6 of the best credit cards for travel purchases — beyond flights and hotels

In my opinion, Hyatt points remain among the most valuable hotel points due to their flexibility.

Award nights start at just 3,000 points for a Category 1 property at the Lowest rate and range up to 75,000 points for a top-tier Category 8 property under Hyatt’s five-tier standard award chart.

I’ve used Hyatt points for everything from inexpensive city breaks to luxury resorts. Some of my favorite redemptions include:

Hyatt also lets you redeem points for Points + Cash stays, suite upgrades, club lounge access and Find experiences. While those options can make sense occasionally, I almost always get the best value by redeeming points for standard award nights.

Related: 22 best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

Despite being one of my favorite hotel credit cards, the won’t be the right fit for every traveler.

The biggest drawback is Hyatt’s relatively small footprint. While Hyatt has more than 1,500 hotels and all-inclusive properties across 80-plus countries, that’s still far fewer than Marriott or Hilton. If you frequently travel to destinations without a Hyatt, you may struggle to maximize the card’s benefits.

Those who prioritize earning the highest possible rewards on everyday spending will likely find better options elsewhere. Beyond Hyatt purchases and spending toward the $15,000 threshold for a second free night certificate, this card isn’t particularly rewarding for dining, travel or everyday purchases.

Finally, travelers looking for premium perks like airport lounge access, annual travel credits and luxury benefits across multiple hotel brands should consider a premium travel rewards card instead.

For most travelers, I think the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card is the better choice than the (see rates and fees).

Both cards help you earn Hyatt points and elite status, but the business version is designed primarily for business owners. It offers bonus categories geared toward business spending and additional benefits for companies, while the personal card provides better long-term value for most travelers, thanks to its annual Category 1-4 free night certificate.

By comparison, I think the World of Hyatt Business card's $199 annual fee is harder to justify year after year because it lacks an anniversary free night. It does offer up to $100 in Hyatt statement credits each anniversary year, but that requires Hyatt spending and there's no way to get outsized value like you might with a free night.

Unless you own a business and can maximize the business-specific earning categories, I’d start with the personal card.

These are hotels that would ordinarily require 3,000 to 25,000 points per night, depending on the property and stay dates. Someone who uses all four free night certificates at the highest-priced properties would save up to 100,000 World of Hyatt points, making this offer worth up to $1,650 (based on TPG valuations).

This is a very strong bonus compared to other historical welcome offers, though not the absolute all-time highest offer for new cardmembers. The best-ever welcome offer included five free-night awards (offer no longer available). Having said that, if you max out the four certificates, this would be considered the most lucrative offer since February.

Despite being a great offer right now, some travelers may prefer to wait until the introductory bonus is awarded in points instead. Unlike free nights, there are no hotel category restrictions for redeeming points. The expiration date for free nights is also stricter.

I’ve carried the World of Hyatt Credit Card for eight years, and it’s one of the few hotel credit cards I have no intention of canceling.

The annual Category 1-4 free night certificate has consistently offset the card’s $95 annual fee, while the elite night credits helped me qualify for Globalist status last year. Add in Hyatt’s strong redemption value, and it’s easy to see why this remains my favorite mid-tier hotel credit card.

If you regularly stay at Hyatt properties, I think the World of Hyatt card deserves a place in your wallet. If you rarely stay with Hyatt, though, you’ll probably get more long-term value from a flexible travel rewards card.

#6205. Arc'teryx Promo Codes & Deals November 2026

Whether you’re a seasoned mountaineer, a proponent of gorpcore, or a mix of both, you’re probably familiar with the Vancouver-based outdoors brand Arc’teryx (Did you know it was named after the Archaeopteryx lithographica, the first reptile to develop feathers for flight?). Famous for its waterproof Gore-Tex shell jackets, down parkas, and—if you’re a Brooklyn hipster—the iconic Bird Head Toque hat, the brand is committed to developing the very best in activewear technology, often testing its gear on the Coast Mountains of British Columbia for durability, comfort, and function.

Founded in 1989 by Dave Lane as “Rock Solid,” the brand started out as a collection of climbing harnesses. After enlisting Jeremy Guard, the company was rebranded as “Arc’Teryx” in 1991, with a new logo: a stylized skeleton of the Archaeopteryx lithographica. In 1998, the brand secured a license for Gore-Tex, launching the iconic Alpha SV jacket. In the last few years, Arc’teryx has made its way into high fashion, capturing the attention of street-style icons behind the gorpcore trend and collaborating with designers like Jil Sander. While Arc’teryx gear does cost a pretty penny, there are all kinds of deals to look out for to help you save big on your next purchase. (While these discounts come directly from the brand, keep in mind outdoor outfitter REI is currently offering significant discounts on various Arc'teryx apparel). Below, find the best Arc’teryx discounts, promo codes, and offers.

Before you commit to buying something full-price, have a look at the Arc’teryx Outlet, where you can score up to 50% off a selection of men's and women’s shell jackets, base layers, and footwear—including products from Veilance, the brand’s more urban-friendly line. Men, for instance, can currently save 30% on the Solano jacket, as well as 65% on the Kragg shoe. For the steepest discounts, keep an eye out for discontinued colors and previous iterations of core products. Keep in mind, though, that all items purchased at the Arc’teryx Outlet are final sale.

Part of Arc’teryx’s commitment to sustainability is ensuring products last for lifetimes. When you trade in gently used Arc’teryx gear, you’ll receive a gift card worth 30% of the original retail value. Trade-ins are processed through the Rebird Resale program—simply complete the trade-in form online to get a shipping label, then package the gear and mail it in, or drop it off in store to save on shipping fees. Only eligible items will qualify for the trade-in, so those that pose hygiene issues, like cotton T-shirts or headwear, are less likely to be accepted. A good rule of thumb is that if you wouldn’t gift it to a friend, it likely won’t be eligible.

Through Arc’teryx’s Pro Program, qualified outdoor experts and community partners—including mountain guides, park rangers, firefighters, ski instructors, and more—can take advantage of special discounted pricing. To apply, fill out an application and verify your professional credentials on the Arc’teryx site.

Arc’teryx offers free shipping on all orders placed within the US—no minimum purchase required. This includes items from the Arc’teryx Outlet, and also extends to free returns within a 30-day window for most purchases. Whether you’re grabbing a pair of merino wool hiking socks or a comfortable jacket for day hikes, the price on the tag (plus tax) is all you’ll be paying.

To get the best possible deal, combine savings strategies. Use trade-in credits from the Rebird program on items already marked down in the Outlet, and check the Outlet regularly, since new styles rotate in often. Sign up for the brand newsletter to receive alerts on upcoming Arc'teryx savings opportunities.

#6204. Finland Is Throwing an Epic Dinner Party for 16 Singles—Here's How to Get Invited

The Nordic countries are well known for their rather gimmicky yet innovative travel campaigns luring travelers to the icy north. From doctors prescribing travel to Sweden as a medical treatment to Oslo's viral mock-documentary narrated by a jaded local called Halfdan. Preceding these by a decade, Danish tour operator Spies Travels famously promoted its ”Do It for Denmark!” campaign focused on Denmark’s low birth rates, offering “ovulation discounts” to couples who proved they conceived on their romantic trip.

Now, Finland has announced it's flying out sixteen international singles this February for a "blind group date with likeminded travelers and local Finnish singles.”

The country is touting the so-called Love At First Bite campaign as an epic blind dinner date, designed to help participants “discover Finnish food, meet new people, and perhaps even find love.” The singles will be divided and hosted in two group dates in capital city Helsinki and Tampere located in Europe’s largest lake district, Finland’s Lakeland region.

Joining the singles over candlelit tasting menus crafted by local celebrity chefs will be local single Finns. Get ready for lots of prolonged eye contact—the Nordic way of flirting—under low light as you bond over the likes of wild trout, reindeer, chanterelle mushrooms, and sea buckthorn. For those heading to Tampere, the destination is monikered the “world’s sauna capital,” so chances of sweating with your fellow single strangers is probably on the menu too.

I’ll admit, when the campaign was launched worldwide, my Finnish friends and I wrinkled our noses in confusion. Romantic and sexy aren’t the first words that come to mind when you think of Finland. And it's not the Nordic country you'd first go to for love if we're talking stereotypes. The Danes have their extroverted charm, the Swedes their chic worldliness, and the Norwegians typically have more money to spend on you. Popular Nordic comedians Helgi and Erlend riff on these regional stereotypes, depicting their Finnish character as stoic, quiet and mentally tough. The very Finnish ethos of “sisu” means grit and the tenacity to push through tough times. But maybe those are qualities you'd want in a lifelong partner as you navigate challenges together.

So the campaign got me thinking a little deeper. Named the happiest country in the world for the ninth consecutive year in a row, Finns are satisfied with their lifestyles firmly rooted in the outdoors, nature, and a slower pace of life. In this contentment is where you’ll find Finland’s hidden sexier side.

In a country of roughly five million, there are two million saunas. And few places are more intimate than sweating together naked in a sauna, dipping in chilly lakes during winter, then warming back up indoors in many more ways. There’s also something rather romantic about grilling wild-caught salmon for two over an open flame in the backcountry.

This isn’t the first time the country has dabbled in an unconventional approach to dating. The viral “Sinkkukori” phenomenon introduced pink shopping baskets as a way for singles to covertly signal their availability. Now Finland is taking a more overt approach to romance. As the well-known nineteenth-century English idiom reminds us, the quickest way to the heart is through the stomach, and Finland certainly wants to put this to the test.

To shoot your shot at finding love in Finland, apply by November 10, 2026 at 11:59 AM Finnish time. All you have to do is make a video answering the question: what would you serve on a dinner date, and why? Just like a proper prospect, Finland would like to know your preferences in advance so it can woo you in the most epic and intentional way. If that isn’t romantic, I don’t know what is.

#6203. KLM Plans 1,000 More Job Cuts

KLM expects to eliminate approximately 1,000 positions through productivity improvements as part of a restructuring announced Thursday.

The Dutch carrier said it would seek to limit the impact through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements and transfers. Other changes include moving about 800 ground services positions to outside providers and transferring 2,000 positions to Air France-KLM, including 1,500 at customer contact center Cygnific.

“But KLM’s future is not guaranteed,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement, citing global instability, high fuel prices, and pressure on the industry.

KLM is targeting a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028, alongside restrained wage growth. It said an additional €1 billion in annual earnings improvement is needed to fund investments.

The changes also affect its European fleet. KLM will replace planned Airbus A320s with Embraer E195-E2s, giving regional subsidiary Cityhopper a larger role. The A321neo will remain, while Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s will be phased out.

The announcement came as KLM reported a third-quarter operating profit of €458 million, up from €352 million a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, operating profit reached €526 million on revenue of €10.9 billion.

Despite the improvement, KLM said profitability remains insufficient to support its investment needs. Higher fuel costs and Middle East flight cancellations weighed on its passenger business, while Transavia faced competition and operational challenges.

“We need to increase it to more than 8% to secure a financially healthy future for KLM,” Chief Financial Officer Bas Brouns said of the airline’s profit margin.

#6202. The Best Way to Eat Swiss Fondue? Floating on Lake Brienz

I could say that I was surprised to find myself and my family floating along in a red Zodiac on the deepest lake in Switzerland, eating cheese fondue and sipping white wine as the sun set. But really, it was all by design. When I designated myself as chief planner for an autumnal family trip to the Alpine nation with my adult children and their partners, I searched for an activity that would knock their socks off. I found it in Interlaken, with a floating fondue experience. Yes, you read that right.

I love Switzerland, and have visited the land where the hills are alive with the sound of cowbells more than 30 times in my life. And while I’ve done many amazing things in and around the Swiss Alps—skiing, hiking, trottinetting, whittling my own Swiss cow from a block of wood—I knew getting my Gen Z crew excited about family time involved finding something a little more unconventional.

We were going to be staying in the Bernese Oberland, a picture-postcard region with legendary sites like Grindelwald, the Jungfrau and Eiger mountains, and Interlaken. Everyone was up for hiking and taking cable cars to waterfalls; paragliding was sadly vetoed. But a unique culinary experience would surely work, I thought—the way to their hearts is through their stomachs.

Luckily, I had heard about a Cheese Fondue Float experience offered by a company called Outdoor Switzerland a few years ago. Back then, it was raclette—toasted cheese scraped onto boiled potatoes—that served as the dish du jour. But fondue, Switzerland’s national dish, is much more well-known, so the company savvily swapped raclette trays for caquelons (ceramic fondue pots). I found the experience listing on Get Your Guide, and reviews praised the change, highlighting the delicious cheese and wine and the gregarious fondue fun. I confirmed a private booking for the six of us a month before we left home, and kept my fingers crossed for good weather.

I needn’t have worried—my prayers were answered with glorious temperatures and bluebird skies on the day of the tour, a leisurely Sunday in September. A five-minute bus ride from downtown Interlaken brought us to the small village of Bonigen, the launch site located on scenic Lake Brienz. After shaking hands with our guide, a tall, friendly Dutchman named Hild, we donned life jackets, listened to the mandatory safety briefing, and stepped into the boat, alternating sides to keep the weight even. Once comfortably settled around the pretty red-and-white-checkered tablecloth, which was already topped with plates, cups, and two fondue pots, Hild slowly rowed us onto the lake.

An overhead shot of the pretty tablescape and gorgeous lake

Lake Brienz is the deepest lake in the country, and it’s surely one of the most scenic too. Moving out from the shore, we encountered spectacular views of towering mountains, their peaks mirrored in the impossibly blue water. I poured the prepared cheese fondue into the heated fondue pots, and the mixture began bubbling, filling the air with a sharp aroma as it warmed into readiness.

The fondue float experience includes white wine (one 500-ml bottle per person), as well as water and hot tea. We took turns pouring wine into our copper cups as my eldest son took command of the Bluetooth speaker, setting a lively mood with traditional Alpine tunes played on accordions and hackbretts (a kind of dulcimer), mixed with the occasional yodel ditty. At one point, our float’s music and laughter brought friendly waves from passengers on a passing cruise boat, along with toots from the ship’s horn. We whooped and waved in return.

Once the cheese was steaming hot, we dipped and swished bread cubes into the melted goodness, savoring the delicious alchemy of bread and cheese alongside celebratory toasts in honor of our family adventure. As the cheese disappeared, the fondue pot heated the remains into what the Swiss call “la réligieuse”—toasted cheese bits that are scraped from the bottom of the pot. We fought playfully over dibs on the last delicious morsels—trust me, they’re good to the last perfectly browned crumb.

Raising a glass to a unique family adventure

The entire experience lasted about an hour and a half, and during that time, the six of us managed to drink all six wine bottles on board. None of us are big drinkers, but the beauty of the surroundings inspired the good times to flow, and, well, so did the wine.

Photos and videos captured our cheesy adventure, but the memory of enjoying such a unique culinary and cultural experience with my favorite people in the world will be forever burned into my mind. You can have a fondue anywhere, but while floating in one of the most iconic locations in one of the most beautiful countries on earth? Even my discerning Gen Z travel companions agreed: “That’s extra.”

The Cheese Fondue Float experience on Lake Brienz in Interlaken is available to book on the Outdoor Switzerland website, as well as on GetYourGuide and Viator. It is offered between September and April, weather permitting. If booking in the colder months, bundle up with coats, beanies, and gloves, as you’ll be out on the water for up to an hour and a half. Private charters are available for groups up to eight people; kids eight years and up are welcome. More of a dessert person? Outdoor Switzerland also offers a Swiss Chocolate Fondue experience. Get cozy under blankets, sip hot tea, and dip marshmallows and fruit into creamy melted Swiss chocolate while a qualified guide rows you merrily along the beautiful Brienzersee.

#6201. The Wonder—and Weirdness—of Exploring a National Park in the Dark

I’ve spent the majority of my life doing outdoor activities: camping, hiking, biking, kayaking, you name it. It’s intrinsically part of who I am, something that defines my siblings and I so deeply it feels like it’s braided into our DNA.

Perhaps that’s because, when I was just two-and-a-half years old, my parents took my siblings and me on a two-month-long road trip from New York to Arizona, hitting dozens of state and national parks on the way. We still talk about that adventure, lovingly referred to as the Out West Trip. It was the first time I visited Utah’s national parks, known as the Mighty 5: Zion, Arches, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, and Bryce Canyon.

Once night falls in Utah's national parks, most travelers head back to their campfires or motor lodges—except for those willing to brave the dark and explore their nocturnal side.

A lot has changed since I first visited. Now, millions of visitors head to Southern Utah every year, flocking to these five well-known national parks in addition to the whopping 46 state parks across the whole of Utah. Even in the staggeringly hot and dry summer season, these protected areas teem with tourists from all over the world—Zion alone reported over 1.4 million visitors in June, July, and August of 2026, while Arches reported over 445,000 in the same season.

Once night falls in the Utah desert, though, the temperatures cool off, most tourists head back to their campsites and motor lodges, and the stars shine through that clear desert sky. All of the Mighty 5 are certified dark sky parks—Utah, in fact, boasts the highest concentration of certified International Dark Sky Places in the world. So maybe it's no surprise that, in recent years, these destinations have embraced night-centric recreation, showcasing a lesser-known version of themselves for those willing to brave the dark.

In Capitol Reef National Park, the The Temple of the Sun summit stands against a sky full of stars.

It's why, nearly 30 years after my first Utah park trip, I decided to return—this time, experiencing Southern Utah’s state and national parks once the sun set. I’m a night owl, but I also wanted to revive that sense of wonder I felt so long ago when I first visited. I knew the parks by day, but by night? They were brand new to me. And so, in late September, my friend Sarra and I plotted a week-long road trip linking four national parks and three state parks in Utah. Our goal was to take it easy during the daylight hours with a gentle hike or two, and store up our energy for a nocturnal expedition come sundown. We wanted to get to know Utah’s parks in a way that too few do.

It’s 9 p.m. when we walk into Capitol Reef National Park with hiking guides Samuel and Suzanne Francis, the married owners of Western Whiptails Adventures. The sun has set by a couple hours; my friend and I rely on flashlights, while our guides trust themselves in the dark. As we begin on the trail, I’m struck by the silence surrounding us, serene in a way I’ve experienced only in the redwoods, where the massive trees cradle you against human noise; by day, the stone of Utah’s parks almost reverberates with the many overlapping voices of the crowd. Now, there is no sound left to bounce.

The view of the Hickman Bridge in Capitol Reef National Park at midnight.

Our goal is to hike to Hickman Bridge, a natural sandstone arch—completely in the dark. It’s a 1.8-mile round-trip that begins with an initial climb on switchbacks, flattens out in the middle, and then resumes a narrower uphill path with a bit of a scramble required to reach the view. It’s a hike that should take about 1.5 hours in daylight. Sam says he and Suz have led hundreds of guided tours throughout the park and surrounding public lands, but nothing quite like this. “Capitol Reef’s landscape takes on an entirely different character at night,” he says.

I feel the ground under my sneakers shift from hard-packed dirt to softer sand as we set out, and the herbal scent of pinon and Utah juniper trees tickles my nose. We’re surrounded by dust and desert, but the area feels alive with the chirping of bugs and rustling of leaves.

Suz leads us to little-known petroglyphs, then points out a site where the Fremont people once stored corn. Sarra and I shine our flashlights and look on in admiration. It’s a respite in the adrenaline-pumping stretch of the hike—we have gained a couple hundred feet of elevation, and I am imagining the drop-offs that I’m quite sure lie beyond the tiny circle of my flashlight. My grip gets tighter and I begin to sweat through my layers, realizing that the dark can't quiet my fear of heights. Suz is up ahead, climbing like it’s second nature: “If you turn your flashlights off, your eyes will adjust,” she says, turning back. I laugh, knowing there's no way I can get myself to follow her advice.

The nearly full moon directly over the sandstone summit in Capitol Reef National Park

A hard-to-find petroglyph site in Capitol Reef National Park

“Many animals in Capitol Reef are nocturnal or crepuscular, especially during warmer months,” Sam says, listing off the species we share the night with as we plod on. “Bats, kangaroo rats, desert cottontails, foxes, desert bighorn sheep, mule deer, or even the rare ringtail.”

Once we reach flatter ground, I concede to turn off my light, blinking to let my eyes adjust. I realize the nearly full moon above is blindingly bright—and yet we can still make out hundreds of glittering stars sharing the sky. “The darkness really offers a unique connection to the landscape,” says Sam. I can't help but agree.

And then we finally catch sight of the stone bridge, bathed in moonlight and backlit by stars, appearing especially mammoth in the low light. We sit beneath it, the silence wrapped around us, the space above looking unimaginably infinite. “I’ve seen this bridge plenty of times during the day,” says Suz, agreeing with me, “but at night, it's even better.”

The starry sky shines over Dead Horse Point State Park, where after-dark activities include scorpion spotting and stargazing.

While Capitol Reef's night hike was nothing short of thrilling, another type of excitement awaits us at Dead Horse State Park. The park is known for its dramatic red-rock canyon vistas and hiking trails that cross them—and yet the evening programming is just as robust, with scorpion searching, stargazing, sunset walks, and astronomy talks all included in the $20 entrance fee. Unlike Capitol Reef, where we were possibly the only visitors on the grounds that night (despite it being open 24 hours), Dead Horse is known for its nocturnal programming (much of which begins around 8 p.m., and runs until the park closes at 10). According to Ally O'Rullian, public information officer at Utah State Parks, Dead Horse Point naturalist programs have “likely included dark sky viewings” since as early as the mid 1970s, and this new slate of activities was added to the regular calendar in 2015 as part of its application for International Dark Sky status. We are far from the only ones out tonight—it feels as though this is how the Dead Horse is meant to be appreciated.

A group of travelers gather around a state ranger as they prepare for a scorpion search

We've opted to go scorpion searching, which is exactly as wacky as it sounds. Scorpions are biofluorescent, meaning they emit a visible bluish glow under UV lights. And so we gather at the Visitor Center, where ranger Jimmy Burch is handing out special flashlights. This is one of the most popular activities at the park, Burch says, and perhaps unsurprisingly, the one with the greatest youth turnout. We do feel like kids, as our group of a dozen or so of all ages start down a gentle, meandering path, shining our torches on brush and rocks to see if we can find anything hiding among them. Shine a UV light directly on a bush with a scorpion in it, Burch says, and it would be nearly impossible to overlook the glowing body within. “If you hear hissing, step away,” he cautions, as we sweep the area. Burch assures us that no one has ever been stung on one of these walks.

We are nearing the end of “scorpion season” in late September, as the weather is getting too cold for the critters to wander freely. In winter, scorpions enter a low-activity state and hide in dark, quiet locations, like underground burrows, conserving their energy against the cold. I wonder if that means we won't see much—but then, after just a few minutes, a boy in my group begins to call out, “Scorpion, scorpion, scorpion!” Burch heads over, congratulatory as he crouches down a few inches away from the tiny, glowing arachnid. The rest of us follow, taking turns leaning closer to take in its luminous body, just a few inches long. It turns out that scorpions are perfectly happy to hang out under the UV light, surrounded by a large group of people taking photos. It doesn't move a single muscle as we pap it in awe.

Setting up kayaks at the edge of the Sand Hollow State Park reservoir, just as the moon begins to rise

Jaw-dropping colors appear in the sky over Sand Hollow State Park and its reservoir.

Ready for something a bit calmer, we make the early morning drive to our final destination: Hurricane, Utah—about 25 miles away from Zion National Park, and home to the lesser-known Sand Hollow. Initially, we had plans to do nocturnal canyoneering in Zion, but when the weather turned, it gave us permission to settle into a slower place.

For the past two years, Sand Hollow State Park—known for its large reservoir set against red-rock cliffs—has been offering a monthly full-moon paddle in the warmer months, to complement the hiking and biking trails that families enjoy year-round.

The paddle is only available from April through September (depending on the weather) and starts at moonrise—which is just after 7 p.m. for us, when our group meets ranger Callie Mallow on the shore of the reservoir. Just on the other side of sunset, the sky still has tinges of light to it, and we can hear the gentle chatter of dozens of other people who are still swimming, fishing, and hanging out on the water's edge as we pull our kayaks into the water. The park is open until 10 p.m., and those accompanied by a ranger can stay even later. I feel as though I'm at an after-hours summer camp, as I notice the people on piers, jumping in the water, and sitting at picnic tables nearby.

Two kayaks at the edge of Sand Hollow State Park reservoir at the end of the moonlit paddle

The night is relatively warm, as we make the gentle paddle out. We take pauses to float and listen to history; Mallow points at an island in the middle of the water: "a family of raccoons lives there", she tells us.

We let our kayaks rest when we near the isle, collecting among the rippling water to watch the moon continue its rise. I hear the water brushing against my kayak, and realize my eyes are now more used to navigating these wild spaces in the absence of the sun.

Our group is substantial. Sometimes there will 30 kayaks or paddleboards on the water at a time, Mallow says. “The moonlit paddle is pretty popular,” Mallow tells us from her own kayak, as we circle the island. "We hope programs like these both spark adventure and curiosity in visitors, and encourage neighbors to fall in love with their backyard.” As we navigate the water, we come across night fishers and a swimmer (“people train for the Ironman here,” says Mallow). I wonder if the scuba divers who were on the shore when we pushed off were entering or exiting. Before this trip, my imagination couldn't have fathomed so many ways to experience these lands after sunset.

As parks get increasingly crowded, I have to wonder if nighttime adventures will become a part of my regular routine. There are always new ways to discover America’s national and state park system—and now, I know that darkness can make even the most familiar places feel like a whole new world. Once you get past the fear of it—the dark, the height, the critters—you are free to soak up the feeling of being so small against the endless night sky, amazed by all the life that continues even once the sun has gone down.

#6200. Why Airports Remove Rubber Deposits From Runways To Keep Jets Braking Safely

eric1207cvb | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Every time a passenger jet touches down, its tires leave behind a small amount of rubber on the runway. Although this is a normal part of aircraft operations, thousands of landings can eventually create a significant buildup, especially where aircraft first make contact with the runway. Over time, these deposits can reduce the surface friction that aircraft tires need to slow down safely.

For airports, removing this accumulated rubber is an important part of routine runway maintenance, helping preserve braking performance, reduce the risk of hydroplaning, and maintain safe operating conditions in different weather. The process involves specialized equipment, careful monitoring, and carefully scheduled maintenance windows, with airports needing to balance effective cleaning against the possibility of damaging the pavement itself.

When an aircraft lands, its tires initially make contact with the runway while rotating at a relatively low speed, then rapidly accelerate to match the aircraft's forward movement. This sudden change creates considerable friction between the tires and the pavement, causing small quantities of rubber to wear away and transfer onto the runway surface. The deposits are particularly concentrated in the touchdown zone, where aircraft wheels first contact the pavement during landing. This area generally extends approximately 150 to 450 meters beyond the runway threshold, although the precise distribution depends on aircraft performance, landing techniques, and operational conditions.

Although individual landings leave relatively little rubber behind, the cumulative effect becomes significant at busy airports handling hundreds of aircraft movements every day. Heavier aircraft such as the Airbus A380 or Boeing 747 can contribute particularly substantial deposits because their tires experience considerable forces during touchdown, making runways frequently used by widebody jets especially important maintenance priorities. The rubber gradually becomes embedded in the pavement's surface texture, particularly when the heat generated during touchdown helps bond the material to the runway. As additional aircraft land, successive layers accumulate, eventually filling small surface irregularities and runway grooves that would otherwise help provide the friction needed for effective aircraft braking.

Runway pavement is designed to provide sufficient friction between aircraft tires and the ground, allowing pilots to reduce speed after touchdown while maintaining directional control. Its surface texture plays an important role in this process, helping tires maintain contact with the pavement rather than sliding across a smoother, potentially slippery surface.

When rubber deposits accumulate, they gradually cover the microscopic texture of the pavement and can obstruct the grooves cut into some runway surfaces. This reduces the ability of the runway to provide consistent friction, potentially making it harder for aircraft to slow down, particularly when braking conditions are already challenging.

The problem becomes especially important during wet weather, when water collects between aircraft tires and the runway. Properly maintained pavement texture and grooves help channel water away from the contact area, reducing the possibility of hydroplaning, a condition in which tires lose effective contact with the surface and braking performance deteriorates.

Research and airport maintenance observations have highlighted how substantial this deterioration can become in heavily contaminated touchdown zones, where friction levels may be 15% to 30% lower than elsewhere on the runway. Consequently, rubber removal is not simply an appearance-related maintenance task but an important measure for preserving the conditions required for safe aircraft operations.

The conductive rubber neutralizes electrical charge in aircraft tires.

Airport operators do not generally wait until rubber deposits become visibly excessive before arranging maintenance. Instead, they use specialized friction-measuring equipment to evaluate runway surface conditions, identifying areas where accumulated contamination or pavement deterioration could affect aircraft braking performance. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) provides guidance through its Advisory Circular 150/5320-12 series, which addresses the measurement and maintenance of skid-resistant airport pavement surfaces.

The guidance considers factors including aircraft movements, pavement characteristics, and the condition of the runway when determining how frequently friction assessments should take place. Inspection frequency increases with the number of daily jet landings. The guidance describes annual measurements for runway ends receiving fewer than 15 daily jet landings, quarterly assessments for those receiving between 31 and 90, monthly assessments for 91 to 150, and weekly measurements where traffic exceeds 210 daily landings.

Aircraft size is another consideration because widebody jets can contribute more substantial rubber deposits than smaller aircraft. The FAA guidance recommends increasing inspection frequency by one level when widebody aircraft account for more than 20% of landings on a particular runway end. When measurements indicate inadequate friction, airports can arrange rubber removal before considering more extensive pavement rehabilitation.

There are several ways airports can remove accumulated rubber, with the appropriate approach depending on the pavement material, the severity of contamination, and the condition of the runway. The FAA identifies high-pressure water, chemical solvents, high-velocity impact using abrasive materials, and mechanical grinding among the available removal techniques. High-pressure waterblasting is one of the most widely used methods because it can remove stubborn deposits without necessarily damaging the underlying pavement. Specialized vehicles direct powerful streams of water onto contaminated areas, breaking away the rubber and exposing the original surface texture and grooves beneath the accumulated material.

Chemical treatments provide another option, either as a standalone technique or in combination with waterblasting. Certain solvents help loosen rubber deposits, making them easier to remove, although airports must carefully consider chemical handling, environmental requirements, and the compatibility of cleaning products with runway materials and painted markings. Mechanical grinding and abrasive techniques can also remove difficult deposits, but they require careful control because excessive treatment could affect the pavement itself. The objective is not to remove layers of runway material but to restore the existing surface texture, ensuring that cleaning operations improve friction without creating additional maintenance problems.

Here is why the composite materials used in the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 make repairs more complex following impact incidents.

High-pressure waterblasting is particularly useful at major airports because it can cover substantial runway areas while targeting rubber deposits in the touchdown zone. The cleaning vehicles are equipped with specialized spraying systems that direct water onto the pavement at carefully controlled pressures, lifting accumulated rubber while preserving the underlying concrete or asphalt.

A notable example can be found at New York LaGuardia Airport (LGA), where rubber removal operations have been organized around the airport's demanding operating schedule. In one documented operation, a contractor used equipment capable of spraying water at approximately 17,000 to 20,000 pounds per square inch, sometimes combining the process with chemical solvents to improve removal effectiveness.

The work is generally concentrated into overnight maintenance windows, when fewer aircraft movements make it possible to close sections of runway temporarily without causing unnecessary disruption to flight operations. At LaGuardia Airport, crews working within approximately five-hour windows could clean one touchdown zone measuring around 50 feet (15.24 meters) wide and 3,000 feet (914.4 meters) long during a night's operation. LaGuardia Airport typically sees narrowbody and regional jets, with its largest operator being Delta Air Lines, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics:

The airport's rubber removal program involves about five to seven cleaning events annually, showing how often the work is needed at a busy facility. Once cleaning is complete, the treated area can be inspected and assessed before returning to normal operations, with maintenance teams checking that the pavement has been adequately restored.

Although removing rubber is essential for maintaining braking performance, the cleaning process introduces another maintenance consideration: protecting the runway pavement from excessive wear. High-pressure water can be extremely effective, but repeated treatments may gradually affect the surface, particularly when equipment operates at unnecessarily high pressures or remains concentrated in one area for too long.

A December 2025 study conducted through Iowa State University's Airport Concrete Pavement Technology Program examined best practices for runway rubber removal, including the effectiveness of different cleaning techniques and their potential effects on pavement condition. The research highlighted the importance of balancing successful rubber removal against the possibility of cumulative damage caused by repeated maintenance treatments.

One important consideration is equipment calibration, since water pressure, vehicle speed, nozzle positioning, and the number of cleaning passes can all influence the final result. Airport operators and contractors must establish suitable operating procedures for different pavement types, while ensuring that rubber is removed from grooves rather than simply cleared from the exposed surface. The research also examined opportunities to improve waterblasting efficiency by reducing operating pressures while maintaining effective cleaning results. This is particularly relevant for airports that repeatedly treat the same touchdown zones, where preserving pavement integrity can reduce the need for expensive repairs and extend the useful life of existing runway infrastructure.

If you’re a frequent traveler, scoring elite status with a major carrier like Delta Air Lines can make your journeys more relaxing and rewarding.

However, deciding which airline loyalty program benefits you the most is difficult. This is mainly due to the variations between complimentary upgrades, bonus points or miles, lounge access and other valuable perks. Plus, is it even worth pursuing elite status?

This guide breaks down Delta’s SkyMiles Medallion program, including its four public elite status tiers, how to earn status in 2027 through both travel and non-travel expenses, and the benefits of each level.

Here is everything you need to know about elite Medallion status in the Delta SkyMiles program.

Delta awards elite status to qualifying SkyMiles members each year. Elite status offers a range of benefits — from seat selection to priority boarding — that make travel more comfortable and convenient.

The airline has four published tiers of elite status:

Delta also has an invite-only status tier called Delta 360. While the airline doesn't publish its standard qualification criteria, big spenders could get an invitation to this very special club. Delta also says, “Members that have reached the 5 Million Miler milestone will receive an annual complimentary invitation for Delta 360° Membership.” That's a pretty sweet perk.

Visit our Delta Medallion glossary page for more details.

Flyers earn Medallion status based on their eligible activity during the preceding calendar year. Delta tracks travelers' activity through Medallion Qualification Dollars, which they earn by flying with Delta and its partner airlines, spending on select Delta SkyMiles American Express cards and booking Delta Vacations packages.

For Delta-marketed flights operated by Delta or a partner airline, members generally earn 1 MQD for every dollar spent on the eligible ticket price (including the base fare and carrier-imposed surcharges but excluding government-imposed taxes and fees). For eligible partner-marketed flights, MQD earnings are generally based on a percentage of the distance flown and the purchased fare class, according to Delta's published partner earning charts.

Note: Delta Main Basic tickets generally don't earn MQDs or qualify for Medallion upgrades.

Related: Your guide to Delta Air Lines Million Miler status

You can also earn MQDs on eligible award tickets and through everyday spending on the Delta SkyMiles Platinum, Platinum Business, Reserve and Reserve Business American Express cards. All four cards offer an annual 2,500-MQD Headstart, while eligible spending earns 1 MQD per $20 on Platinum cards and 1 MQD per $10 on Reserve cards.

Your status is valid through Jan. 31 of the following year. For example, travelers who qualify in 2026 will earn 2027 Medallion status, which would be valid through Jan. 31, 2028.

You must meet the applicable Medallion Qualification Dollar thresholds each calendar year to maintain that status.

Delta used to have several ways to earn status, but now the carrier uses only MQDs as qualification criteria. Below are the requirements to obtain 2027 Medallion status:

Delta did not raise the status requirements for 2027 status.

Here are some key benefits of each of Delta’s status tiers.

This is the entry tier in Delta’s program, and you’ll receive benefits like:

Delta’s mid-tier status includes Silver Medallion benefits, plus:

In addition to the Gold Medallion perks, you’ll also get the following:

You’ll get everything detailed above, plus some even better perks:

Check Delta’s website to review the full list of benefits available to SkyMiles Medallion members.

To make it easier to earn elite status, Delta gives eligible frequent flyers who also hold the following cobranded cards a head start on MQD metrics with a boost of 2,500 MQDs (per eligible card type) toward status qualification at the start of the year (and each year thereafter, until further notice):

Since the MQD head start is awarded per eligible card type, you’ll enjoy more than one 2,500 MQD boost if you have multiple eligible cards. Additionally, you’ll be able to enjoy bonus MQDs based on everyday spending on these cards.

Specifically, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $10 spent. Meanwhile, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $20 spent.

Technically, you could earn Delta Medallion status without ever stepping on a plane, simply by putting enough eligible spending on a cobranded credit card. But that doesn't necessarily make it a good strategy,

Even with the MQD Headstart, reaching the higher status tiers through credit card spending alone requires a large financial commitment. Before putting everyday purchases on a Delta card to chase status, consider whether the rewards and benefits justify the cost, when there are lots of other travel credit cards that could offer better returns for you personally.

If you earned Delta elite status in 2025, it’s valid through Jan. 31, 2027. If you qualify in 2026, your status will last until Jan. 31, 2028.

It’s critical to consider how much you’ll be traveling in the future to decide if Medallion status is worth it. If you push hard to reach Diamond Medallion status, the valuable perks outlined above apply only when traveling.

With the high MQD requirements, you would need to spend a significant amount of money with the airline or on a cobranded card to earn this top-tier status. So, you should ensure you're traveling enough to enjoy it.

That said, if you wind up within striking distance of the next tier, consider whether the benefits are worth it for you personally. There’s no reason to go out of your way for perks that don’t matter to you. Pursuing elite status with an airline you can’t realistically fly regularly isn't a great move. Look at Delta’s offerings from your home airport and whether it would be feasible to rely on that airline.

This elite-status hobby has many trade-offs, and one of the most common is deciding whether to use your preferred airline or hotel chain when neither is the most convenient nor the cheapest. Would you book a one-stop Delta flight if Southwest Airlines had a cheaper, nonstop option? If the answer is no, it may not be worth going out of your way to earn Delta elite status (or any elite status, for that matter).

The final consideration involves travel rewards credit cards. Many airline cobranded cards offer perks that mirror what you’d enjoy as an elite member. For example, the includes a free checked bag worldwide and a second checked bag when flying domestic, priority boarding and a 20% inflight savings in the form of statement credit. The card has no annual fee for the first year, then a $150 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Meanwhile, when you fly with Delta, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card provides 15 Sky Club lounge visits each year (Feb. 1 through Jan. 31). Cardmembers also qualify for various complimentary seat upgrades and receive an annual companion certificate (valid for round-trip domestic and short-haul international flights to Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America in economy, Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select or first class). To earn unlimited Sky Club visits each year, the total eligible purchases on the card must equal $75,000 or more between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31 each calendar year.

If you can pay a flat annual fee for one of these cards and gain access to perks that matter to you without going out of your way to earn elite status, that may be a good plan.

Delta Medallion status can make flying more comfortable, particularly if you're a frequent Delta customer who can take advantage of all the perks. But the value of those perks really depends on how often you fly and how much you're willing to spend to earn them.

For most travelers, the goal shouldn't necessarily be "reach Diamond Medallion." Instead, focus on the status tier that offers benefits you'll actually use and avoid spending more or booking less convenient flights just to earn a higher level of status.

If you’re considering switching your loyalty, we hope this detailed review of Delta’s elite status program has helped you make your decision.
