#6179. We Tracked The World's Longest Airbus A321XLR Flight: Here's The Detour It Takes Every Day

On October 25, IndiGo started operating its flights between Mumbai Airport (BOM) and Amsterdam Schiphol Airport(AMS) with the Airbus A321XLR, replacing the leased Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners previously used on the route. At approximately 3,707 nautical miles (6,865 km), this is now the world's longest scheduled route operated by the A321XLR, with a scheduled flight time of around 10 hours from India to the Netherlands.

However, the actual distance flown is considerably longer due to airspace restrictions across the Middle East and South Asia. Using the Simple Flying Flight Tracker, we examined the routing of flight 22 from Amsterdam to Mumbai on November 1, as well as the flight times recorded during the aircraft's first 11 days on the route. Interestingly, the data shows that although the A321XLR is smaller and generally slower than the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, its average flight time to Amsterdam has been shorter.

On November 1, IndiGo flight 22 departed Amsterdam at 2:31 PM local time, operated by an A321XLR registered VT-NLC. According to our flight tracking data, the aircraft spent approximately nine hours and nine minutes in the air before landing in Mumbai at 4:10 AM local time the following morning. Rather than following the shortest possible route toward India, the aircraft followed a more southern trajectory through Europe and the Middle East.

After departing Amsterdam, the aircraft headed southeast across Central Europe before continuing toward Turkey and Iraq. From there, the route passed through the Gulf region and Oman, avoiding Iranian airspace, before continuing toward India's western coast and eventually Mumbai. The tracking data shows how the aircraft avoids both Pakistan and Iran, despite these countries lying along the more direct route between Mumbai and Amsterdam.

The distance between Mumbai and Amsterdam is about 3,707 nautical miles (6,865 km) along the shortest route. However, according to Aerospace Global News, the necessary detours can increase the actual distance flown to approximately 4,200 nautical miles (7,778 km), or around 13% longer. This puts the flight much closer to the A321XLR's advertised maximum range of 4,700 nautical miles (8,704 km).

IndiGo's 8-hour Bali flights showcase the A321XLR's potential to transform aviation route planning as we know it.

One of the main reasons for IndiGo's detour is the ongoing closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian airlines, in place since April 2025 following rising tensions between the two countries. According to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the restrictions apply to aircraft registered in India, as well as those owned, operated, or leased by Indian carriers. Pakistan has since extended the restrictions several times.

At the same time, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has also made flying through Iran increasingly difficult. Although Iranian airspace is not subject to the same ban for Indian airlines, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) currently advises operators to avoid Iranian airspace at all altitudes.

For IndiGo, Pakistan's restrictions and the security situation in the Middle East considerably reduce available routing options between India and Europe. The airline must therefore follow a longer route, which increases fuel requirements and operating costs. The implications are particularly significant for the A321XLR, as the aircraft has far less flexibility to carry additional fuel and passengers on such a long flight than a widebody such as the Boeing 787-9 previously used on the route.

We tracked a Widerøe Dash 8 through 17 sectors in one day. The shortest flight lasted seven minutes.

Although Airbus advertises the A321XLR with a range of up to 4,700 nautical miles (8,704 km), the actual range depends on several operational factors, including passenger weight, cargo, fuel reserves, and weather conditions. The additional distance flown between Mumbai and Amsterdam consequently puts the aircraft much closer to its operational limits. To ensure that the flight can be completed nonstop, IndiGo reportedly restricts the number of seats it makes available for sale.

According to avicionline, IndiGo is currently selling fewer than 140 seats on the Mumbai-Amsterdam leg, despite its A321XLRs having a total capacity of 195 passengers. The aircraft are configured with 12 IndiGoStretch business class seats and another 183 economy class seats, meaning that over 25% of capacity is reportedly unavailable for sale. However, this restriction is not necessarily identical in both directions, as the aircraft's fuel requirements may differ depending on weather and other operating conditions.

Compared with the 787-9 previously operated on the route, this represents a considerable reduction in available capacity. The Norse Atlantic Airways aircraft offered 338 seats, including 56 premium and 282 economy class seats, according to IndiGo's original route announcement. While the A321XLR already has 143 fewer installed seats, additional restrictions on the Mumbai-Amsterdam leg mean almost 200 fewer seats may be available than on the previous widebody operation.

Interestingly, analysis of Flight Tracker data indicates that in the first 11 days of A321XLR operations, the aircraft spent less time in the air on flights from Mumbai to Amsterdam than the Boeing 787-9. Between October 25 and November 4, flight 6E21 recorded an average airborne time of nine hours and 36 minutes, approximately 20 minutes shorter than the average of nine hours and 56 minutes recorded by the 787-9 during its final nine flights. However, the opposite was true in the other direction: the A321XLR averaged nine hours to fly from Amsterdam to Mumbai, compared with eight hours and 31 minutes for the 787-9.

Looking at the individual flights, the fastest A321XLR service from Mumbai to Amsterdam was recorded on October 28, when VT-NLD completed the journey in nine hours and 19 minutes. The longest was the first flight on October 25, when the same aircraft spent nine hours and 52 minutes in the air. For comparison, the longest 787-9 flight during the period examined took 10 hours and 15 minutes on October 20. On the return journey, the fastest A321XLR service took eight hours and 32 minutes, while the longest required nine hours and 14 minutes, compared with a range of eight hours and 19 minutes to eight hours and 43 minutes for the 787-9.

However, this does not necessarily mean the A321XLR is operating more efficiently or at higher speeds than the 787-9. The two aircraft were operating at different times of day, with the 787-9 previously scheduled to depart Mumbai at 12:25 PM and Amsterdam at 8:35 PM local time, compared with 6:25 AM and 2:15 PM for the A321XLR. The comparison also covers two different periods around the start of the winter schedule, meaning wind conditions, air traffic restrictions, and the actual routings flown may have differed. The 787-9 also generally cruises faster than the A321XLR, making it difficult to attribute differences in airborne time to the aircraft types themselves.

Ultra-long-haul flying keeps pushing further. Singapore Airlines’ nonstop service between Singapore and New York is one of the longest commercial flights in the world, and Qantas’ Project Sunrise aims to link Sydney with London and New York nonstop using specially configured Airbus A350-1000s. Other marathons include Qantas’ Perth to London route and Air New Zealand’s Auckland to New York flights. Whether you were on board for 18 hours or followed a long-haul journey on the Simple Flying Flight Tracker, tell us the longest flight you’ve taken or tracked, and what made it memorable.

According to flight tracking data, IndiGo has already used four different Airbus A321XLRs on its Mumbai–Amsterdam service since October 25. In addition to VT-NLD, this includes VT-NLA, VT-NLB, and VT-NLC, with all four operating at least two flights from Mumbai to Amsterdam during the first 11 days of operations. VT-NLC has been the most frequently used aircraft, completing four services in each direction, while VT-NLD operated three flights to Amsterdam and VT-NLA and VT-NLB operated two each.

Although four aircraft appear in the flight-tracking data, the schedule allows IndiGo to operate both directions with the same aircraft within about 24 hours. On November 1, for example, VT-NLC landed in Amsterdam shortly before noon local time, before departing again at 2:31 PM. This left approximately two hours and 33 minutes between landing and takeoff, after which the aircraft arrived back in Mumbai at 4:10 AM local time the following morning.

The relatively short turnaround times allow IndiGo to operate the daily service without dedicating several aircraft exclusively to the route. Meanwhile, the airline has continued rotating its A321XLRs across other international services, including flights to Athens and Istanbul Airport (IST), where the aircraft type is also being deployed. The Mumbai-Amsterdam route nevertheless represents a considerably longer operation than those services, making it particularly dependent on the aircraft's available range and the routing restrictions currently affecting flights between India and Europe.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6177. Singapore Airlines’ New Business Class Finishes Look Cheap, Mismatched

Earlier I covered how Singapore Airlines unveiled its new first & business class, which should enter service in 2027 (hopefully). These products look like very nice improvements over the existing cabins, even if they’re not revolutionary.

That being said, I have to give Singapore Airlines some tough love on the new business class seats. Let me acknowledge that I’m a huge fan of Singapore Airlines as a brand. Any list I keep of the best airlines in the world (whether it’s the best airline brand, best first class, best business class, best inflight service, best inflight entertainment, etc.) has Singapore Airlines on it… that’s how highly I think of the brand!

But I’m also honest, regardless of how it fits my preconceived notions of a brand. I feel like I’m saying what everyone else is thinking, seemingly except for most influencers who are in Singapore for the launch event, who are just casually glossing over this… so much for attention to detail!

When I think of Singapore Airlines, the first thing that comes to mind for me is how deliberate the airline is. I don’t think there’s an airline that’s more intentional with every aspect of its guest experience, from the tone of voice with which staff speak, to warm and elegant design.

I’d say Singapore Airlines’ new first class actually looks really on brand. It’s a nice evolution of what the carrier has historically offered — it’s warm and elegant without being outdated.

And then you move to business class, and it looks like Scoot and Spirit Airlines had a baby. The gray and black is generic, the yellow accents look cheap, and then there’s so much going on with the blue and white bulkheads (if that’s actually how they’ll look).

And the Scoot reference isn’t even sarcastic. For those not familiar, Scoot is Singapore Airlines’ low cost carrier, and look at the seat finishes you’ll find there!

Usually there’s some consistency between seat finishes and wider branding, including the livery, flight attendant uniforms, etc. In this case, it’s not only not aligned, but they seem at odds with one another. There’s otherwise not a hint of yellow (or neon green, or whatever that is) in Singapore Airlines’ branding.

What so bizarre to me is how the first and business class finishes are completely mismatched, and you wouldn’t assume they belonged to the same airline. That’s because Singapore Airlines worked with different design firms (separate from the seating manufacturers as such) for the two cabins.

BMW Designworks was behind the business class seats, while PriestmanGoode was behind the first class seats. I think it’s safe to say there was no coordination between the two. I guess the argument from executives is that they want the cabin to look more modern and high tech, and go after a younger crowd, but I just don’t follow the logic.

It’s clear that Singapore Airlines put many years of effort into this product, and frankly I’m just surprised that Singapore Airlines executives signed off on this. Am I just in the minority in thinking this isn’t a good look for the airline? Did some marketer assure Singapore Airlines executives this was great branding, and they were wrong? Or did everyone just independently decide that this looks great?

If they at least eliminated the yellow stripes, it would no longer look cheap, but would instead look generic. I’m just surprised that this is the conclusion they came to.

Singapore Airlines of course had a big media event in Singapore to celebrate the launch of this product. I don’t attend media events, just as a general policy, because I don’t find them to be a great use of time. But I certainly do enjoy seeing the coverage from others.

What I find fascinating is the inherent bias that exists when someone is invited to something. For example, if you look at the comments on my post about the new cabins, the single thing most commented on by OMAAT community members is how bad the business class colors look.

If you watched the videos on social media about this, there’s oddly no commentary on that. Admittedly I haven’t seen all the coverage, but the worst coverage I’ve seen is someone saying they “don’t mind” the colors, and that it’s a “big departure” from the old look. Okay, that’s not exactly an endorsement.

I also haven’t found a single person who attended the event who said “I love the new colors,” which probably tells you everything you need to know. For that matter, it’s one thing if people acknowledged “I realize the colors might not look good in pictures, but in person, it’s a different story.” But I haven’t heard that either.

To me this gets at the rather complicated relationship between so many brands and influencer types. If you can say all the things you love about the product, shouldn’t you also feel totally comfortable criticizing the parts of the experience you don’t like, though?

While we’re on this topic, let me add one more point. Being able to sit in seats at media events like this is of course cool, but it really doesn’t actually give you an impression of what it’s like to fly in a product, and that’s why it’s not something I particularly value, as an experience.

Of course a big business class seat is comfortable when you sit in it for a minute, and you’re filming content. But the real test of a product is when you spend hours in the seat, when you recline the seat into a bed, when you try to move your laptop around while you’re being served a meal, etc.

I once had the opportunity to spend a night in an aircraft seat on the ground (I can’t really say more, since I signed an NDA, but it was to provide feedback to a seating manufacturer). To me that was fascinating, because it really gives you an understanding of what the experience is like. My feeling about the seat was very different after being in the seat for many hours vs. when I sat down.

Singapore Airlines has unveiled its new cabins, and there’s a lot to be excited about, as the hard products look very nice. However, Singapore Airlines’ new business class cabin finishes are a real mystery to me, because the yellow stripe looks cheap (I mean, it seems to be inspired by the carrier’s low cost subsidiary), and completely mismatched with first class.

The airline used different design firms for first class and business class. For an airline so focused on attention to detail and being very deliberate in terms of design, this strikes me as a misstep. Anyway, Singapore Airlines, I still love you and think you’re one of the best airlines in the world…

Where do you stand on Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat finishes? Does anyone love them?

#6176. Livery of the Week: JetBlue’s Florida Panthers Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Since the beginning of its operations in 2000, New York-based airline JetBlue has always considered South Florida as one of its primary markets, with a presence at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood Airport that has grown during the past 25 years to include up to 25 aircraft based overnight at the airport and over 2,000 people supporting its operations in Broward County.

As a sign of its commitment to the South Florida community, JetBlue has announced a multi-year extension for an expanded partnership with the Florida Panthers, the NHL’s southernmost franchise that captured back-to-back Stanley Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. The partnership will see JetBlue present a newly redesigned Champions Club at the Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise, Florida, home of the Panthers, and to celebrate the announcement, the airline unveiled a special Panthers-themed livery for one of its Airbus A320 aircraft.

The new livery draws its inspiration from the Panthers’ jersey, therefore sporting the iconic Panthers’ red across the entire fuselage, with the outline of a golden panther all across the central part of the fuselage, right next to JetBlue’s logo. The Panthers’ shield logo is on the aircraft tail in navy and gold.

Bold red letters spelling FLORIDA appear on the bottom of the aircraft, where there’s also a leaping cat, the team’s logo. More symbols of the Panthers and the State of Florida appear in other parts of the fuselage: a simplified Florida flag appears near the front of the aircraft together with a palm tree and a hockey stick, which represent the secondary logo for the team.

“South Florida has been part of JetBlue’s story since our very first flight more than two decades ago, and we’re continuing to build on that history in a big way as Broward County’s largest airline,” said Marty St. George, JetBlue’s president, in a press release. “The Panthers know a thing or two about winning in South Florida, and we’re bringing that same energy as we expand our network, elevate the customer experience and deepen our commitment to the community. ‘Go Cats Go’ is a fun way to celebrate our shared passion for South Florida and team up with a franchise that knows how to make some noise.”

The aircraft chosen to display this special livery is an Airbus A320, registered as N784JB, delivered to the airline on Feb. 11, 2011.

The original name of the aircraft was “Blue And Infinity And Beyond,” which has been changed to “Go Cats Go” following the repainting in this new livery.

#6174. When Is An Airport Lounge Visit Not Worth It? Here’s How I Decide…

It goes without saying that a lot about the passenger experience when traveling by air has changed over the decades, both for better and worse. I think perhaps one of the most fascinating transformations we’ve seen over the years involves airport lounges, and how their purpose has completely flipped.

I’d like to talk about that in a bit more detail in this post, and share my approach to using lounges. Let me emphasize that there are of course all kinds of lounges out there, from international first class lounges, to international business class lounges, to Priority Pass, membership, and credit card lounges. This post is primarily about lounges that fall into that last category, in terms of being pretty widely accessible.

Look, I’m not trying to sound like some boomer talking about how things were in “the good old days” (nothing against boomers… hi, dad!), but I think it’s interesting to compare how things were 15-20 years ago, to how they are today.

Back in the day, airport lounges — even the most basic ones — were primarily about escaping the hustle and bustle of the terminal, and having a quiet place from which to work, with free Wi-Fi and easy access to charging ports. At the time, free Wi-Fi and charging ports in terminals were incredibly rare. The food in most standard domestic lounges sucked — it was typically cubed cheese, snack mix, and not a whole lot else.

It also goes without saying that lounges were mostly very poorly monetized. Airport real estate is incredibly expensive, and lounges were primarily a cost center for their operators, as part of an overall value proposition for travelers.

Fast forward to today, and look at the state of lounges in the United States. Lounges have much better food than they used to, and they also have much better amenities than they used to. Also, exponentially more people have access to the lounges than they used to. They’re actually pretty nice destinations in airports.

The catch is that they’ve completely lost their initial purpose — they’re no longer a place you go to escape the crowds, and quite to the contrary, they’re often the most crowded place in a terminal. In many lounges you’ll find every single seat occupied, and even a very long waitlist to get in.

Obviously this is great for monetization, since lounge operators maximize their return by having the lounges utilized as much as possible, so that the cost can be divided by the highest number of people possible. Ironically, we’ve also seen terminals largely get much nicer over the years. It’s nowadays common to see free Wi-Fi and charging ports throughout terminals, and it’s usually not too hard to just find a quiet place to sit, with more peace than you’d find in a lounge.

Back in the day, if I had lounge access, my obvious move was always to use the lounge if I had time. I mean, that seems like a pretty obvious move, right? After all, you get access to something “premium,” so you want to make the most of it. Most people with TSA PreCheck don’t say “meh, you know, I think I’ll skip that today and go through the regular line.”

At the same time, I think one has to step back and look at things objectively. At times it almost feels like people use lounges religiously in order to justify the annual fees on their credit cards, and so they can talk about how they’re eating for “free.”

You’ll often see people on social media essentially call airport lounges upper middle class airport cafeterias, and that’s probably not actually too far off in terms of how they’re practically used… and there’s nothing wrong with that!

Personally, for places with consistently crowded lounges, my approach to lounge use is pretty straightforward:

Honestly, this is one of the reasons I really love grab & go lounges, where you can pick up something to take with you. To me that’s the ideal setup, since it serves the purpose I’m actually looking for from lounges — if a lounge is going to be crowded, I’d rather just be able to grab what I’d like, and head somewhere quiet.

As someone who loves coffee, it’s why I also appreciate when lounges have great coffee to go. It’s typically the item I most want to consume at airports, and the wait for a cup of coffee at an airport can often be quite long early in the morning.

The lounge crowding issue nowadays is only made worse by the number of people who are watching videos and making calls with no headphones in lounges.

The whole concept of airport lounges has changed massively over the years. Monetization of lounges has largely gotten better, as they’ve become a key component of the credit card race that we’re seeing between airlines and card issuers.

That’s a double edged sword. On the one hand, lounges have become higher quality, on average. On the other hand, demand for them has also increased massively.

For the most part, lounges are no longer a place you go to escape the bustle of the terminal, and to use free Wi-Fi and charge your electronics. Now they’re a place you go to eat, drink, and wait in line.

The way I’ve used lounges has definitely evolved over the years, and it’s one of the reasons I appreciate the grab & go concept that we’re increasingly seeing. Unless I’m hungry or thirsty, I prefer just finding a quiet gate area.

What do you make of how airport lounges have evolved, and has your approach to using them changed?

#6172. How To Combine Marriott Bonvoy Points Between Accounts For Free

The major hotel loyalty programs all have different policies when it comes to combining points between accounts belonging to different members.

For example, Hilton Honors lets you transfer points to any other member online, and you can transfer up to 500,000 points and receive up to two million points per account per calendar year. Meanwhile World of Hyatt lets you transfer points to any other member online as well, with the ability to give or receive up to 525,000 points per year.

Marriott Bonvoy is the world’s largest loyalty program, so how does the program’s policy on combining points compare? Not very favorably, but it can still prove to be quite useful. I’d like to go over the details of how this feature of the program works.

Marriott Bonvoy lets you combine points between accounts at no cost, with the following restrictions:

There’s no need to be related to the person you’re sharing points with, or even to share the same address. Rather you can transfer your points to any member.

The only limitation is how long accounts have to be active:

Qualifying activity includes any earning or redeeming of points, with the exception of gifting or transferring points, receiving points as a gift or transfer, or earning points through social media programs.

Along those lines, it’s also worth pointing out that combining points with a member won’t count toward extending the expiration of your points, if that’s something you’re going for (Bonvoy points expire after 24 months of inactivity).

It’s possible to combine Marriott Bonvoy points between accounts either by phone or via an online tool, so let’s go over both of those options.

It’s possible to transfer points to another Marriott Bonvoy member at this link. The member looking to transfer their points (rather than the recipient) should log into their account at that link, and they’ll then be brought to the points transfer tool.

On that page you’ll have to enter the recipient’s first and last name, Marriott Bonvoy number, and how many points you want to transfer (between 1,000 and 100,000).

You’ll then be asked to receive a verification code, either by email or text.

You’ll then receive confirmation that your request has been made. While the transfer tool suggests that it could take up to one hour for points to post, in reality they typically post instantly.

If for whatever reason you don’t want to use the online tool to transfer points to another Marriott Bonvoy member, you can continue to do this by phone. Here’s how the process works:

Now that we’ve established that you can transfer points, perhaps the bigger question is why you would want to. There are some circumstances where combining points between Marriott Bonvoy accounts could make a lot of sense:

Ford transfers 100,000 Bonvoy points to me every year. Why? Because he has a sizable Bonvoy points balance, I have the higher status with Marriott, and we usually travel together. There’s more value in having Bonvoy points in my account rather than his, so that we can take advantage of elite perks when redeeming points.

While Marriott Bonvoy isn’t the most generous when it comes to letting members combine points between accounts, this is still a functionality worth being aware of. There are plenty of circumstances where it could make sense to combine points, whether you’re looking to maximize elite benefits or book travel for others.

The major catch is the restriction on how old the accounts have to be, plus the limit on how many points you can transfer, and how often you can transfer points.

Have you ever transferred Marriott Bonvoy points? What was your experience like?

Royal Caribbean's newest megaship is set to make its U.S. debut this weekend.

Passengers will board Legend of the Seas, the cruise line's third Icon Class vessel, at Fort Lauderdale's Port Everglades on Sunday for a pre-inaugural three-night trip to the Bahamas.

The cruise line added the departure ahead of the ship's previously announced Nov. 11 inaugural voyage from the cruise hub, giving travelers an early chance to experience its newest Icon Class ship.

The sailing will include a stop at Royal Caribbean's private island destination, Perfect Day at CocoCay, followed by a day at sea before returning to Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11.

At 248,633 gross tons, Legend of the Seas is the world's largest cruise ship, sharing the title with its two same-size Icon Class sisters, Icon of the Seas and Star of the Seas. The vessel can accommodate up to 7,600 passengers and approximately 2,350 crew members.

Like its sister ships, Legend of the Seas features eight neighborhoods, seven pools and a lineup of family-friendly attractions, including Category 6, a six-slide water park. The ship also introduces several new experiences, including the Hollywood-themed Hollywoodland Supper Club and additional dining options in the AquaDome.

Related: Royal Caribbean cruise ships from newest to oldest — a complete list

Legend of the Seas debuted in Europe in summer 2026, sailing seven-night Western Mediterranean itineraries from Barcelona and Rome before crossing the Atlantic to begin its Caribbean season.

Following two initial Bahamas sailings, Legend of the Seas will operate six- to eight-night itineraries from Fort Lauderdale to Western and Southern Caribbean destinations — including some places, like Aruba and Curacao, that don't normally see much action from Icon Class ships. Depending on the sailing, it'll also make port calls in Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and Mexico. Plus, every sailing will visit Perfect Day at CocoCay.

Rates for six-night trips begin around $1,000 per person, and eight-night trips begin around $1,400. However, prices differ greatly based on your chosen itinerary, room type and dates of travel.

#6169. Qatar Airways & Hans Zimmer Unveil “Burgundy Symphony” Sonic Identity

Qatar Airways has introduced a new signature soundtrack, which can be heard on flights as of today. As someone who cares so much about airline boarding music that I keep a list of my favorite tunes, it’s something I’m both excited and sad about…

Qatar Airways has partnered with Oscar and Grammy award-winning composer Hans Zimmer for a new sonic identity for the airline, featuring a signature sound “that will elevate the passenger experience onboard and beyond.” This collaboration was first announced back in July 2025, but the music has now been released, as of November 2026.

You’re almost certainly familiar with Zimmer’s work, even if the name doesn’t ring a bell, as his music has been featured in everything from The Lion King, to Gladiator, to Pirates of the Caribbean, to The Da Vinci Code.

This new music will be played as the boarding and landing music on Qatar Airways flights, and will also be released as a full musical album on major streaming platforms, and across the carrier’s social channels.

The music is described as being “inspired by Qatar and its culture,” and it features a “Burgundy Symphony” album, which is a five-track album that encapsulates the airline’s wider sound identity and signature sound elements.

The album is intended to capture the rhythm of travel through five original tracks, each reflecting a different stage of the journey:

You can hear the entire album below, with all five tracks (in order). The music is no doubt beautiful, don’t get me wrong — Zimmer is a generational talent, who has arguably revolutionized the sound of modern cinema.

But I just somehow don’t find it to be as distinctive as the previous track. But maybe my feelings about that will change over time. I will say, the music is incredibly relaxing, and I’ll definitely be listening to this in the background while working.

As someone who loves airline boarding music, I’m of course delighted when airlines invest money into that aspect of the passenger experience (and my gosh, I can’t imagine how much money Qatar Airways is spending to get a whole album of Hans Zimmer music). It shows such an attention to detail that you don’t find on many airlines.

That being said, I adore Qatar Airways’ old boarding music, created by local Qatari composer Dana Al Fardan, and I just find it to be so incredibly calming and relaxing. The initial track was “The Awakening,” the second track was “The Dawn,” and the third track was “The Ascent.”

So I’m sad to hear that these will no longer be played, though at the same time, the new tracks are lovely as well. I can’t help but wonder if this development is almost a competitive response to airline startup Riyadh Air, which revealed its high profile brand sonic before even launching operations.

We know the two carriers are sort of going at one another, with Riyadh Air CEO Tony Douglas having stated that it’s “haram” that “the number one premium passenger for Qatar Airways, are Saudi nationals,” and Qatar Airways has responded with some pretty shady ads.

Qatar Airways has partnered with Hans Zimmer on its new sonic identity, including the introduction of a new boarding music track. As a self proclaimed connoisseur of boarding music, I’m very excited to see this collaboration, though I’ll miss Dana Al Fardan’s trilogy. Oh well, I guess I can always still listen to it at home!

What do you make of Qatar Airways partnering with Hans Zimmer?

#6168. The Airbus A350 Has Become The New Flagship Of Some Airlines While Others Stick With The Boeing 777

InsectWorld & Markus Mainka | Shutterstock , Simple Flying

Air Canada is about to take its first Airbus widebody in nearly three decades. Emirates, meanwhile, added 65 more Boeing 777-9s last November to an order book that now stands at 270. Same industry, same decade, opposite flagships. According to Business Traveller, Air Canada's eight A350-1000s begin arriving in the second half of 2030, while Emirates says its first 777-9 should land in the second quarter of 2027.

The split is not about brand loyalty, and it is messier than the headline suggests. Qatar Airways flies the A350-1000 and has ordered the 777-9. Emirates, the world's biggest 777 operator, also flies A350s. Behind those choices are fleet age, delivery schedules, route networks, passenger capacity and, in one particularly important case, an engine. The timing of each airline's decision matters almost as much as the aircraft itself.

Qatar Airways was the A350-1000's launch operator, putting it into service in February 2018, as Simple Flying previously reported. Japan Airlines(JAL), Delta Air Lines, Air Canada, and Qantas have since built parts of their long-haul plans around the larger Airbus, and British Airways flies it too. Riyadh Air and Philippine Airlines have also ordered the type.

The Boeing side has a different starting point. Emirates operates the largest 777 fleet on Earth, about 140 aircraft, based on the 119 777-300ERs, 10 777-200LRs, and 11 freighters. United Airlines flies nearly 100 777s and no A350s at all. American Airlines is retrofitting its 777-300ERs, while Lufthansa is due to become the first airline to fly the 777-9 in 2027. The 777-9 first flew in January 2020 and remains uncertified.

Timing accounts for much of the difference. By June 2026, the A350-1000 had 367 orders and 114 deliveries. The 777-9 was still uncertified and targeting a first delivery roughly seven years late. Airlines with aging 777-300ERs could not wait for Boeing's schedule to settle. Others had enough life left in their fleets to take the risk.

JAL offers the cleanest example. Its A350-1000 entered service between Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND) and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in January 2024, and daily Los Angeles flights followed on June 30, 2025, according to Japan.travel. Delta will add 20 A350-1000s from early 2027 on top of 41 A350-900s already flying. Delta says the new jet burns more than 20 percent less fuel per available seat mile than the aircraft it replaces, and it will debut a next-generation Delta One Suite with a flat bed more than three inches (7.6 cm) longer, giving over six and a half feet (two meters) to stretch out.

Air Canada's reasoning is the most revealing. The A350-1000 is a logical stand-in for the 777-300ER, with a 19 to 25 percent cut in fuel burn per passenger-nautical mile and a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) instead of the 777 family's 8,000 feet (2,438 meters).

A firm delivery slot mattered more to Air Canada than a bigger airplane on paper. Even so, the airline is not leaving Boeing: it operates 19 777-300ERs and expects 14 787-10s, so the A350 is diversification, not defection. The most dramatic conversion belongs to Qantas, because it is retiring a beloved superjumbo years ahead of schedule.

The 777X is nearly ready for service, how will it fare against Airbus's A350?

According to Executive Traveller, Qantas will gradually phase out its 10 A380s from 2028, roughly four years earlier than a plan that pointed to fiscal 2032. Qantas took its first A380 in September 2008 and its last in December 2011, so the oldest are approaching two decades of service. Lufthansa and Etihad Airways look set to keep their superjumbos into the early 2030s, while Korean Air and Qatar Airways are likely to follow Qantas out. CEO Vanessa Hudson cited rising maintenance costs and high fuel prices tied to the Middle East conflict. The A350-1000 will take over the flagship routes from Sydney to Singapore, London, and Los Angeles.

The transition away from the A380 will not be without capacity challenges. According to Qantas, its A380s have 485 seats, compared with an indicative capacity of more than 250 seats for the planned A350-1000LR replacements. The timing also presents a challenge: as Hudson reportedly said the additional replacement aircraft would not arrive until after 2030. In the meantime, 787s are expected to cover A380 services to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and Johannesburg.

Qantas expects its 12 Project Sunrise A350-1000ULRs to help offset the loss of A380 capacity. Some will operate Perth–London and Auckland–New York services, freeing up 787s for other routes. Designed for ultra-long-haul flights such as Sydney–London and Sydney–New York, the aircraft completed its maiden flight on June 2. Its additional 20,000-liters fuel tank supports flights of up to 22 hours, helping Qantas expand its ultra-long-haul network.

Consider two routes. Dubai–London, at roughly 2,900 nautical miles (5,370 km), favors the 777-9's approximately 16% seating advantage, as capacity helps reduce cost per passenger. Perth–London, at around 7,800 nautical miles (14,450 km), favors the A350-1000, with a range of 8,700 nautical miles (16,112 km), compared with 8,000 nautical miles (14,816 km) for the 777-9.

Airbus also notes that carbon-fiber composites account for 53% of the A350-1000's structural weight, helping reduce fuel consumption and maintenance requirements. The same industry, but very different economics. The A350 therefore has an advantage on longer routes, particularly where range and delivery timing matter. Yet some of the world's biggest airlines continue to favor Boeing.

For Emirates, the answer is largely about scale. Its order for 65 more 777-9s, worth US$38 billion at list prices, pushed its 777X total to 270, with first deliveries expected from the second quarter of 2027. The 777-9 seats 375 to 450 passengers against 350 to 410 on the A350-1000, and on dense trunk routes that gap is significant. Emirates chairman Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum has also said the airline wants manufacturers to build larger aircraft, and Emirates holds options to convert some orders to the 777-10 or 777-8. According to Executive Traveller, it plans to keep its A380s flying until 2040.

American Airlines took a middle road. Its first retrofitted 777-300ER, which began flying from New York to Buenos Aires on September 2, offers 144 premium seats, including 70 Flagship Suites, across a fleet of 20. Flagship First will no longer be sold on those aircraft for travel from November 19. United Airlines' picture is stranger. As of June 30, the airline still lists 45 A350-900s as firm commitments but assigns no delivery dates, amid a $175 million dispute with Rolls-Royce. United's position was considerably different in 2022. According to Reuters , the airline was then considering a triple-digit widebody order involving either 787s or A350s.

Kirby's comments reflected the scale of United's fleet-renewal ambitions, although the airline ultimately committed to 100 787s in December 2022. United has since built a 787 order book of 146 firm commitments, which gives it an easy way out. One name keeps turning up in the background: Rolls-Royce. The engine choice on the A350-1000 has become part of the fleet decision itself.

The list is dominated by Qatar Airways' and Cathay Pacific's flights to North America.

The A350-1000 has a single engine option, the Trent XWB-97, and Emirates president Tim Clark has called it defective, with engines that, by one account, stay on the wing for only about a quarter of the time Emirates needs between maintenance visits. Airbus said this month that a durability package aims to double time on the wing from 2028, though that improvement has not yet been demonstrated in airline service. Rolls-Royce has committed £1 billion across its Trent Engine family, with much of it aimed at the XWB-97, a sign of how seriously it takes the problem.

Delivery certainty may still outweigh the criticism. Emirates reportedly weighed an order for at least 30 A350-1000s, and Simple Flying previously explored why the logic works: the Boeing 777X remains unavailable, while the A350-900 already performs well in Dubai, and the two A350 variants share a type rating and systems architecture, so pilots move between them with minimal extra training. Emirates counts 13 A350-900s in service and 52 on order. Even the Boeing camp's flagship customer is quietly buying Airbus. The planemaker lists certification and first delivery of the Qantas-bound A350-1000ULR for 2027, so the long-range case is about to move from demonstration to service.

Neither aircraft has to win every route. For airlines, the choice comes down to range, capacity, costs and availability. In some cases, the smartest move is not choosing one over the other, but using both where they make the most sense.

Cathay Pacific appears on the A350-1000 customer list alongside Qatar and also among 777-9 customers, including Singapore Airlines, Lufthansa, and British Airways. Qatar Airways, which has flown the A350-1000 since 2018, has 124 777-9s on order. The usual logic is straightforward: the larger 777 suits the busiest routes, while the A350 can cover missions where range and efficiency matter more. Airbus is also studying a stretched version, informally called the A350-2000, to fill the gap between the A350-1000 and the 777X, although a formal launch depends on how airlines assess the market once the 777X enters service.

Airbus will likely have well over 150 A350-1000s flying by the time Boeing delivers its first 777-9 in 2027. That gives the A350 a clear advantage: airlines can look at years of operating experience rather than projected performance figures. Airlines needing aircraft now have few practical alternatives to the A350-1000, and the choice gets harder for deliveries between 2027 and 2030. Air Canada's slots only begin in late 2030, showing how far ahead some large widebody campaigns are being planned.

Boeing still leads the order book, with more than 520 777-9s against 367 A350-1000s. Airbus, however, has already delivered 114 A350-1000s. The next few 777-9 deliveries will therefore be important beyond the headline numbers. If Lufthansa's first aircraft slips again, airlines with aging 777-300ERs will have another reason to look at Airbus. If Emirates turns its reported A350-1000 interest into a firm order, the decision becomes harder to describe as a simple Airbus-versus-Boeing split.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Emirates is flying about 30 a350-900 with another 43 examples to follow. Churing out articles is one thing but, quality of the article should improve.

#6166. Combative LaGuardia ATC Berates Southwest Pilot Over Taxiway Mistake

The pilots of a Southwest Airlines flight departing New York LaGuardia (LGA) made a mistake. What’s wild to me is how unprofessionally the air traffic controller handled that mistake, though, and the clear joy he got from being able to chew out the pilots…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an incident that happened shortly after 7PM local time on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at New York LaGuardia Airport.

A Southwest Boeing 737-800 was getting ready to depart to Dallas Love Field (DAL), and was just getting permission to taxi to the runway, which is when the issues started:

Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541, runway 13, give way to an E170 off the left, taxi via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22.”Southwest pilot: “Taxi runway 13 via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22, give way to E170 off our left, Southwest 4541.”

The Southwest plane then started taxiing, but immediately cut off the Embraer E170 it was supposed to give way to on the taxiway. That was probably a dumb error (more on that in a bit), but that’s when the air traffic controller really got excited:

Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541.”Southwest pilot: “Southwest 4541, go ahead.”Air traffic controller: “Did you give way to the 175 we told you about?”Southwest pilot: “Uh, sorry, we were looking at a different one. We’ll still be on B. Are we clear?”Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541, hold there. Show me the 175 that you were looking out for.”Southwest pilot: “We’re looking at the Delta colors to the left, Southwest 4541.”Air traffic controller: “So that’s the one we told you to give way to and you cut them off, right?”Southwest pilot: “Affirmative, Southwest 4541. Where would you like us to go?”Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541, possible pilot deviation, advise ready to copy a phone number.”

The Southwest pilot then copied down the number, and then the air traffic controller broadcast on frequency that “Southwest looks like just decided to do whatever they want.”

There are two issues here — the mistake on the part of the Southwest pilots, and how the air traffic controller responded.

Obviously the Southwest pilots screwed up here, as they did cut off the Embraer. As much as Southwest pilots are known for their speedy taxis, I’d be willing to bet this wasn’t intentional, because if you try to fight a NYC-area air traffic controller, you’ll lose every time. 😉

My guess is that the pilots were genuinely confused by the word order of the instructions, and didn’t fully process the instructions until it was too late (which isn’t to excuse it, but just to try to make sense of how this happened).

The instructions were to taxi to “runway 13, give way to an E170 off the left, taxi via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22.” Based purely on those instructions, it wasn’t entirely clear where the Embraer would be, since the instruction to give way was given after the runway assignment.

It seems like a clearer way to describe that would be to give the taxi instructions, and then explicitly say where the plane is that they should be giving way to. So something like “runway 13, taxi via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22, give way to the Delta colors E170 off on your left on A.”

But the real issue was the laser focus that the controller had on just talking down to these pilots and proving a point. He literally stopped traffic so that he could win an argument. By all means give the pilots a number for a possible pilot deviation, and discuss this stuff off frequency. But to stop traffic, argue with the pilots, give them a number, and then throw in another insulting comment, is just uncalled for and incredibly unprofessional.

Compare this to an incident at Boston Logan (BOS) a few weeks back, which I’d argue was more serious. An Etihad Boeing 787 entered a runway without permission and caused a go around. Shocking as it might be to some New York area controllers, the Boston controller didn’t take it as an opportunity to insult someone on frequency, and stop traffic. Instead, he handled it professionally, kept planes moving, and then they got a number for a pilot deviation. That’s how it should be handled.

The pilots of a Southwest Boeing 737 chose the wrong airport to make a mistake at, as it quickly turned into the highlight of the air traffic controller’s day. The air traffic controller stopped traffic so that he could school pilots and give them a number for a possible pilot deviation, rather than keeping planes moving and then discussing this off frequency.

What do you make of this LaGuardia ATC interaction?

#6164. Atmos Rewards Summit Card 3x Points On Foreign Purchases: Any Catch?

The $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) is the premium personal credit card of Atmos Rewards, which is the combined loyalty program of Alaska & Hawaiian.

There are lots of reasons to get this card, from a huge welcome bonus, to a great return on spending, to valuable perks just for being a cardmember, like free points sharing and waived partner award booking fees. It’s a card I’ve already applied for.

In this post, I’d like to talk about what might just be the most interesting aspect to spending on the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, which borders on seeming too good to be true. Specifically, I’m talking about how the card earns 3x points on all foreign purchases, with no caps, which is a pretty unheard of bonus category.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card offers 3x points on eligible foreign transactions, with no caps. This applies to both the primary cardmember and to any authorized users (authorized users can be added to the card at no extra cost). Specifically, eligible foreign purchases include:

In the interest of being thorough, let me copy and paste the portion of the terms addressing this:

3 Points for eligible Foreign Transactions: Earn 3 points for every $1 spent on eligible foreign transaction Net Purchases (1) made in a foreign currency, or (2) made in U.S. dollars if the transaction is made or processed outside of the United States and US Territories. Bank of America is not responsible for how foreign transactions are billed to the card.

Let me emphasize that the card has no foreign transaction fees, so not only are you not paying those fees, but you’re being rewarded very handsomely. The exchange rates used by the card are also totally fair, and competitive.

Personally, I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so I’d consider that to be a 4.5% return on all foreign purchases, which is unrivaled. If you have an eligible Bank of America account, you can even get a 10% relationship bonus, meaning you could net 3.3x points per dollar spent.

While there are some cards that might be slightly more rewarding for specific categories of foreign spending — like dining, airfare, or hotels — there’s not another card that’s broadly this rewarding for all foreign spending.

Keep in mind that this is only the start of the rewards you get for spending on the card:

Admittedly this is a very specific situation, but if you were to spend $60,000 abroad, you’d earn 180,000 Atmos Rewards points, 30,000 Atmos Rewards status points (not including the 10,000 status points boost the card offers annually), and a 100,000-point Global Companion Award.

If you want to take it a step further, those 40,000 Atmos Rewards status points are enough to earn Atmos Rewards Gold status, which gets you oneworld Sapphire, offering perks like priority services and lounge access. That’s a pretty incredible setup, eh?

As you’d expect, there are a lot of questions about the Atmos Rewards Summit Card 3x points on foreign spending:

“I’ve looked but I couldn’t find what the terms are for the 3x points on foreign purchases. Is there an annual limit? Does it need to be combined with domestic spend?”

“Let me get this straight – any transaction outside the US will be in the 3x category? Is this capped? As someone living in Europe, that could make this card extremely valuable for me…”

Officially, there are no limits on how much you can spend abroad. Of course to get this card, you need to be eligible for credit cards in the United States, which requires having an address in the country, among other things.

As I look at the terms, there’s nothing there stating any limits as to how much you can spend abroad, both in absolute and relative (to domestic spending) terms. In practice, there are plenty of Americans living abroad who use US credit cards (given how much more lucrative they are than most foreign cards) without any issues.

So I don’t think there’s a catch here, but I will say this (and I’m not trying to fear monger, but am just trying to address the only potential concern) — banks can shut down your credit cards at will, and decide they no longer want to do business with you.

In the past, I’ve read reports where credit card issuers have shut down accounts because too big of a percentage of spending was consistently abroad. That’s far from consistent, though, and I’ve also heard of people using their card living abroad for a decade without an issue.

My point is to say that based on how things currently stand, I think this benefit is as good as it sounds, and I wouldn’t expect any major changes (though who knows, maybe at some point down the road we’ll see a cap on how much foreign spending can earn bonus points).

Many people may wonder if this is sustainable in the long run, so let me point out a few things:

My point is simply to say that this doesn’t strike me anywhere near the top of the list of unsustainable credit card benefits, though we’ll see how this plays out.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card offers 3x points on foreign spending, with no foreign transaction fees and no caps. This is an unheard of bonus category, and makes this by far the best card for foreign spending.

What makes this even better is that beyond the 3x points, you also earn one status point for every $2 spent, and if you spend $60,000 in an anniversary year, you can receive a 100,000-point Global Companion Award. This return on spending is every bit as great as it sounds, and this is the card to have in your wallet if you travel abroad a lot.

What do you make of the Atmos Rewards Summit Card 3x points on foreign purchases?

One important nuance is that although many regions around the world impose interchange fee caps, those caps generally do not apply to U.S.-issued cards. (Fees still tend to be lower outside of the U.S., however.) It is entirely possible that 3x (or 3.3x) on foreign purchases will turn out to be an unsustainable perk because it does not align with the underlying unit economics of a foreign purchase. However, the same could be said of 5x on airline purchases (Platinum Card) or 4x on hotels (CSR). In general cards offer generous bonus categories and accept that, for certain customers, they may not recover the full costs of doing so. As someone living in Europe, I am certainly maximizing this very unique and rewarding bonus category.

#6163. Southwest 737 Flew 44 Times Before Wind Damage Was Found

A Southwest Boeing 737 MAX 8 flew 44 times before maintenance crews discovered tail damage that investigators traced to a thunderstorm more than a week earlier. In a final report released Thursday, the National Transportation Safety Board said the damage went undetected through a scheduled maintenance check and caused a standby rudder control unit to operate abnormally.

The damage came to light after Southwest flight 746 experienced unexpected rudder movements on May 25, 2024, while flying from Phoenix to Oakland, California. All 175 passengers and six crew members were uninjured. The aircraft, registered N8825Q, sustained substantial damage.

The NTSB traced the damage to the night of May 16, when the jet was parked in New Orleans, and thunderstorms brought gusts of up to 73 knots, or about 84 mph. Investigators said the wind likely moved the rudder enough to damage ribs inside the vertical stabilizer where the standby rudder control unit was mounted.

At the time, Boeing’s 737 maintenance manual called for a special inspection after an extreme wind event but gave no wind speed at which the check was required. The manual listed signs such as an aircraft moving over its wheel chocks or leaving tire skid marks.

Southwest also lacked a process to notify maintenance control when a parked aircraft had been exposed to extreme winds. The jet flew the next morning without the inspection.

Over the next week, the aircraft completed 38 flights with no reported rudder or yaw damper problems. It then underwent scheduled maintenance in Houston on May 23, including a test of the standby hydraulic system. The procedure required a mechanic at the tail to verify that the rudder moved in response to pedal inputs.

Hangar video showed the rudder moving to the right but failing to move to the left. Investigators said no one was at the tail to verify the movement. Southwest’s maintenance records showed the test was signed off as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The NTSB could not determine whether the test worsened the existing damage.

On the fourth flight the next day, a crew disconnected the yaw damper after reporting that it was overcorrecting in turbulence. The yaw damper uses the rudder to counter side-to-side motion.

The jet flew one more leg with the system listed as inoperative. It then passed a functional test, and the yaw damper was returned to service before Flight 746.

On the Oakland flight, the captain noticed momentary stiffness in the rudder pedals while turning onto the runway. Shortly after reaching 34,000 feet, he felt what he described as “a small amount of Dutch roll.” Both pilots felt the pedals move, and the oscillations recurred after the crew descended to 32,000 feet.

Flight data showed one episode of rudder and pedal oscillations lasting about 20 seconds, with no significant change in heading or bank angle. Investigators found that the abnormal movement appeared in the data from the first flight after the Houston maintenance check, before crews reported it. They observed it only when the yaw damper was engaged.

Southwest removed the aircraft from service after it landed in Oakland. The airline later inspected the rudder control unit mounting areas across its 737 MAX fleet and found no similar damage. It also added individual mechanic sign-offs to the hydraulic test and set up a process to alert maintenance control after extreme winds. Boeing revised its maintenance manual to require the special inspection at a wind threshold of 65 knots, or 75 mph.

#6162. My 9 Favorite Hotel Toiletry Brands, From Aesop To Le Labo, And More

Luxury hotel brands try to differentiate themselves in all kinds of ways. One (arguably) minor way they do so is by partnering with other luxury brands on their toiletry and skincare lines. While I’m not suggesting that you should pick a hotel brand because of the toiletries that they offer, I think I’m not alone in preferring some brands to others.

In this post, I’d like to share my favorite hotel toiletry brands, and then I’m curious to hear what brands OMAAT readers prefer. To be clear, my rankings are based purely on my perception of products and brands, from the packaging, to the scent, to how it feels using them, to memories I associate with them. I’m not claiming any authority with my opinion, so please don’t ask me to defend my preferences!

Still, I’m sure I’m not alone in getting more excited about some toiletry brands than others. With that out of the way, below are some of my favorite hotel toiletry brands (let me also emphasize that not every single property belonging to these groups has the brand standard toiletries).

Le Labo generally supplies toiletries for EDITION and Park Hyatt hotels, as well as select Fairmont properties, and it’s probably my single favorite toiletry brand. I love how there are different scents, and how they’re often customized for individual hotels (with the branding on the bottles even reflecting that). I enjoy the scents, and also appreciate that they seem to be fairly mild.

Bamford toiletries are generally available at ultra-luxury hotel group Capella, and sister brand Patina. I absolutely love Bamford, and find the product scents to be pleasant, and I also like the simplicity of the branding. For airline geeks, Bamford is also nowadays the premium toiletry partner of Cathay Pacific, so don’t be surprised if you see these products in Cathay Pacific lounges, and onboard the carrier’s flights.

Within the past few years, Ritz-Carlton has started partnering with Diptyque on toiletries. What an absolutely massive upgrade this is, compared to the previous Asprey Purple Rain collection, which I personally found to be completely unremarkable. I find Diptyque to have a very pleasant scent without being overpowering. It’s something I otherwise associate with Qatar Airways, as it’s the only major airline to partner with the brand. Speaking of changes in recent years in the luxury Marriott portfolio, St. Regis has moved to SACHAJUAN, which I find to be unmemorable.

A few years ago, Waldorf Astoria made the switch from Salvatore Ferragamo toiletries to Aesop toiletries. I’d consider that to be a significant upgrade. I love the scent of Aesop, and it can’t help but always remind me of Cathay Pacific back in the day (which, as noted above, has now switched to Bamford).

I love BVLGARI toiletries, including the packaging, scent, and feeling of using them. The catch is that while many hotels have BVLGARI toiletries, there’s not much consistency as to which brands have them. Yes, as you’d expect, BVLGARI hotels have these products, but that’s a small hotel group, with under 10 properties. On top of that, you’ll find BVLGARI toiletries at select properties of Four Seasons, Rosewood, and more.

Acqua Di Parma is another one of my favorite hotel toiletry brands, in terms of packaging and scent. The catch is that there’s not a major hotel group that consistently stocks these products, though they’re common enough among hotel groups that I feel good about including it on the list. For example, while not brand standard, the St. Regis Venice uses Acqua Di Parma products.

Molton Brown makes great products (I particularly like the soap). While no major hotel group consistently has Molton Brown products, I find that they’re pretty common at luxury hotels, including at many Marriott Luxury Collection properties.

I think Byredo is worth mentioning, as you’ll find the Bal d’Afrique product line at many InterContinental properties, and the Le Chemin product line at many Luxury Collection properties. While I don’t like this quite as much as some of the brands mentioned above, I appreciate that it’s often available at more mid-range properties, where you won’t typically find brands like Aesop and Le Labo.

Admittedly this is a bit lower end than the other options, but I wanted to also throw in a toiletry brand from a more mid-range hotel brand. For upscale hotels, I’d say that MALIN+GOETZ, available at Le Meridien properties, is probably my favorite line.

The above are nine of my favorite hotel toiletry lines. As you can see, some are pretty consistently available at select hotel brands, while others are frequently offered, though not consistently at any brand. I don’t claim that my opinions are right, but the above are the toiletry brands I’m typically most excited to see at hotels.

What are your favorite hotel toiletry brands?

Read the label! So many mentioned in the post and comments are made in China by Sysco Industrial Supply, not the brands. Marriott is a big offender, smart to partner with Sysco, Hunter Amenities, La Bottega, etc. who license some really great brands, but they are not the original formulations, and while close - beware of lesser quality ingredients or added chemicals to increase the shelf life and global distribution.

@lucky if you don't already know, every toiletry you listed has a special version produced just for use in the hotel that is MUCH cheaper than the real product you can buy at a store. The ingredient quality is way way lower. The brands lend their name to a third party producer to make a product that costs as much as 1/10th of what the real product costs. They are basically just buying advertising rights on cheap generic stuff.

I find if I use hotel toiletries for more than a few days in a row I start to get skin irritation. At home, I buy low irritation body wash without harsh sulphates etc, which most body wash has. Would be nice if hotels stocked those kind of products that were better for your skin - perhaps some of these do, but its often unclear.

My first introduction to Le Labo was in 2012 at the Park Hyatt in Abu Dhabi. I did buy Bergamotte 22 on a regular basis for a long while after, so both brands got a positive effect from that stay. Does it make me pick a Park Hyatt? Probably not in and by itself, is it part of my positive brand perception of PH? For sure.

I just carry my toiletries. I have sensitive skin so I like to use natural and very basic toiletries which have as few chemicals as possible. I’ve found that Soul Tree is fantastic and doesn’t react with my skin. For scalp, I’m partial to Olaplex. For fragrances, Le Labo and Dyptique - I would not recommend either for toiletries since that’s not their forte. Therefore, I wouldn’t choose the hotel based on toiletries.

Recently, TPG launched its  inaugural State of Loyalty report, a "data-backed look at consumer loyalty, industry trends, the best loyalty program benefits and how far your points, miles and dollars go these days."

Inside our comprehensive report, there are some interesting data points to look at, like which hotel loyalty points have increased or decreased in value over the year, the average points and cash price for hotels across the major loyalty brands, and our takeaways about what it all means.

It's a nice deep-dive into the world of loyalty — and a great weekend read with a strong coffee in hand.

Here's the other hotel news you need to know this week.

Aman has been on a significant expansion streak of late. Now, the luxury hotel brand has its eyes set on Puerto Rico with the announcement of Amantaru in Cabo Rojo. Though no opening date is available, we do know the hillside resort near the ocean will feature a hotel and residences, a wellness center, bars and restaurants and more in the Escencia development on the Southwestern coast.

Wyndham is making a big play in the luxury hotel space with a new partnership with HotelREZ Hotels & Resorts. The partnership will bring more than 40 independent luxury hotels into Wyndham's Registry Collection Hotels Brand by early 2026. For fans of Wyndham Rewards, this means exciting (dare I say unexpected?) locations to earn and burn points, like The TownHouse Mykonos in Greece, TreeHouse Villas Koh Yao in Thailand and Galgorm Resort in Northern Ireland.

Viceroy Park Avenue is now accepting reservations from Feb. 1, 2027, starting at $850 per night.

What's old is new again in St. Augustine, Florida, where the nearly 140-year-old Casa Monica Resort & Spa has emerged from a makeover with a new name: Grand Bohemian Casa Monica. The 137-room hotel, the first to join Marriott's Autograph Collection in 2010, now features Moroccan- and Spanish-inspired interiors, jewel tones, intricate tilework and original art. Guests can also enjoy the revamped Soltana Pool Lounge, complete with a new Moroccan-inspired bar, Mediterranean bites and cocktails made for sipping in the Florida sunshine.

There are few things I like in life more than hotel merch. It's a fun way for those of us who are travel-obsessed to inject a little hotel love into our everyday lives at home. For example, my Corgi's dog bed is from The Beverly Hills Hotel and my favorite hat was a gift from the Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Landaa Giraavaru.

Now, another brand I love, Raffles, has launched an online shop: The Little Shop by Raffles. Opening up just in time for the holidays (hey mom, you reading this?!), fans of the brand can now order everything from luxury linens to pajama sets and outfits, suitcases, fragrances and more.

“For more than a century, Raffles has inspired a sense of discovery and an instinct for the extraordinary, Claudia Kozma Kaplan, Raffles chief brand officer, said in a statement. "The Little Shop is an invitation to bring that world home through a curated collection of distinctive pieces, created by Raffles and in collaboration with a selection of houses we deeply admire."

#6159. What Are The Best Seats To Book On A Widebody Long-Haul Flight?

There is no single answer for where you should try to sit on a long-haul widebody flight because it all depends on what sort of traveler you are and what you want to prioritize. The best seat depends on whether you care most about sleep, legroom, getting off quickly, or relaxing. Whatever you prioritize, you'll have to trade off other aspects, such as convenient access to the toilet or the best window views.

Undoubtedly, the best place to sit in a widebody flight is in first or business class. Economy class varies a lot depending on where you sit, so this article focuses on that.

The first step in choosing the right seat for your economy class widebody flight is understanding how the cabin works. This is because an economy class cabin is so large on a widebody aircraft that it acts more like a set of mini-cabins, which are broken up by exit rows, galleys, toilets, and more. Some superjumbos also have an economy class enclave on the upper deck. Each mini-section of the economy class cabin is suited to different passenger archetypes.

The table below shows what you can expect in each part of the economy class cabin, making use of insights from Seat Compare:

Less busy, rapid service, helps with sleeping, and you can get off quickly

Proximity to the galley and curtain behind the premium classes

Lots of choice; often you don't have to pay too much extra for seat selection

The most activity and busiest part of the cabin will make sleeping difficult

Proximity to the galley and toilets. You may get meal service last

Rarely found due to the commonality of putting premium classes on the upper deck, and the small number of double-decker jets still flying.

Additional room, better views out of the windows, small economy class cabin

Stairs that can lead to separate boarding, and it takes longer to get off the aircraft.

In modern aviation, most airlines now expect you to pay extra to choose a specific seat. Some of the most in-demand seats, such as the exit row, cost more, though still well below premium economy or business class. As a result, an additional option opens up, particularly for solo travelers. That is to refuse to pay for seat selection and gamble that you won't get put right next to the toilet.

The most well-known path to extra legroom in economy class is to book a seat in the exit row. The extra few inches of legroom makes the seat feel closer to premium economy. It is ideal for taller passengers and often means you won't need to get up to let fellow passengers out.

Please note that these seats come with responsibility in the event of an accident. Each airline has a different minimum age to sit here, usually between 15 and 18 years old, and you also need to be physically able to operate the emergency exit.

This isn't the only reason that the exit row can be a poisoned chalice. First, aviation rules mean you can't keep any bags under the seat in front of you, as these could cause an obstruction if the aircraft must be evacuated. You'll need to be organized if you want a specific device, book, or magazine during takeoff and landing. Exit-row seats can also frustrate some passengers. These seats are fixed, often with no recline and armrests that can't be moved. The armrests also make the seat a little narrower than normal. Robustly built passengers may find this cramped. The tray tables are built into the armrest rather than on the back of the seat, which can make for an odd eating experience. For some passengers, these downsides will be irrelevant, but for others, they make exit row seats hellish.

Finding the best seat in the house can be tricky.

A poor night's sleep on a red-eye long-haul flight can steal a day from your hard-earned vacation time, making it a priority for many economy class passengers. Yet, given the inherent discomfort and crowding of economy class cabins, this can be impossible. Some seats within the class will still give you the best chance of sleep.

The first step is to secure a window seat. You'll have a wall to lean on or wedge a pillow or sweater against for additional comfort. It also means you won't be woken up when the other passengers in your row want to use the bathroom. The window seat allows you to control the blinds, though an eye mask is always a good idea.

The table below uses data collected by Simple Flying to show the window dimensions of various widebody aircraft. Pick a flight with a large window if you want to get the best views:

10.7 inches x 18.4 inches (27.2 cm x 46.7 cm)

9.5 inches x 13.5 inches (24.1 cm x 34.3 cm)

10 inches x 15 inches (25.4 cm x 38.1 cm)

9 inches x 12.3 inches (22.9 cm x 31.2 cm)

The best spots are toward the front of the economy class cabin, in front of the wings due to the engine noise, although not far forward enough to be disturbed by cabin crew clattering around in the galley. This spot, near the plane's center of gravity, also helps you avoid turbulence that can jolt you awake. Another great spot is a mini-cabin, a smaller economy class enclave formed by galleys, exit rows, and other objects that divide the cabin. These mini-cabins have fewer people, so they have less activity that could disturb your sleep.

Another popular seat that is available throughout the aircraft is the aisle seat. It has numerous benefits. Most obviously, it is more spacious than the average economy class seat, as you can enjoy some of the room in the aisle when passengers and cabin crew aren't coming past. That gives the impression of more width than the basic amount that the seat offers.

You'll find deplaning much easier, as you won't have to wait for the passenger next to you to finish before you can move. That makes the seat ideal if you have a connecting flight or need to get to your accommodation quickly. The seat also lets you access the bathroom easily, although you will also have to move whenever the other passengers in your row need to get up. Likewise, you can easily access the overhead bins, but will be disturbed when the passengers next to you need their items.

Yet, the aisle seat usually isn't ideal for passengers who want to be undisturbed or enjoy a good night's sleep. Due to the size of long-haul economy class cabins, there will constantly be other passengers and flight attendants traveling down the aisle. They could bump into you and wake you from your slumber.

Which seat should you choose for your next long-haul flight?

No seat combines everything you want to avoid on long-haul widebody flights like the final row of economy class. As you board, you may struggle to find space for your bags as the overhead bins may be partially filled with airline emergency equipment. During the flight, you'll often have no or limited recline because the seat is directly against a wall. You'll also often be close to noises and smells from the lavatory and galley. If there is a queue for the lavatory, it will always be directly next to you.

It is also common for meal services to work from the front to the back of the aircraft. Along with the wait, the best options may already be taken by the time the trolley gets to you. Finally, the rear of the aircraft is set back from its center of gravity, so you'll get the worst turbulence. The problems continue when it's time to get off the aircraft. You will often be one of the last people off the aircraft. That can cause problems if you have a tight connection. You also won't be able to get ahead of the rush to deal with immigration controls, which can cause even more delays.

The middle seat anywhere on the aircraft is also a must-avoid. You'll feel cramped between two other passengers and have no window view. This seat can become a disaster if the passengers on either side of you are large individuals. As with the window seat, you'll have to disturb the passenger next to you whenever you want to get up.
