#6158. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Through 11:59PM ET on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is tiered, as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses. With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

Do you plan on buying IHG points with a bonus?

#6156. Introduction: An Orient Express Adventure Via Africa

Welcome to my next trip report series, covering a trip that I recently wrapped up, which will include reviews of flights and a cruise. This will be a relatively short series, since the trip didn’t last that long, and had a specific purpose. However, as usual, I tried to take an unconventional routing to get to and from the destination, so I could review new experiences.

You can expect reviews of Air Algerie and Royal Air Maroc business class, as well as a review of Orient Express Sailing Yachts, which is Orient Express’ new cruising venture. In this post I’d like to share a basic outline of the trip, and then I’ll have individual review installments in the near future.

The primary reason for this trip was simple, and it was to take a cruise with Orient Express Sailing Yachts. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry, and in particular, the increasing number of new lines associated with existing luxury hospitality brands.

Prior to this year, I hadn’t taken a cruise with any cruise line since I was a child, so I’ve been curious to check this all out. At the beginning of the year, I reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, which was surprisingly lovely, and a very nice reintroduction to cruising.

Then over the summer, I reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which was definitely upmarket, but had some growing pains.

The newest entrant into this market is Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and arguably it takes luxury cruising to a new level, so you can expect a full review of the experience. Full disclosure — Ford was invited on the sailing (so traveled as a guest of Orient Express) and I tagged along. I’ll still review the experience objectively, of course, but I’ll say upfront that Orient Express simply nailed it, and this matched the feedback Ford has received from clients who have sailed with the company.

Anyway, we sailed with Orient Express Sailing Yachts on a four night journey that started in Marseille, France, and ended in Malaga, Spain, so we needed to position to and from there.

I’m of course always looking for an interesting airline angle when I travel long haul, since my goal is always to try as many new airline products as possible. So rather than flying to Marseille and from Malaga on the “typical” airlines (Air France, British Airways, Lufthansa, etc.), I tried to see if I could instead check some airlines off my list that I’ve been wanting to try. I accomplished that, and below is what my routing looked like.

While I sent Ford direct, I booked a four segment routing for myself, spread across three different tickets.

I had heard a lot about Air Algerie over the years (and not in a good way!), so I decided I finally had to give the carrier a try. Air Algerie typically has very high business class fares, despite the carrier’s lackluster product.

However, I found one decent fare on the carrier’s only route from North America, from Montreal (YUL) to Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, that doesn’t start where I’d like to start, and it doesn’t end where I’d like to end, but that has never stopped me if the price is right. 😉

This included a flight in Air Algerie’s Airbus A330-900neo business class across the Atlantic, and then a connecting flight in Avion Express’ Airbus A320neo business class for the short hop in Africa (this was a wet leased flight operated on behalf of Air Algerie). So I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day) 10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

From there, I of course had to get from Tunis to Marseille (MRS), so I had booked Tunisair’s A320 business class for $270, with the following schedule:

10/04 TU902 Tunis to Marseille departing 1:05PM arriving 3:40PM

Unfortunately I ended up being downgraded shortly before departure due to an aircraft swap. That’s because the flight was swapped to a wet leased Fly2Sky Airbus A320, and I guess they don’t offer business class on those planes. I’m still waiting on any sort of a refund.

Suffice it to say that the outbound wasn’t that smooth, between Air Algerie just royally sucking, and Tunisair downgrading me. I’m happy I had the experience, though!

I should also mention that I had to position to Montreal, so I did that in Air Canada Rouge economy, and flew the following for 11,500 avianca lifemiles plus $54 in taxes & fees:

10/04 AC1651 Miami to Montreal departing 7:55AM arriving 11:28AM

The return portion of our trip was a little more straightforward. Our priority was to get home the same day as our cruise arrived, since we wanted to minimize time away from our kids, and had a family event the next day. So we booked the one routing that would best get us home the same day, which was on Royal Air Maroc, from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN) to Miami (MIA), with the first flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class, and the second flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class.

I booked one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM 10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

On this trip, we just had a single hotel night ahead of our cruise in Marseille (in order to build in a buffer), and we decided to stay at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. I booked this using an IHG free night award, and it cost 60,000 points before applying the award, so I just had to redeem the difference in points.

I had intended to review the hotel, but I have to apologize, it just didn’t end up working out (since I pride myself in thoroughly reviewing hotels). To be honest, I was dead tired from the journey over, and then we had some drama to deal with back at home most of the afternoon. Then the next morning I prioritized sleeping in, as I was just getting over a cold, rather than getting up at 5AM so I could photograph all parts of the hotel.

So I’m sorry about that. My conclusion is that the hotel has a central location, and from the outside you’d think it’s super charming, but the interior feels mismatched and rather uninspiring and generic.

We had an absolutely amazing time cruising with Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and I was blown away by the experience. What I was less impressed by was my flights to and from Europe, which I routed via Africa in both directions. Air Algerie was downright terrible, while Royal Air Maroc was just unnecessarily bad.

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Your Chase Ultimate Rewards card can help you earn bonus points in more ways than one — provided you remember an extra click before checkout.

Chase has an online shopping portal, called Shop and Earn, that lets eligible cardholders collect bonus Ultimate Rewards points when shopping at over 1,000 online retailers. Those bonus points stack with the points, miles or cash back you earn from your credit card, meaning the same purchases are doing double duty.

It's a small habit with a surprisingly satisfying payoff. Here's how to make sure those extra points actually land in your account.

Like other portals, Chase Shop and Earn is easy to use, but the order matters: Instead of beginning at a retailer's website, sign into your Ultimate Rewards account, find your preferred merchant within Shop and Earn and click through to its website.

You then shop and check out as usual, while Chase tracks the purchase and awards the advertised bonus points.

There are strong odds that you can earn on nearly any purchase, given the large number of participating websites. Advertised rates range from 1 to 15 bonus points per dollar spent, although participating stores and payouts change regularly.

These portal rewards are added on top of the points your Chase card normally earns. For example, if a retailer offers 5 bonus points per dollar spent through Shop and Earn, a qualifying $100 purchase would earn 500 bonus Ultimate Rewards points, plus the rewards earned from paying with your card. You may also be able to combine these earnings with Chase Offers for even more returns.

If you repeat this strategy every month, with a little extra shopping around the holidays, you could earn thousands of Ultimate Rewards each year, putting you closer toward your next award flight, hotel stay or other redemption.

The Shops at Chase is a separate offering for eligible Chase cardholders. While Shop and Earn acts as a shopping portal that awards bonus Ultimate Rewards points for qualifying online purchases, The Shops at Chase is an actual shopping marketplace. Through The Shops at Chase, cardholders can buy a curated selection of products using their Chase credit card and/or Ultimate Rewards points.

Related: Why I choose to earn Chase Ultimate Rewards points over Amex Membership Rewards points

Shop and Earn is available to cardholders who have at least one Chase credit card that's part of the Ultimate Rewards family. Some popular examples include:

Note that cobranded Chase airline and hotel cards aren't eligible for Shop and Earn.

If you're an eligible cardholder, there are several different pathways to access Shop and Earn from your online Chase account or mobile app. Personally, I find the easiest method is to go directly to ultimaterewardsearn.chase.com. There, you'll sign in to your account and select your eligible Chase account (if you have multiple qualifying cards).

You can also access Shop and Earn by navigating through the benefits sections of your online accounts or the Chase mobile app.

Offers sometimes vary by card, so it can be worth checking each of your eligible accounts before choosing a payout. Shopping aggregators like Cashback Monitor quickly display earning rates for different Chase cards as well as what you'd earn by using alternative shopping portals.

Aggregators are also a good way to determine if the Chase portal is the best option for your particular purchase. Sometimes, other portals offer a stronger return than Chase Shop and Earn, though this will depend somewhat on how you value Ultimate Rewards.

Related: Reasons to choose the Chase Sapphire Preferred over the fancier Chase Sapphire Reserve

Once you're on the Chase Shop and Earn website, you can search by merchant using the search box on the right, or you can scroll down to browse the stores currently offering elevated earning rates.

If you shop with a particular retailer regularly, click the heart icon to add it to your favorites and monitor its offers more easily.

When you're ready to shop, click on the relevant retailer's name. That will lead you to a screen outlining different earning rates by purchase type, as well as any additional terms and conditions for that specific merchant.

Pay attention to excluded products or brands, restrictions on coupon codes and other exclusions.

Related: How to redeem Chase Ultimate Rewards points for maximum value

Shopping portal bonuses rely on browser tracking, so a few small mistakes can prevent your purchase from qualifying.

If you close out of the window, there's no guarantee your visit will be tracked correctly for your rewards. When in doubt, you can always restart the process from Chase Shop and Earn.

You'll also want to pay close attention to terms and conditions. Chase doesn't normally award points on gift cards or purchases made with specialized coupon codes (in my experience, promo codes advertised directly on the merchant's website are usually allowed). Orders that are canceled, returned or otherwise refunded also won't qualify.

Chase says bonus points may appear as pending on your Shop and Earn shopping details page within 15 days, though in my experience, it often takes just a day or two. You should also receive an email confirming the purchase and the points earned.

Even when you can see the transaction was accurately tracked, points may take up to 60 days to fully post to your account. If they still haven't appeared by then, you can follow up with Chase via the phone number on the back of your card or through the online secure message center. You'll need the merchant name, purchase date, order total and ideally an e-receipt or confirmation email.

Points you earn with Shop and Earn typically appear as pending on your "Rewards Activity" page within a few days, though it can take up to two billing cycles for your bonus points to post.

If you're shopping online without checking Chase Shop and Earn, you could be leaving free travel on the table. Returns go further than simple cash back, and the math is simple: Even small transactions snowball into larger balances that can lead you to some serious redemption power.

#6150. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Countries? One Carrier Has A Huge Lead

I don’t want to bury the lede — in posts, I often reference how Turkish Airlines flies to more countries than any other airline in the world. However, how many countries does the airline actually fly to, and how far ahead of competitors is Turkish Airlines? I thought that would be interesting to explore…

Turkish Airlines has the record for flying to more countries than any other airline in the world. That has been the case for a long time, and in late 2024, the Star Alliance carrier made it official, with a Guinness World Record in the category of “most countries flown to by an airline.” The airline has flown to more countries than any other airline since 2012, and has a sizable lead over competitors.

Just how many countries does Turkish Airlines fly to? This is where it always gets tricky as to what you count. If you count active flights operating at the moment, the airline flies to 117 countries. However:

As you’d expect, when you’re an airline serving virtually every corner of the globe, there will always be some suspended services due to geopolitical factors, etc. What’s cool is that Turkish Airlines is also far from done with its expansion, as the airline still has big growth plans. It’ll be fascinating to see just how many countries the airline eventually serves.

What’s perhaps most impressive about Turkish Airlines’ record for serving the most countries is just how far ahead of competitors the airline is. Turkish Airlines is 30+ countries ahead of the next airline when it comes to countries served.

Does anyone want to take a guess as to which airlines are next on the list? Here are a few general thoughts that come to mind:

With that in mind, which airlines serve the most countries, aside from Turkish Airlines? According to flightconnections.com, here are some observations:

As you can see, that means Qatar Airways serves the most countries after Turkish Airlines, while Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, are currently tied for third place.

Meanwhile it’s impressive that Emirates serves so many countries when you consider that the airline just flies wide body jets. If you combined the networks of Emirates and flydubai (both are owned by the government, but the airlines are run separately), then the combined airline would have close to as many destinations as Turkish Airlines.

Let me of course also acknowledge that the number of countries served and number of destinations served is very different, and US carriers would do much better by the latter metric. And if the question is the number of premium destinations served, then there’s only one right answer. 😉

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 13 most “global” airlines, in terms of countries served (I had to include KLM as well, since it ties Air Canada and Delta, even if it doesn’t lead the way among European carriers).

Turkish Airlines sets the world record for serving the most countries in the world. The airline actively flies to 117 countries, but including suspended routes, serves 130+ countries. That puts the airline way ahead of the next carriers by this metric, which include Qatar Airways at 86 countries, followed by a tie between Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, at 80 countries.

Are you surprised by the airlines serving the most countries?

#6149. Why Boeing 777 Freighter Conversions Are A Stopgap Built On A Shrinking Supply Of Used Jets

The Boeing 777 is helping the global air cargo industry address a growing shortage of large freighters, but the aircraft providing that additional capacity are becoming very difficult to find. As passenger airlines retain their widebody jets for longer and new-build freighters face production and delivery constraints, three conversion programs are competing to turn used 777s into dedicated cargo aircraft. The irony is that the industry's immediate solution depends on an aging aircraft supply that cannot be replenished indefinitely.

For cargo operators, converted 777s offer an attractive way to obtain substantial payload capacity without waiting for a new-generation freighter. However, their fuel consumption, acquisition costs, and remaining service lives raise questions about their long-term commercial viability. With the Airbus A350F approaching entry into service and the 777-8F still in development, the converted 777 looks like a temporary answer to a problem that will require a more permanent solution.

Growing interest in Boeing 777 passenger-to-freighter (P2F) conversions is closely tied to a shortage of available large widebody freighters. Cargo airlines need more capacity, but the transition from existing production programs to next-generation aircraft has created a gap they can't fill immediately. Production constraints, certification delays, and changing emissions requirements have made used passenger aircraft an important source of additional capacity.

The 777-300ER variant is particularly attractive because of its large fuselage, substantial structural capabilities, and established operational history. Originally designed for long-haul passenger services, the aircraft offers the dimensions and performance needed for demanding cargo operations. Converting an existing passenger aircraft also lets operators add capacity without waiting for a completely new aircraft to be manufactured.

However, the supply of suitable aircraft is becoming a major limitation. Passenger airlines are keeping their 777-300ERs in service longer, partly because delays affecting replacement 777X aircraft have disrupted fleet-renewal plans. This means conversion specialists must compete for a relatively small number of aircraft that are young enough, structurally sound, and economically viable to modify. The question is whether the remaining supply can support the ambitions of the companies developing these conversion programs.

Three companies have emerged as the principal players in the 777 conversion market: Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), Mammoth Freighters, and Kansas Modification Center (KMC). Although all three target the same broad market, their programs involve different 777 variants, engineering approaches, and development schedules. Their progress also illustrates how quickly the industry is trying to expand conversion capacity before suitable passenger aircraft become even harder to source.

IAI was the first to establish a commercial operation with its 777-300ERSF, also known as the Big Twin. The aircraft entered commercial service in September 2025, with operators including Kalitta Air, Fly Meta and Challenge Group. Mammoth Freighters subsequently secured Federal Aviation Aviation (FAA) certification for its 777-200LRMF in April and delivered the first converted aircraft to Jetran on August 21 for DHL Air UK operations. The company is also developing the larger 777-300ERMF. Meanwhile, KMC is pursuing its 777-300ERCF, which uses a distinctive forward cargo-door design intended to reduce structural weight.

Commercial operations since September 2025

Developing a lightweight forward cargo-door solution

These programs are also expanding geographically. In October, IAI, Ascent Aviation Services and World Star Aviation announced the commencement of 777-300ERSF conversions in North America, with the first aircraft arriving at Ascent's Marana facility in Arizona. The site is expected to operate two parallel conversion lines. Mammoth has also expanded into China through a partnership with STAECO, where the first 777-200LR entered conversion last month. A second line is planned for 2027.

These investments show confidence in the converted 777 market, but adding conversion lines does not automatically increase the number of available aircraft. Companies still need to acquire passenger jets, and customers must be willing to pay substantial sums to secure them.

Boeing is pushing hard to get its answer to the new generation of cargo aircraft out of the factory. However, the 777X delays have trapped its promise

The financial appeal of a passenger-to-freighter conversion is straightforward: an operator buys an existing aircraft, modifies its interior and structure, and puts it into cargo service without paying for a brand-new production freighter. However, the purchase price represents only one part of the investment. The aircraft must undergo extensive structural modifications, maintenance inspections, and potentially expensive engine work before it can begin earning revenue.

According to aircraft consultancy IBA, a half-life 777-300ER converted into a freighter can cost approximately $75 million to $80 million, including the aircraft and conversion work. The investment can approach $100 million if the GE90-115 engines require shop visits. These costs are high, particularly when the resulting aircraft retains the operating characteristics of an older passenger jet rather than incorporating the latest generation of engines and aerodynamic improvements. The aircraft must also have sufficient remaining structural life to justify the expenditure.

Fuel consumption becomes particularly important when operators deploy converted freighters on long-distance routes with high utilization. At the TIACA Air Cargo Forum, Airbus freighter-marketing executive Bernard De L'Estoile described conversions as only part of the solution, arguing that fuel burn matters most when converted aircraft operate frequently over long distances,Air Cargo News reported. His comments should be read in the context of Airbus selling a competing new-build freighter, but the underlying economic issue matters regardless of the manufacturer's commercial interests.

The difference becomes clearer when comparing the Mammoth 777-200LRMF with the next-generation alternatives:

A converted 777 can remain attractive on routes where operators need substantial capacity but cannot justify the investment in a new aircraft. Its economics become less convincing when it flies long-haul services almost continuously, where small differences in fuel consumption accumulate over hundreds of operating hours. The commercial sweet spot is consequently likely to be routes with moderate utilization, not the most demanding intercontinental cargo networks. But if converted aircraft aren't the best long-term option for those networks, what will replace them?

The long-term answer lies in purpose-built freighters designed around modern engines, improved aerodynamics, and dedicated cargo operations. Airbus and Boeing are both developing aircraft to replace older widebody freighters, but their delivery schedules mean converted 777s will remain relevant during the transition. The A350F is currently further along in its development program, while the 777-8F is expected to arrive later in the decade.

Airbus achieved a major milestone on September 29, when the A350F completed its maiden flight. The aircraft flew for four hours and 10 minutes, beginning a flight-test campaign expected to last more than nine months. Airbus is targeting initial deliveries in the second half of 2027, although some industry observers believe the program could slip into 2028. The manufacturer had secured 115 firm orders from 14 disclosed customers by the end of August. The A350F offers a maximum structural payload of 111 tonnes and a range of 4,700 nautical miles, with Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines.

Boeing's competing 777-8F is designed to carry even more cargo, with a maximum structural payload of approximately 118.2 tonnes and a range of 5,000 nautical miles. Based on the 777X family, it incorporates a composite wing and GE9X engines, offering improved efficiency compared with the current-generation 777F. Boeing also advertises 17% more cargo volume than the existing 777F. However, the program has experienced delays, and the manufacturer is targeting deliveries around 2029, approximately two years after the expected first delivery of the 777-9. Boeing had 81 firm 777-8F orders according to the October industry comparison.

The transition will not happen overnight. Even after the first A350Fs and 777-8Fs enter service, production will need time to ramp up, and operators will need time to integrate the aircraft into their networks. That is why converted 777s have an important window to generate revenue, but the length of that window depends on whether the new-build programs meet their delivery commitments. Another complication is that the existing 777F production line has received additional time, potentially changing conversion demand.

Cargo flats are getting older, and the end is getting further out of sight. With delays more common than ever, when will cargo operators modernize?

Passenger-aircraft availability is becoming the biggest constraint on the conversion market. Strong demand for the Boeing 777-300ER has kept residual values relatively high, while 777X delays have encouraged passenger airlines to retain their existing widebody fleets. Some carriers have even invested in additional cabin refurbishments rather than retiring aircraft they originally expected to replace.

This situation creates competition between passenger airlines and freighter conversion companies. A 777-300ER that remains commercially useful in passenger service may generate more value for its existing operator than selling it to a lessor or conversion specialist. The aircraft's age is not necessarily a reason for retirement, particularly when replacement capacity is unavailable. As a result, conversion companies cannot simply purchase as many aircraft as their production facilities can accommodate. They must wait for suitable jets to become available and compete with other buyers.

Boeing is also developing its own freighter production strategy. The FAA granted Boeing an exemption allowing up to 35 additional 777Fs to receive their first airworthiness certificates between January 1, 2028, and January 1, 2031. This provides a temporary extension to the existing production program while operators await the 777-8F. According to Cirium's October 2026 analysis, the extension could influence conversion demand because some customers were waiting for clarity on continued factory-built 777F availability before making purchasing decisions.

However, the waiver does not eliminate the feedstock problem. Cirium reported 86 firm orders across the IAI, Mammoth and KMC conversion programs, while noting that securing individual aircraft for all those commitments remains challenging. The additional 777F production also represents a limited extension, not an unlimited source of new capacity.

The implications are significant for lessors and operators. If used 777 prices continue to rise, conversion costs could exceed what customers are willing to pay, especially when engine maintenance is included. Meanwhile, the A350F and 777-8F will eventually offer more attractive operating economics for airlines flying intensive long-haul networks. The remaining question is whether conversion specialists can deliver enough aircraft before feedstock scarcity and new-build competition make further expansion increasingly difficult.

The 777 conversion market is entering a period in which demand alone will not determine its success. Cargo operators still need large widebody aircraft, and converting existing passenger jets can remain economically attractive in specific markets. However, the availability of suitable airframes, the cost of engine maintenance and the operating efficiency of older aircraft will increasingly determine which conversion programs can remain competitive. The industry is facing a rather unusual situation: it needs more converted 777s, but the aircraft required to produce them are becoming more valuable to their existing owners.

Upcoming milestones include the A350F's anticipated first deliveries in the second half of 2027 and the 777-8F's expected arrival around 2029. In the meantime, IAI, Mammoth Freighters and KMC will need to secure additional passenger aircraft while managing conversion costs and production schedules. The FAA's allowance for 35 additional 777Fs also gives cargo operators another option during the transition, potentially moderating demand for converted aircraft.

Converted 777s will remain an important part of the global freighter market, but they are unlikely to be the industry's permanent answer to the shortage of large cargo aircraft. Their greatest value may lie in connecting two generations of freighters, providing capacity while manufacturers work through development and production challenges. Whether this bridge can be extended will depend less on how many conversion facilities open and more on how many suitable passenger 777s are available for conversion.

#6147. Hotel Refills Toiletries From Ketchup-Style Bottles—This Is Why You Can’t Trust What’s In The Shower

This upscale hotel’s housekeeping cart looks ready to dress a hamburger: red, yellow and white squeeze bottles lined up beside the guest supplies. The red one says “Body Wash.” In the shower, the bottles say Klur. Travel journalist Scott Mayerowitz photographed the setup and compared it to the condiments at McDonald’s. He’s glad the hotel is refilling its toiletries. I’m looking at the same photo and wondering how guests are supposed to know what they’re actually washing with. A post shared by Scott Mayerowitz (@globetrotscott) His follow-up photo on LinkedIn shows Klur Repose shampoo, conditioner and body wash in the shower, in the Clary Sage + Lavender scent. My guess, eyeballing the hallway and bathroom, is the Omni Boston Hotel at the Seaport. Readers familiar with the property can confirm or correct that. A September review documents Klur toiletries there, and Klur supplies Omni more broadly. The red squeeze bottle isn’t literally unlabeled. It’s self-labeled. The bottle identifies as body wash. What it doesn’t show is whose body wash. The contents may be genuine Klur, though it seems odd if it were that it would be in a ketchup squeeze bottle. Best case, this looks cheap. They went to the trouble of selecting a branded amenity for the bathroom, then made the refill process look like the back of a burger joint. I’ve Reported This At Hyatt Hotels, Too In May 2025, I wrote about Hyatt Regency San Francisco’s ketchup-style refill jug. A reader photographed an unbranded squeeze container being carried with housekeeping supplies. Guests could see the dispenser in their bathroom, but couldn’t identify the product supplying it. Then, in December, a reader found condiment containers on a housekeeping cart at Hyatt Place Phoenix Mesa. That cart also had a toilet brush beside fresh towels, which didn’t improve the presentation. At Hyatt’s Wild Palms Hotel in Sunnyvale, California, a reader photographed DRIFT bulk toiletries on housekeeping carts while the guest bathroom bottles displayed Jonathan Adler branding. The hotel advertised Jonathan Adler amenities. When One Mile at a Time followed up in January, Ben reported that the labels had been removed from the bulk jugs, and published new photographs. The hotel was still advertising Jonathan Adler. And at the Suining Marriott in China, management there actually acknowledged swapping out cheaper stuff. A guest found FORMETURE products instead of Marriott’s thisworks amenities. The general manager said the owner had changed products to save money. The hotel denied that the replacement was counterfeit, saying it was a legitimate product with quality documentation. It promised to restore the brand standard, and the guest received 8,000 points. Does This Break Any Rules? Klur’s hospitality products are is sold in bulk refill containers. I’d expect those to be used rather than squeeze bottles. Putting a different product into a Klur-labeled bottle could create a misbranding problem. Handling cosmetics under conditions that could contaminate them can violate adulteration rules. And passing off a cheaper product as the promised brand could also run afoul of Massachusetts law against deceptive business practices. Bulk Toiletries Leave More For The Guest To Worry About I’ve been criticizing this move for years. Buying larger containers can reduce packaging (but they can opt for single use biodegradable packaging too). It also lets hotels spend less on toiletries. I’ve shown a Sheraton’s bulk toiletries sitting beside disposable plastic cups, with plastic water bottles elsewhere in the room. They were surely using bulk toiletries out of an ideological commitment to end plastic use. The refill routine adds opportunities to mix up products or introduce contamination. TA 2023 study of 104 hotel soap dispensers in Germany found bacterial contamination in 70.2% of refillable pump dispensers, compared with 10.6% of nonrefillable press dispensers. Bottles that can be opened can be tampered with, and I’ve found supposedly secured dispensers left unlocked. And housekeeping has to remember to fill them. I once returned to the same room at a Marriott Courtyard a week later and found the bath gel dispenser still empty. It had been empty throughout the previous stay, too. You usually discover that problem after you’ve gotten into the shower. Hotels have also given up something that helped sell both the stay and the toiletry brand. I started using Aesop after staying at the Park Hyatt Tokyo. Taking a little bottle home extended the experience and introduced me to a product I still use. #6146. Confused Air France Pilots Make Wrong Turn After Takeoff From LAX, Leading To Close Call

An Air France Airbus A350 departing from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) made a wrong turn after takeoff, sending the plane dangerously close to the path of an American Airlines Airbus A321. The way the pilots responded to this isn’t exactly great, though one thing is for sure — there seems to be a recurring problem involving runway 24L departures from the airport, whatever the cause may be.

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the audio and a visualization of an incident that happened shortly after 12AM on Saturday, November 7, 2026. It involves Air France flight AF28, which was operating to Papeete, French Polynesia (PPT).

LAX has four parallel runways, and the Air France A350 was cleared for takeoff on runway 24L, on the north side of the field. The Air France pilots were instructed to initially fly to the DLREY fix, instructions which they correctly read back.

Once through the DLREY fix, they were instructed to climb via their assigned SID (that they had received with clearance), but then the pilots suddenly made a turn to the left. The issue is that an American A321 had been cleared for takeoff on runway 25R just moments earlier, and that’s to the south of runway 24L.

So when the Air France pilots started turning to the left, they went directly into the path of the American plane. Fortunately the air traffic controller quickly caught this, but it created a traffic alert, and the planes had less than a mile of separation.

Mistakes happen, but what’s strange here is how this was handled after the initial incident. The air traffic controller asked the Air France pilots why they made a turn. The Air France pilot responded “standby,” which is fair enough. Pilots are supposed to be focused first on aviating, then on navigating, and then on communicating.

Moments later, the air traffic controller followed up and asked what departure the pilots had been instructed to fly. Once again, the pilot responded “standby one.” I do think the air traffic controller should’ve been a bit more patient here when a pilot is asking him to hold on for a second. At the same, the Air France pilots seemingly just kept stalling, and seemed to be unable to answer the question.

Of course we don’t know what was going on in the cockpit (it’s possible they were dealing with something else), but the controller wasn’t asking a complicated question. The pilots ended up getting a phone number for a possible pilot deviation.

It’s truly a mystery what caused the pilots to make that left turn, especially since they were flying to Tahiti, which is basically a straight westbound departure (and in the middle of the night, it’s not like you typically need to vector to the east when departing LAX).

Regardless of how good a system looks on paper, you of course have to consider human factors, and how systems are actually perceived. For reasons that are somewhat of a mystery, there seem to be repeated issues with planes departing from runway 24L at LAX making a turn to the left, and turning into the path of planes departing from runway 25R.

Just a couple of weeks ago, I covered how a TAP Air Portugal Airbus A330neo departing runway 24L at LAX made an unauthorized left turn immediately after takeoff, putting itself in the path of another jet.

Heck, just a couple of months ago, an Air France Boeing 777 departing runway 24L at LAX made an almost identical mistake, and turned left right after takeoff, when it wasn’t supposed to.

That’s only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the number of these incidents we’ve seen. I’m not sure what exactly is going on here, and if it’s a case of pilots programming their computers for a departure from runway 25R, only to get assigned runway 24L, or what.

But either way, it seems something should be done here. As redundant as it might sound when you’re sending pilots to a specific fix (which already tells them which direction they should go), it almost seems like air traffic control needs to add in a warning about not making a left turn without authorization. I mean, it sounds silly, but…

An Air France Airbus A350 departing LAX made an unauthorized left turn after takeoff, sending it right into the path of a departing American Airbus A321. The pilots really seemed to struggle with answering air traffic control’s basic questions, though I don’t know what was actually going on in the cockpit.

What’s so strange is how there seem to be repeated issues with departures from runway 24L, as we’ve now seen this “unauthorized left turn” situation from this exact runway several times in recent weeks alone.

What do you make of this LAX runway 24L issue?

#6144. Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card Review: Worth The $95 Fee For The Free Night

Marriott has co-branded credit cards issued by both American Express and Chase, and it can be tough to figure out the differences between these cards. This is my review of the most popular mid-range Marriott credit card in that portfolio, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card. It’s a card that many Marriott guests will likely want to have, if eligible.

Let’s dive into the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card’s details to see whether it’s worth it and who it makes the most sense for.

Link: Learn more about the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card

Before I get into my full Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card review, here’s a brief look at the card’s key details:

I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card welcome bonus, card eligibility rules, and fees. After all, these are important factors that cardmembers consider when applying for cards. Now is an especially good time to apply, thanks to the current offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is currently offering a multi-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn three free night awards. The bonus is broken down as follows:

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each, given all the great ways there are to redeem them. While the maximum value of this offer is 150,000 points, I wouldn’t value the bonus quite that high, given the limited flexibility (you need to redeem the free night award within a year, you’re capped at properties costing 50,000 points, etc.).

However, if it were worth 150,000 points, I’d consider that to have a value of $1,050, and that doesn’t factor in the potential airline statement credits.

If you’re applying for the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, the general Chase application restrictions apply. There aren’t too many direct, consistent rules, but considerations include Chase’s 5/24 rule (which isn’t always enforced), being able to get up to two Chase cards every 30 days, etc.

Beyond that, since both American Express and Chase issue cards for Marriott, there are some pretty complicated restrictions regarding eligibility for this card, so see this post for more details.

To summarize the very basics, you can’t get the welcome bonus on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card if:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card has a $95 annual fee. You can add authorized users at no extra cost. That’s an incredibly reasonable annual fee, given the amount of annual fee inflation we’ve seen over the years on other cards.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s an excellent card for purchases abroad. That means you can earn rewards on your foreign spending, without having to pay any fees that will offset those rewards. In particular, it’s a good card to use for foreign Marriott spending.

While I wouldn’t recommend using the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card for your everyday spending, there are potentially some situations where it could make sense. Let’s go over the rewards structure of the card, including the bonus categories and other incentives to spend.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 6x Bonvoy points for spending at Marriott-family hotels globally. For many people, this will be a worthwhile bonus.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, that’s the equivalent of a 4.2% return on hotel spending. While there are other great cards for hotel spending, some people will want to use this as their card for Marriott spending.

Keep in mind this is on top of the standard points that you can earn for Marriott Bonvoy hotel stays. At most brands, Bonvoy members earn 10x points per dollar spent, and that’s before elite bonuses, which range from 10-75%. So as a Bonvoy Silver member paying with the card (the minimum status you get with this card), you’re looking at earning 17x points per dollar spent at most brands, minimum.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 3x Bonvoy points on dining, gas station, and grocery store purchases globally. This only applies to the first $6,000 spent on combined purchases in those categories annually, and after that, you’ll earn 2x Bonvoy points on those purchases.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, the 3x points is like the equivalent of a 2.1% return on eligible gas, grocery, and dining spending. While there are still more rewarding cards for spending in the categories of dining, gas stations, and groceries, this is about as good of a rewards structure as you’ll see on a Bonvoy credit card.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 2x Bonvoy points on all other eligible purchases. I don’t consider 2x points per dollar spent to be especially compelling since I value that at a return of 1.4 cents per dollar of spending, and there are better cards for everyday spending.

How would I approach the value of Marriott points? As mentioned above, based on my valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each. I’m not going to suggest that Bonvoy points are my favorite points currency — they’re not — but the reality is that Marriott has a huge global portfolio, and many of the properties are quite decent.

Generally you’ll find that Bonvoy award stays cost anywhere from 10,000 to 200,000 points per night, though some hotels do fall outside of that range. You can maximize value by taking advantage of the fifth night free benefit, which is open to elite members.

This is an extreme example of value, but take Hotel Cala di Volpe, a Marriott Luxury Collection hotel in Sardinia, which is the brand’s most expensive property in summer. I just pulled up a five night redemption (including a fifth night free) for 776,000 Bonvoy points. By my valuation, that’s like $5,432 worth of points.

Meanwhile the cash rate at the hotel is 4,161 EUR ($4,639) per night, so those same five nights would cost you $23,195. Talk about huge savings!

One unique thing about Bonvoy points is they can also fairly efficiently be converted into airline miles. You can transfer your rewards to dozens of different airline programs, and a vast majority allow a 3:1 transfer ratio. On top of that, you get a bonus of 5,000 airline miles for every 60,000 Bonvoy points you transfer. In other words, with most programs you can convert 60,000 Bonvoy points into 25,000 airline miles, which is potentially a decent value.

For more details, see my guide to redeeming Bonvoy points.

One of the primary reasons to consider getting the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is how the card can help you earn elite status in the Bonvoy program. Status starts to get valuable around the Bonvoy Platinum tier, when you become eligible for perks like complimentary breakfast and valuable room upgrades.

One of my favorite perks of having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is that you get 15 elite nights toward status annually just for having the card.

Note that several co-branded Marriott credit cards offer this, and you can only receive the benefit once per year on a personal card. In other words, if you have three Marriott personal cards, then you wouldn’t get 45 elite nights.

However, you could earn 15 elite nights from this personal card and 15 elite nights from a business card, so that you’d earn 30 elite nights in a year. The ideal setup would be to have a personal card in conjunction with the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more).

This makes it more attainable to earn Platinum status, which requires 50 elite nights. If you had the Bonvoy Boundless Card, you’d only need 35 more elite nights, and if you also had the business card you’d only need 20 more elite nights.

Note that if you really want to maximize elite nights with personal credit cards, the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) offers 25 elite nights per year, which is the most elite nights you’ll get with any Marriott credit card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers one elite night for every $5,000 spent on the card. Any elite nights earned this way will be credited to your account within eight weeks of the last day of the calendar month in which you qualify.

Personally, I think spending $5,000 to earn one elite night is a lot, but everyone’s situation will differ, and for some people, this could make sense if you’re otherwise close to earning status. This is the only Marriott credit card that offers bonus elite nights for spending.

Perhaps this is a bit redundant, but just for having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card you receive Silver elite status in the Bonvoy program. Now, don’t get too excited, as this doesn’t exactly come with that many benefits.

Marriott Silver elite status ordinarily requires 10 elite nights, and comes with perks like 10% bonus points on hotel stays, priority late check-out, and free Wi-Fi. So it’s better than nothing, but that’s about all I can say.

If you have the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, you can earn Marriott Gold elite status if you spend $35,000 on the card in a calendar year. This status ordinarily requires 25 elite nights. Bonvoy Gold elite status gets you benefits like 25% bonus points on hotel stays, 2PM late check-out, a room upgrade subject to availability, and more.

In addition to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card spending bonus categories and ability to earn elite status, there are some other major perks to having the card. This is where the card’s annual fee becomes really easy to justify, in my opinion.

The real perk that makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card worthwhile is that you get a free night award every year on your account anniversary, valid for a one-night hotel stay at a property costing up to 35,000 points.

It’s also possible to top off Marriott free night awards with up to 25,000 additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. This means you could redeem a free night award plus 25,000 points to stay at a hotel costing 60,000 points per night.

This is an exceptional deal, and I think this card is worth having. Marriott is the world’s largest hotel chain, so regardless of your preferred hotel program, just about everyone may find themselves in a situation where this could come in handy.

I consistently redeem this certificate at hotels costing $250+ per night. Based on my valuation of 0.7 cents per point, I’d consider the free night award to be worth around $245, more than double the annual fee… that’s awesome!

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers auto rental collision damage waiver coverage. Decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

Coverage is provided for theft and collision damage for most cars in the United States and abroad. Do note that within the United States, coverage is secondary to your personal insurance, though. Of course you’ll always want to check the guide to benefits for all the details.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers a variety of protection when traveling. Among these features are:

Make sure you check your cardmember agreement and guide to benefits for all of the details, since there are terms to be aware of.

Personally, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card isn’t a card that I would be using for my everyday spending. However, I think the card is worth having, given that it offers a free night certificate on your account anniversary every year, which should more than justify the annual fee.

If you’re going for status, the 15 elite nights toward status annually is incredibly valuable as well, and makes it easier to earn Platinum status.

I think there’s absolutely merit to picking up the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, though I’d say that the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) might be the best alternative to consider. While the card is issued by American Express and has a steep $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees), there are lots of reasons to consider this card, including:

Obviously this card won’t be for everyone, and the fee is steep. However, I do think the perks add up, and if you’re involved quite a bit in the Bonvoy ecosystem, it’s easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re not actually that committed to the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem, there are lots of other great cards to consider. In particular, these are cards with relatively reasonable annual fees and great rewards structures, and they’re very well rounded:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is a great card with a reasonable annual fee, and offers an annual free night award and 15 elite nights toward status annually. This is an especially good time to apply, given the welcome offer that’s currently available.

For those looking to earn Bonvoy points, this is also one of Marriott’s better credit cards for being rewarded, between the points and additional elite nights. However, this still isn’t the card I’d be used for my everyday spending. Instead, this is a card you get for the perks it offers, as it can make sense to hold onto this card even with minimal spending.

If you want to learn more about the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, follow this link.

To occasional hobbyists: With the card's 15 Elite Night Credits (ENCs), if you stay 10 nights per year, you earn Gold status. You receive better WiFi, a potential non-suite upgrade, and 2pm checkout. Not much. If you stay fewer than 10 nights, you should ask yourself what the practical effect is. If your nights hit 20, then those combined with this card's 15 ENCs plus the Amex business version's 15 ENCs get you to Platinum. So, at 20+ nights, practical effects kick in. Set your expectations.

#6143. Airport Lounges Just For Singles—A Boarding Pass, A Cover Charge, And A Chance At Finding Love

A traveler wants major airports to open lounges just for single people: pay to get in, meet other singles, and skip the guessing about whether someone wants to be approached. The comments immediately went to (a) married men and (b) Minute Suites. I don’t think the idea is crazy. A boarding pass, TSA screening and lounge access already do some pre-qualifying of potential dates and mates. Add people going to a location where everyone’s signaling they’re open to meeting someone solves the coordination problem. I wonder if it would make more sense to test it inside an existing lounge rather than signing an airport lease for a singles club though. Professional pickleball player Shelby Bates lays out the proposal in an Instagram reel tagged at Atlanta’s airport. She names New York JFK, Atlanta and Los Angeles, proposes an admission fee, and suggests activities, a communal table, speed dating and televisions showing sports (so you already know what team someone likes before making an approach). There needs to be a lounge for single people. A fee to get in. You’re going in there with the mindset that you’re single. Everyone else in there is single. People can approach you, talk to you. She figures she needs to get in touch with an airport CEO. Watch Shelby Bates propose airport lounges for singles But Will The Men Even Be Single Or Just Take Off Their Wedding Bands? Some people love the idea. Others point out that a person can be flying alone without being single, or that the person you meet may live 2,000 miles away – airports are optimizing for long distance relationships. Then there are these: @mauriciopaiz: “Just spent the night in ATL… they should promote the minute suites a bit more 😂” @chinedumikwuakor: “Just gonna be a bunch of married people in that mix lol.” @motobecanegt: “ ‘So, where do you live?’ ‘2000 miles away from you.’ ‘Oooh, we should date.’ ” @mikelyonsphotography: “They are there, it’s called… ‘United Club’.” He then offers to meet her at an airport that weekend. @taliafvr92: “Ugh no!!! I love being single and left alone in the lounge” There’s Already Some Sorting Happening I’ve written about airport lounges and PreCheck as filters for potential dates. A staffed public venue behind security, with cameras and airport police available, has advantages for a first meeting. Travelers have been screened for weapons. Flying and paying for lounge access also let you infer someone’s resources. It’s imperfect information. And a security checkpoint doesn’t get you a full background check (PreCheck is at least going to cover many offenses). Priority Pass would be an interesting addition. If the lounge was accessible that way, it would attract guests whose cards cover their visits. Then the premium credit card it’s attached to serves as a rough signal of creditworthiness (of course Priority Pass also sells memberships directly). The strongest filter would be wanting to meet someone. Earlier this year I wrote about a woman who got an Amex Platinum card to network with rich people in lounges and made “0 connections”. Everyone was eating, scrolling or sleeping. A designated singles space changes that expectation. People still get to decline an approach, and staff would need to deal with anyone who won’t take no for an answer. But you’re no longer trying to work out whether the person beside you wants to talk or finish a presentation. Most lounges might not have enough room, but what about the new 55,000 square foot United Club in Houston? Another benefit is that your flight departure serves as a natural end to that first conversation. Or, if things are going well, missing the flight adds real dramatic tension and a story to tell you grandchildren. People Have Been Trying This For Years Excluding couples and families shrinks the customer base for a lounge. That doesn’t kill the idea if enough people were uniquely motivated by the concept. The operator still needs enough compatible people present at the same time. Age, attraction, orientation, relationship goals and boarding times all winnow down the dating pool. The operator would need rent, buildout cash and a revenue share. They’d cover staffing and food costs. You’re going up against Chase, American Express, Capital One, Airport Dimensions, TAV Services and others bidding for the space. Priority Pass could help supply visits and revenue. But when entry is included with a card, some people will come for the food and drinks and not actually be open to date. People have been trying versions of this for years. In 2015, Lounger proposed matching travelers who had lounge guest privileges with people who wanted to join them. I’ve also covered AirDates, Wingman and the idea of selling introductions through seat assignments. Calls for designated singles lounges were turning up in New York Times airport romance coverage last year. In this reel’s comments, GateF8 showed up to promote its airport connection app. Bates said she’d try it on upcoming trips. I actually think an airport singles event in a lounge would be interesting just for the buzzworthy media coverage it could generate. It may be a collossally bad idea on an ongoing basis but as a one-off it’s surely worth the earned media. In this reel’s comments, GateF8 showed up to promote its airport connection app. Bates said she’d try it on upcoming trips. I actually think an airport singles event in a lounge would be interesting just for the buzzworthy media coverage it could generate. It may be a collossally bad idea on an ongoing basis but as a one-off it’s surely worth the earned media.

After a six-year hiatus, American Airlines’ most exclusive lounge offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) is back in business.

This week, the carrier reopened Flagship Dining at LAX. That’s American’s a la carte restaurant-style experience, which is available to customers flying in its most premium seats.

It had been closed since 2020 but is now open again after a face-lift.

And it also has a new access policy at LAX — and at the two other American hubs that offer the service.

American now offers Flagship Dining at three of its hubs:

At those airports, you'll find the a la carte dining experience is available within its Flagship Lounge, AA's premium lounge that's open to premium cabin passengers and AAdvantage elites taking long-haul flights.

Instead of grabbing food at the buffet, Flagship Dining offers flyers a sit-down meal with table service — we’re talking a full menu with coursed-out dishes, all complimentary.

In the past, the airline limited access to Flagship Dining to passengers flying in its Flagship First cabin on the Boeing 777-300ER or Airbus A321T aircraft.

But as the carrier gets set to phase out its international-style first-class cabin, access to Flagship Dining is opening up to more passengers.

In September, American began allowing passengers in its Flagship business-class cabins to sit for its exclusive dining experience.

If you’re flying out of DFW, MIA or LAX, you can have a Flagship Dining meal if you are:

That change is especially notable at LAX, because it allows business-class passengers to use Flagship Dining on certain transcontinental flights. To get in, you'll need to have a ticket that's marketed as "Flagship" (domestic first-class tickets won't be enough).

Like with any restaurant or airport lounge, space is limited. You can join the waitlist for a table after arriving at the Flagship Lounge in LA, Dallas and Miami.

American used to offer Flagship Dining at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). Today, the carrier instead operates its three premium lounges (Greenwich, Chelsea and Soho) in Terminal 8 with partner British Airways.

Meanwhile, its newest Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) features a la carte dining within the main club.

Speaking of American’s “Flagship” product, the end is rapidly approaching for Flagship First.

Nov. 19 will mark the last date AA offers long-haul first-class as a stand-alone product on its 777s.

Those jets are getting refreshed with new interiors, with the airline ditching first-class and adding the highest business-class seat count it's ever offered.

American will phase out Flagship First on transcontinental service in March.
